This study introduces a novel statistical technique for analyzing Alzheimer's disease clinical trials, with a specific focus on assessing the efficacy of treatments on trial endpoints. The method employs a natural cubic spline to model disease progression, utilizing baseline covariates and random walk components to account for unmeasured covariate drifts. The authors demonstrate the approach through simulations and by applying it to the analysis of a pivotal Phase 3 trial for the Alzheimer's drug aducanumab.

A central challenge in the theory of rare events is determining the most probable path to an event's occurrence. This path is defined as the least-action trajectory that connects stable states within a system's landscape. While the Freidlin-Wentzell framework provides a robust mathematical foundation for locating this path, it has historically been difficult to apply to high-dimensional systems. This study introduces a fresh numerical strategy capable of extending the method to arbitrary dimensions. The approach employs a global optimization algorithm to identify the path of minimal cost. Its efficacy is demonstrated by resolving a previously unsolved case study in geophysics: the mechanism of tropical cyclone genesis.

This study examines the relationship between the $L^{\infty}$ bounds of solutions to the parabolic complex Monge-Ampere equation and those of the corresponding time-independent equation. Furthermore, it explores the connection between the $L^{\infty}$ bounds of the parabolic complex and real Hessian equations. These findings are applied to establish $L^{\infty}$ bounds for the parabolic complex Monge-Ampere equation.

We demonstrate that the complexity class CFAL, comprising the regular functions calculable in alternating linear-time, can be characterized by the strong normalization of a specific lambda-calculus. This system features function abstraction and application, alongside a restricted form of recursion. Furthermore, we establish a dual result: the class REG of all regular functions is exactly the set of regular functions that normalize strongly within the more expressive System F. These findings extend previous work by the second author, who previously showed that the class RAL of rational functions calculable in alternating linear-time corresponds to the strong normalization of System F enhanced with specific recursion mechanisms.

This work examines the relationship between Itô and Stratonovich integrals, where the integrands take the form of polynomials derived from conditional distribution flows. We establish that itô-to-Stratonovich correction terms can be expressed as conditional expectation values of polynomial flows, specifically utilizing the solution to the associated conditional diffusion equation. Furthermore, we present a flow of probability kernels defined by conditional distributions and demonstrate its evolution as the solution to the so-called conditional Liouville equation.

We establish a framework for analyzing the asymptotic properties of discrete groups through the use of metric spaces, introducing a new class of uniform metric spaces termed "standard," which encompasses both bounded coarse structures and proper metric spaces. This introduction allows us to define standard frameworks spaces for groups, which serve as tools to study large-scale group properties by examining the geometry of their Cayley graphs. We demonstrate that the standard framework spaces of groups are uniquely determined by their large-scale geometry, meaning any isometry at infinity preserves these structures. Additionally, we establish connections between standard spaces and the $C^*$-envelopes of groups, showing that the latter's Gelfand spectrum is isomorphic to the standard metric space associated with the group.

This study introduces an auxiliary, end-to-end cross-domain text-to-SQL text-linguistic framework designed to jointly address multiple tasks within the domain, including textual entailment, question classification, and slot detection. By integrating these tasks into a unified multi-objective optimization goal, the model enables the shared representations to be trained simultaneously. Empirical results indicate that this approach not only achieves superior performance on the textual entailment and question classification tasks compared to existing methods but also significantly enhances slot detection accuracy when applied to cross-domain text-linguistic scenarios.

This study addresses the multi-robot navigation challenge within an information-centric framework. We introduce a predictive approach that integrates probabilistic robot-localization estimates with a model-based navigation strategy to account for uncertainties in robot dynamics. The core of this method is a risk-aware Model Predictive Controller (MPC) designed to ensure safe, collision-free paths are maintained despite uncertainties in the dynamics model. To facilitate this, the MPC employs a risk-aware cost function that balances the need for safe navigation with the desire for high-speed movement. The proposed framework is validated through simulations involving a fleet of 100 robots operating in a 2D environment.

Grant-free access is a vital technique for enabling massive machine-type communication (mMTC) within 5G and future networks, allowing devices to transmit data without reserving specific resources. This paper introduces a two-stage, non-orthogonal sequence design method tailored for this environment. Initially, it employs a genetic algorithm to select an optimal subset of available sequences, and subsequently, it uses a simulated annealing algorithm to fine-tune the phase shifts of those selected sequences. The proposed method is evaluated against standard non-orthogonal multiple access (NOMA) systems regarding their bit error rate (BER) and computational complexity. Simulation results demonstrate that the new approach achieves a substantial reduction in BER with only a marginal increase in complexity.

This work presents the thermodynamic consistency of various commonly used models for describing humid air. We introduce a reduced-order model (ROM) for humid air properties that leverages the thermodynamic state equation developed by Chung et al. (2010). This formulation allows for the direct calculation of all humid air properties using only two independent state variables. Furthermore, we conduct a comparative analysis of different humid air modeling approaches, evaluating their accuracy and computational performance.

While automatic speech recognition (ASR) has become a standard component in dialogue systems, its output uncertainty poses significant challenges for downstream modules like the dialogue state monitor (DSM). This study investigates how to effectively leverage ASR uncertainty within the DSM process. We introduce a novel framework that integrates Word Confusion Networks (WCNs) into a Conditional Random Field (CRF) model to represent ASR uncertainty. In this hybrid WCRN-CRF architecture, the WCNs serve as input features to enhance DSM accuracy. We evaluate our approach on the IWSIT2 2016 dataset and demonstrate that the WCRN-CRF model outperforms both a standard baseline and an alternative modeling strategy that utilizes acoustic uncertainty.

This study presents a novel, mathematically rigorous framework for analyzing the dynamics of general sliding mode controllers, covering both chattering and sliding regimes. We demonstrate that the specific sliding mode attractor is determined by the geometric arrangement of the system's vector field relative to the switching manifold. Furthermore, we prove that the resulting dynamics within this attractor can be generated by a smooth system of ordinary differential equations if and only if the system remains unchanged under a specific class of generalized coordinate transformations. Finally, we establish that the set of all such universal entry frameworks is dense within the collection of all possible smooth systems equipped with chattering sliding modes.

We introduce an optimized method for evaluating entanglement within a two-qubit system where each qubit is realized as an optical system using two photons. In this approach, the state of the two-particle wave function is projected onto a basis defined by photon-number distributions, which are recorded via a multiphoton detector array. This measurement protocol necessitates only a single instance per experimental run, offering a significant advantage over conventional quantum information techniques that typically demand multiple copies of the resource state and extensive post-processing. We demonstrate the utility of this measurement scheme by generating and assessing the entanglement of optical qubits.

This research investigates the characteristics of non-axisymmetric magnetic fluctuations in the JET tokamak, specifically focusing on those with a single helical symmetry. The study analyzes data from a single-channel magnetic probe positioned in the edge region, which captures signals from both edge-localized modes (ELMs) and inter-ELMs. During inter-ELMs intervals, the observed non-circularly symmetric fluctuations exhibit a helical symmetry matching the rational surface topology and possess a frequency spectrum that is highly dependent on the safety factor ($q$). The amplitude of these fluctuations increases as the discharge progresses toward an ELM event. The findings indicate that these pre-ELMs fluctuations likely originate from the non-linear interaction between the primary ELM mode and a secondary mode characterized by a single helical symmetry. Theoretical models suggest that this secondary mode is a resistive ballooning mode, which can be excited by the ELM mode when the ELM mode's amplitude becomes sufficiently large.

Continual learning (CL) addresses the challenge of sequentially learning new tasks while retaining knowledge from previous ones, avoiding catastrophic forgetting. Recently, large-scale pre-trained models have been integrated into CL to mitigate this forgetting, yet their efficacy remains debatable. This study presents a straightforward baseline that challenges the necessity of applying pre-trained models in CL. Specifically, we examine a simple approach combining Elastic Weight Consolidation (EWC) with an online pre-training strategy. Our results demonstrate that this method surpasses existing state-of-the-art techniques across multiple CL benchmarks. Furthermore, we provide comprehensive analyses to deepen the understanding of the limitations of current pre-trained model applications in CL. Our findings suggest that pre-trained models are not always optimal for CL, highlighting scenarios where simpler, non-pre-trained alternatives are superior.

Social media platforms host a vast array of user-generated content, including multimodal posts consisting of images and text. Although such content is often benign, it can also be hateful, posing significant risks to marginalized groups. This study addresses the challenge of detecting hate speech across these multimodal social media inputs. We introduce a novel framework called UMHI (Unsupervised Multi-Modal Identification), which is designed to identify hate speech in a label-free environment. By leveraging the semantic connections between textual and visual data, UMHI effectively filters out non-hate content. We have constructed a novel dataset, the UMHI Multi-Modal Dataset, comprising 100,000 label-free images and texts. Experimental results demonstrate that our model achieves superior performance compared to existing methods, achieving a 10.2% increase in F1-Score and a 10.2% increase in F1-Score. We anticipate that this framework and dataset will advance the field of identifying label-free multimodal hate speech.

This study examines how varying degree distributions influence the synchronization of Type-I neurons within random networks. We analyze both independent and coupled scenarios, focusing on two distinct coupling mechanisms: diffusive coupling, which accounts for total current exchange between neurons, and inhibitory coupling, which models the release of inhibitory neurotransmitters. Our findings indicate that while diffusive coupling allows both scale-free and inhomogeneous random networks to synchronize near the neuron firing threshold, inhibitory coupling enables only inhomogeneous random networks to achieve synchronization at this threshold. Furthermore, we explore the synchronization phenomena in the context of a network containing a hub neuron.

Automated program repair (APR) tools typically rely on identifying and substituting buggy code snippets with correct ones. However, these tools often fail to fix code that is syntactically valid but semantically incorrect. To address this, we introduce an approach to automatically generate "antagonistic" inputs that expose such semantic flaws. By provoking these issues, the generated inputs force the buggy code to malfunction, thereby revealing the specific defects. We integrated this technique into a standard APR framework, resulting in significant performance gains on a subset of the Big-Bug benchmark where semantic errors occur.

This work introduces a novel method for determining the achievable rate region within Gaussian interference channels featuring two-way communication. By leveraging concepts from information theory, the study defines the spectrum of interference data and demonstrates that the boundary of the channel's capacity region can be expressed as the optimal resolution of linear constraints involving the maximal eigenvalues found in this spectral representation. This proposed approach offers a distinct alternative to standard information-theoretic techniques, which rely on constructing bounds based on single-user capacity limits derived from auxiliary channels. Furthermore, the study provides a concrete instance where this spectral method yields a capacity-bound closure that supersedes the sum-rate attainable via traditional spectral bounds.

This approach leverages the full three-dimensional geometry of the event by integrating over all final-state particles within a specific rapidity interval. The magnitude and orientation of this vector in three dimensions are determined by the event's azimuthal angle and the topological quick-boost (top-quick) angle, respectively. The top-quick angle quantifies the flow direction in three dimensions and is calculated as the average longitudinal momentum per particle in the event's central plane. The rapid onset of the COVID-19 pandemic has created an urgent demand for non-intrusive, privacy-focused methods to detect the disease. This study introduces a novel framework for privacy-aware early diagnosis of COVID-19, utilizing deep learning on chest X-ray data. This approach is designed to mitigate privacy risks by minimizing the exposure of sensitive patient information. We validate the efficacy of this framework using a comprehensive dataset of 11,308 chest radiographs labeled for both COVID-19 and non-lung conditions. Experimental results indicate that the proposed method achieves superior accuracy compared to existing techniques, reaching 96.1% precision for COVID-19 detection and 95.1% for non-lung detection.

Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have become a vital tool for analyzing graph-structured data across various domains, including wireless communication systems. In this paper, we present a new framework for distributed GNN inference within wireless transmission environments. This approach leverages the graph model to facilitate data exchange among nodes and uses the GNN architecture to compute node features based on local information and received transmissions. We analyze the convergence behavior of this framework and demonstrate that it achieves convergence to a stationary point of the GNN objective function. Furthermore, we establish a connection between our proposed framework and existing distributed optimization algorithms, showing that specific instances of the framework correspond to well-known methods for solving optimization problems. Finally, we apply this framework to a wireless resource allocation problem, demonstrating its effectiveness through a concrete application example.

This study examines spatial clustering patterns in homicide rates across 242 municipalities within the Brazilian province of Goiás between 2002 and 2014, utilizing data from the Brazilian Institute of Geography and Statistics (IBGE) and the Brazilian Ministry of Public Security. The analysis employs the Global Moran's I index to assess overall spatial autocorrelation and the Local Indicators of Spatial Association (LISA) to identify specific clusters. The findings indicate a significant positive spatial autocorrelation in homicide rates, with a concentration of high-high clusters observed in the central region of the province. Furthermore, the study highlights a strong correlation between homicide rates and the proportion of the population aged 15 to 29, while also noting that this age group's presence serves as a significant explanatory factor for variations in homicide rates across municipalities.

This study introduces a novel optimization framework for deep neural networks that dynamically adjusts the learning rate based on the specific characteristics of input data. By integrating data-driven metrics, the algorithm enhances training efficiency and accelerates convergence. Empirical results demonstrate significant improvements in convergence speed and final model accuracy. Specifically, the method achieves a 1.5-fold reduction in training time for the MNIST dataset and a 1.5-fold reduction for the CIFAR-10 dataset while surpassing existing SOTA techniques. Additionally, the code implementation is available at https://github.com/AniruddhaKumar1999/SSAGNN.

This paper introduces a new category of self-exciting dynamical systems, characterized by a feedback loop where the system's state influences the timing of external shocks. We establish the existence and uniqueness of a stationary distribution for these systems and demonstrate that they can exhibit both stationary and non-stationary behaviors. Specifically, we prove that if the system is non-stationary, it possesses a unique ergodic regime. Finally, we present a specific application of this framework to financial econometrics.

Respiratory motion remains a significant challenge in MRI, particularly for abdominal and thoracic imaging. While 4D MRI sequences are typically employed to compensate for this motion, they necessitate breath-holding, which is unfeasible for many patients. This study introduces a free-breathing 4D (3D+respiration) T2-weighted turbo spin-echo (TSE) MRI sequence designed to address these limitations. The technique utilizes a retrospective motion correction algorithm that relies on respiratory gating and a self-navigation approach. A 1D navigator echo is periodically acquired during the main scan to generate self-navigation signals, which are then used to bin k-space data according to the patient's breathing cycle. The resulting motion-corrected 4D (3D+respiration) datasets were evaluated in 10 healthy volunteers using a 3T scanner. Results demonstrated that the mean scan time was 15 minutes and 30 seconds, with a 95% coverage of the liver and spleen. Knowledge distillation (KD) represents a powerful method for compressing deep neural networks (DNNs) by transferring knowledge from a large teacher model to a smaller student model. However, most current KD approaches fail to account for the specific data flow inherent within the network architecture, resulting in suboptimal compression outcomes. This paper introduces InDistill, a data-flow-aware distillation framework designed to maintain the original information pathways between the teacher and student. By ensuring the student replicates the teacher's input-to-output processing flow, InDistill facilitates more effective knowledge transfer. Experimental evaluations across various classification and object detection tasks demonstrate that InDistill consistently outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods.

This paper addresses the query regarding whether every topological plane function possessing a single critical point and yielding a topologically similar level structure can be considered a submersion at infinity. We provide a negative answer for functions exhibiting linear-like behavior at infinity. Additionally, we present a method for constructing examples that refute this question in the broader, nonlinear-like scenario.

This study employs a spatially explicit, individual-based model to analyze how plant dynamics in arid environments respond to seasonal grazing by non-resident herbivores. These models simulate the specific behavior of dry-land ecosystems where herds migrate in and out, leaving no ecological footprint behind other than direct consumption. Plant dynamics are governed by a delicate balance between the destabilizing force of overgrazing and the stabilizing influence of self-organization into vegetation patches. We demonstrate that even moderate levels of external grazing can suppress the emergence of these patterns, resulting in vegetation degradation. Furthermore, we examine the impact of varying herd sizes and grazing intensities, revealing that larger groups exert a more profound destabilizing effect than smaller ones under identical per-plant bite rates.

This paper examines the performance of CountSketch when applied to adaptive data, where the order of entries is chosen by an adversary to maximize error. We demonstrate that CountSketch performs comparably well in this challenging scenario, provided the number of samples is sufficiently large. Specifically, we establish that with a sample size of $m = \Omega(\frac{\sqrt{d}}{\epsilon^2})$, CountSketch achieves an $ \ell_2$ error of at most $\epsilon$ with high probability. This result holds even against an adaptive adversary, matching the sample complexity required for the data to be processed under random conditions. In contrast, we prove that no other data structure can achieve an $ \ell_2$ error smaller than $\epsilon$ with high probability using fewer than $m = \Omega(\frac{\sqrt{d}}{\epsilon^2})$ samples, even when the data arrives randomly. These findings confirm that CountSketch is optimal for processing adaptive data streams within the error tolerance of $\epsilon$ up to logarithmic factors.

We introduce ipie, a newly developed software package for density-functional theory that employs the auxiliary-field quantum Monte Carlo method. Designed to handle large-scale calculations efficiently, it leverages both CPU and GPU parallel computing architectures. Built with a user-centric approach, ipie offers extensive flexibility in handling various functionals, operators, and stochastic integrators, while also supporting custom source code extensions. This package features a range of built-in observables and provides multiple input methods, including command-line, Python scripting, and JSON files. Additionally, ipie offers comprehensive documentation and multiple testing tools to assist users in verifying their setups.

This paper introduces a quantum algorithm designed to resolve the Prisoner's Dilemma, demonstrating that it can achieve a superior collective outcome for the participants. The method leverages the quantum cloud to execute operations at remarkable speeds, with the process described in detail alongside a full analysis of its computational complexity.

This study examines a two-tiered market featuring a continuum of buyers and sellers, alongside a finite group of market makers. These intermediaries operate by purchasing assets from sellers and offering them to buyers at a markup. The analysis focuses on equilibrium scenarios where both parties aim to maximize income. We demonstrate that, under these conditions, both market makers and individual sellers are guaranteed to achieve the highest possible income potential. Furthermore, we establish that the aggregate surplus in this equilibrium is identical to that of a direct market, bypassing the need for intermediaries.

We introduce a new approach to solving the problem of abstractive document condensation, which involves generating concise summaries for a collection of documents that collectively preserve essential information found in the originals. Our method centers on a planning-based framework utilizing a specialized parameterized function called the Acquired Entity Prompts (AEP) to effectively measure how much crucial data remains during the summarization process. This approach is grounded in a novel, computationally efficient acquisition metric that identifies important entities within a source document based on their significance across the entire document set. By planning for information preservation using this AEP planning signal, our method successfully targets these key entities. Empirical results demonstrate that this strategy produces high-quality summaries and achieves state-of-the-art performance in condensing documents.
This paper establishes sufficient criteria for the differentiability of an $n$-dimensional real-valued function, leveraging the known differentiability of its associated $(n-1)$-dimensional function.

Vocal entrainment, the unconscious synchronization of speech patterns between conversing individuals, serves as a crucial social bonding mechanism. While prior research has largely focused on linear vocal features, this study introduces a novel methodology to measure vocal entrainment within dyadic interactions by analyzing the co-occurrence of nonlinear dynamic structures. We propose a context-sensitive approach that calculates the similarity between speakers' nonlinear vocal trajectories at corresponding time points during conversation. This methodology was applied to examine vocal entrainment in 17 couples engaged in natural, face-to-face dialogues. Results indicate a statistically significant correlation between the degree of vocal entrainment and established interpersonal relationship metrics. These findings offer fresh insights into the mechanisms of vocal coordination and open new avenues for automated social bond evaluation in conversational agent design.

This work introduces the $\lambda\mu\mu$-calculus as a categorical characterization of quantum control, specifically targeting quantum interactions within the unitary sphere. We define categorical models for this calculus that correspond to symmetric monoidal closed categories equipped with a special structure, a concept we term a "unitary sphere with extra structure." In these constructions, abstraction and application align with standard categorical constructs, while the calculus' fold operation is modeled as a specific morphism. We demonstrate that consistency within the $\lambda\mu\mu$-calculus ensures that a time-like interaction reduction—representing a complete computational step—produces a unitary transformation. Consequently, this establishes a robust foundation for the categorical study of complete reduction steps in quantum computation.

The dynamics of two interacting quasiparticles within the fractional quantum Hall regime are examined using the time-dependent variational principle (TVDP) applied to a Hamiltonian that accounts for quasiparticle quasihole interactions, quasihole-quasiparticle couplings, and their mutual movements. By extending the TVDP framework to a wave function incorporating relative and center-of-mass degrees of freedom, we derive analytical expressions for the energy spectrum and excitation modes. These results offer refined estimates for the single-quasiparticle energy and velocities of two-quasiparticle transitions, surpassing previous approximations.

This article introduces a finite element method tailored to resolve a variational inequality representing a two-dimensional Stokes model for ice flow over an uneven, impermeable base. Leveraging the fact that the ice's bottom shear stress remains constant, the authors formulate a reduced problem that is semicoercive. They subsequently develop and rigorously analyze a mixed finite element method for this inequality, ensuring the necessary conditions for the Lax-Milgram theorem are satisfied. Finally, the authors present numerical simulations that validate their theoretical findings.

Galactic outflows are prevalent in star-forming systems, yet their role in regulating star formation remains debated. We present DUVET, a project utilizing the ALMA interferometer to map the kinematics of molecular gas and dust in the nearby galaxy NGC 4945. This galaxy exhibits a high star formation rate relative to its mass, a starburst core, and a prominent outflow. Our study reveals that the outflow's star formation rate is approximately 10% of the galaxy's total rate, with the outflow's morphology indicating a bipolar structure. This structure aligns with the galaxy's bar and its molecular gas distribution, showing that outflowing gas moves away from the core along the bar's major axis. Furthermore, we found that the outflowing gas is significantly colder than the static gas, with temperatures around 10 K compared to roughly 20 K elsewhere. These findings suggest that NGC 4945's outflow is a key mechanism in suppressing star formation, a conclusion supported by our 3D radiative transfer simulations.

This study examines an anomalous finding from the STAR collaboration at RHIC, where the triangular flow $v_3$ in Cu+Cu collisions exceeded that in Au+Au collisions by approximately 20%. We evaluate this discrepancy using a multiphase transport model, accounting for variations in initial spatial anisotropy and the medium's equation of state. Our results indicate that initial geometric anisotropy alone cannot account for the observed effect; however, incorporating a first-order phase transition successfully reproduces the anomaly. This phenomenon arises because the pressure buildup during the phase transition in the quark-gluon plasma drives a more pronounced expansion in Cu+Cu collisions compared to Au+Au ones, thereby enhancing the initial anisotropic momentum anisotropy into final-state triangular flow.

This paper introduces a new concept called Simultaneous Robotic Structure Identification (SiRi), which unifies the tasks of identifying a structure and learning a policy for robotic systems. By leveraging the equivalence between policy learning and structure identification, we develop a simultaneous approach that iteratively refines both the model's structure and the policy. We demonstrate that this method is effective for identifying constant and time-varying dynamics in robotic systems, even when the true structure is initially unknown. Furthermore, we establish theoretical guarantees regarding the convergence of our proposed identification algorithm.

Pre-training is a crucial step in deep learning for semantic segmentation, yet the optimal approach remains undefined. While prior research has explored using image classification for this purpose, we investigate the potential of pre-training with monocular depth estimation instead. Our findings indicate that depth pre-training outperforms classification in terms of final accuracy and reduces computational costs. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the superior results stem from the depth network's ability to learn more diverse features compared to classification models. Finally, we confirm that this pre-training strategy is broadly applicable across various backbones and network architectures.

In this study, we establish sharp lower bounds on radii within the class of starlike log-harmonic mappings, demonstrating that our findings significantly broaden the results previously achieved by Bohr, Nesharovsky, and others. Furthermore, we apply these findings to derive enhanced outcomes for improved Bohr radii concerning the classes of starlike and convex functions.

Kendall's tau serves as a standard nonparametric measure of rank correlation, yet its standard estimator exhibits slow convergence. We introduce a weighted estimator that achieves the optimal nonparametric rate of $\sqrt{n}$ for sample-dependent correlation functions. Additionally, we derive optimal local rate-of-smoothness conditions and closed-form formulas for various kernel choices. Our asymptotic results are validated through simulations, and we demonstrate the method's effectiveness in a regression framework.

This paper introduces a comprehensive framework designed to analyze privacy risks within edge intelligence applications for vehicular networks. The proposed model integrates three core components: (1) a privacy assessment framework that evaluates the privacy levels of edge intelligence, (2) a threat model defining adversaries, and (3) a risk calculation method. The authors develop a unified privacy framework capable of evaluating both local training and federated learning scenarios. In federated learning specifically, the model assesses the privacy levels of various update aggregation strategies, including FedAvg, FedProx, and FedAvg++. Furthermore, the study quantifies the privacy risk of these edge intelligence implementations against defined threat scenarios. The findings indicate that while edge intelligence inherently offers higher privacy levels than federated learning, the latter can surpass it under specific conditions.

By integrating the curvature of the Euler topology with the principle of conformality, the method generates a mesh that is both curvature-aware and geometrically accurate. The resulting surfaces are rendered using the Shading Language within the framework of the graphics API known as the OpenGL. The implementation, which is freely available on the GitHub repository of the author, allows users to customize the generated meshes by adjusting the meshing density and the curvature influence. This study examines a system of ordinary differential equations representing a predator-prey model with a strong Allee effect. The primary objective is to analyze the dynamics of this system, specifically focusing on the influence of the Allee effect on the predator's viability. The study reveals that the system's behavior is highly dependent on parameter values, exhibiting a rich variety of limit cycles, homoclinic orbits, and regions of multi-stability. Furthermore, the authors explore the implications of these findings for ecological theory and their application to real-world population management.

The aspect pivot algorithm iterates by pivoting on aspects of the simplex tableau rather than individual variables, with the number of aspects equaling the count of constraints. The presented upper linear complexity bound is approximately 1.44 times that of the standard simplex algorithm's worst-case linear complexity, which is 2m, where m denotes the number of constraints. The paper also outlines the aspect pivot method and its application to the linear complementarity problem. This study determines the NK_1-K\"{u}rner modules of the ring M of 2\times 2 matrices with entries from a graded integral domain R, under a specific set of assumptions. Consequently, we demonstrate that the NK_1-K\"{u}ner module of this modular group, denoted B(R), is isomorphic to the NK_1-K\"{u}ner module of R itself.

The measurement of the top quark mass stands as a primary objective in current top quark research. In recent years, numerous experimental groups have analyzed top quark production alongside a jet, known as $t\bar{t}j$ events, to extract this mass. This approach is favored because it leverages abundant data and minimizes systematic uncertainties. However, such a determination relies on the assumption that the quark-level mass, $m_Q$, serves as a proxy for the physical pole mass. This study examines off-shell contributions within $t\bar{t}j$ events and their impact on the extraction of $m_Q$. We find that these off-shell effects are substantial, reaching approximately 3 GeV, and that their precise quantification is essential for accurately extracting the mass.

The rapid advancement of deep learning has fueled significant progress in face recognition, yet this capability has also introduced substantial security risks, particularly through the widespread misuse of face synthesis and deepfake technologies. While recent research has explored using pre-trained models for detecting face forgery in zero-shot scenarios, this study critically examines the effectiveness of Vision Transformers (ViT) in this specific domain. Our analysis reveals that ViTs underperform compared to Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) in zero-shot settings, primarily due to their inability to effectively leverage prior knowledge from non-face datasets. Consequently, we propose a novel ViT-based architecture designed to enhance zero-shot detection capabilities. Our experiments demonstrate that this new model not only surpasses existing methods but also exhibits superior generalization across various unseen datasets.

This paper introduces a deep reinforcement learning framework designed to develop an autonomous driving agent capable of navigating a simulated highway environment. The agent leverages a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) to process visual data from a camera mounted on the vehicle, enabling it to detect and track surrounding objects. By employing a reward function grounded in real-world driving metrics, the model was trained using the Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient (DDPG) algorithm. Experimental results indicate that the trained agent successfully mastered the task of self-driving, achieving an average speed of 76.44 mph.

Asynchronous parallel multi-objective evolutionary algorithms (AP-MOEAs) are widely adopted for their efficiency in handling large-scale optimization challenges. However, asynchronous execution introduces evaluation time bias, where individuals with shorter evaluation durations are assessed more frequently than those taking longer, skewing the selection process. This phenomenon can result in the premature neglect of high-quality solutions. This paper introduces a frequency-oriented parent selection mechanism designed to counteract evaluation time bias by balancing the number of parental selections. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms existing selection strategies in terms of both solution quality and convergence speed.

This study reports the observational verification of the exoplanet OGLE-2017-BLG-1434Lb, a frigid super-Earth with a mass of 2.64 ± 0.14 M⊕ orbiting the host star OGLE-2017-BLG-1434. While the initial discovery of this system was made by KMTNet, our verification utilized high-resolution imaging from the Keck II Telescope equipped with adaptive optics. We successfully resolved the separation between the host star and its planetary companion, achieving a measurement of the microlensing event's finite source effect. This analysis yielded a finite source scale factor of ρ = 0.101 ± 0.006, a result consistent with prior findings from the KMTNet collaboration. Furthermore, our precise measurement of the angular Einstein radius, θE = 0.41 ± 0.04 mas, has enabled the calculation of the host star's mass (M⋆) as 0.64 ± 0.04 M⊙. We identify a critical concentration threshold of $x_c \approx 0.15$; for $x < x_c$, the Ce sublattice remains unpinned by the Rh moments, whereas for $x > x_c$, the sublattice becomes locked to them. This transition is attributed to the emergence of a magnetic order within the Rh sublattice at higher Rh concentrations.

A $\beta$-shift space is defined as a symbolic system of shift-invariant subshifts associated with a pair of real numbers $(\beta, c)$, where $\beta > 1$. We define an $\beta$-shift space as avaricious if it possesses a word that appears with positive frequency in every other word within the space. Our results demonstrate that for a specific class of $\beta$-shift spaces, a gap exists in the set of word frequencies, preventing the existence of a single word with positive frequency in all other words. Consequently, we prove there are intermediate $\beta$-shift spaces that fail to be avaricious.

The LHCb collaboration presents updated measurements of the CP-violating angle $\phi_s$ through the analysis of $B_s^0\to J/\psi\pi^+\pi^-$ decays, utilizing data collected from Run 1 and Run 2 of LHCb. This combined dataset comprises 3 fb$^{-1}$ from 7 TeV proton-proton collisions and 9 fb$^{-1}$ from 8 TeV collisions. The analysis incorporates a comprehensive model of the $\pi^+\pi^-$ mass distribution, accounting for resonances such as $f_0(500)$, $f_0(980)$, $K^*(892)^0$, $K^*(892)^0(\text{crossed})$, $f_0(980)$, and $f_0(1500)$ to ensure precision. Two independent methods are employed to extract $\phi_s$: one utilizes an amplitude-dependent fit to the distribution, while the other relies on an isobar model. Both techniques yield consistent results, leading to a final determination of $\phi_s = 0.089 \pm 0.010 \pm 0.010$ rad.

This study evaluates the efficacy of employing pre-trained models on large-scale datasets to enhance image recognition performance on smaller target datasets. Specifically, we examine two transfer learning strategies: fine-tuning and pseudo-labeling. Our findings indicate that fine-tuning is the superior approach, yielding results that are both more accurate and computationally efficient compared to pseudo-labeling. Additionally, we assess the impact of varying the source dataset and the initial model architecture on performance, concluding that both factors are significant. Finally, we identify a clear relationship between the magnitude of performance gains and the scale of the source dataset used.

This study explores the enumeration of arcs within the two-dimensional space over a finite field, $\mathbb F_q^2$. We establish an algorithm capable of enumerating all arcs of any specified length $n$, provided that $n$ does not exceed $q+1$. Furthermore, we present an algorithm with a time complexity of $O(q^2)$ for enumerating all maximum-length arcs.

This study explores triangles within the triangular lattice, a topic of growing interest due to its connections with computational geometry and cryptography. We begin by defining three categories of triangles based on the parity of their area and subsequently derive formulas for counting triangles with a specific (and constrained) area. We then establish the minimum possible area for triangles that possess a given side length. Finally, we demonstrate how to generate such triangles efficiently and efficiently, which has significant applications in the field of cryptography.

This paper introduces a graph neural network parameterized hardware accelerator designed to address these challenges. The proposed architecture leverages a hardware-software co-design methodology, utilizing a programmable dataflow engine to facilitate flexible and efficient computation. This approach enables the simultaneous training of both the graph structure and the associated neural network weights. We utilize deep Chandra X-ray data to examine the galaxy cluster RXCJ0232.2-4422, revealing a complex structure characterized by multiple subclusters and a cooling core. Our analysis identifies three distinct subclusters: one located in the southern region, another in the northeast, and a third in the northwest. These substructures are spatially separated from the main cluster core, suggesting they are not the primary drivers of the observed cooling core dynamics. Additionally, we detect a large-scale X-ray filament extending from the northern subcluster toward the northwestern one. This filament appears to be a continuous structure resulting from the merger of the northern and northwestern subclusters.

The Legendre Memory Module (LMM) serves as a leading recurrent neural network architecture, utilizing a polynomial approximation to model long-term dependencies. Although its non-recurrent memory retrieval phase allows for efficient GPU parallelization, the memory encoding stage remains inherently sequential, creating a significant bottleneck for large-scale deployment. This work introduces a novel parallelization strategy for LMM training that achieves near-perfect speedup on multi-GPU systems. Additionally, we present an optimized kernel implementation that further accelerates the previously serial components. Experiments on the WikiText-103 dataset demonstrate that this approach maintains identical model accuracy while substantially reducing training time.

Weakly-interacting massive particles (WIMPs) have long been the favored candidate for dark matter, yet recent findings from direct detection, collider, and indirect detection experiments have significantly tightened constraints on this model. This paper reviews the current status of WIMP searches, explores potential extensions to the standard framework, and outlines future experimental directions. It also examines alternative scenarios, specifically focusing on the axion, a particle that could serve as dark matter through a different mechanism.

This study investigates a naming convention model featuring name-linguistic consistency, where agents maintain a name for each of their traits. Interacting with others triggers communication that may lead to trait renegotiation; simultaneously, agents occasionally switch traits to ensure local diversity. We analyze the dynamics of naming evolution under these conditions using both numerical simulations and an analytical framework. Our results indicate that while agent migration can impede global consensus on language, a specific balance of parameters ultimately fosters consistency.

Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) have recently emerged as a powerful tool for addressing various challenges in physics and engineering. However, their susceptibility to spectral bias—where models struggle to learn high-frequency details—poses significant limitations. This study investigates the effect of incorporating momentum into PINNs, demonstrating that it markedly accelerates the learning of these high-frequency components. This finding is supported by theoretical analysis, numerical experiments, and a comparison with alternative optimization strategies. Ultimately, the research confirms that implementing momentum enhances PINNs' efficiency and efficacy when learning complex physics-based phenomena.

This study examines stability within a system of coupled waves traveling through a viscous medium, modeled by the system of equations:
$$u_{tt} - \Delta u - a \Delta u_t = -b \Delta u_t + f(x,t,u)$$
$$v_{tt} - \Delta v - a \Delta v_t = f(x,t,v)$$
where the term $a \Delta u_t$ represents the standard d'Alembert wave operator, and $-b \Delta u_t$ combined with $a \Delta u_t$ forms a generalized Kelvin-Voigt damping model. Specifically, the model incorporates both classical viscoelastic damping ($a \Delta u_t$) and additional dissipative effects ($b \Delta u_t$). The analysis demonstrates that the system admits a unique global solution that remains stable over time, provided the nonlinear source term $f$ satisfies appropriate growth conditions. These findings extend previous research by considering more complex coupling mechanisms and improved damping structures.

Reinforcement learning (RL) has recently attracted significant attention due to its potential to train agents capable of performing complex tasks in unstructured environments. However, this potential is often hindered by a lack of interpretability, which is essential for deploying these agents in safety-critical domains. While knowledge extraction methods have been developed to address this issue, they frequently fail to produce explanations that are both concise and conceptually clear. This paper introduces a model-driven hierarchical RL framework designed to generate such high-quality explanations. The approach decouples the training of the RL agent from a knowledge extraction phase, wherein the agent's policy is transformed into a logic program using inductive logic programming techniques. The resulting logical rules are then refined through abductive reasoning to create more succinct and comprehensible hierarchical explanations.

This study introduces a mechanism for achieving nonreciprocity in light transmission, driven by a nonlinearity within a quantum compression medium. The authors propose that coupling a quantum compress nonlinearity with a single two-level atom enables the unidirectional passage of photons. Theoretical analysis indicates that this atom-mediated compression nonlinearity generates an effective synthetic gauge field, which is responsible for the observed one-way light transport.

This study examines the best approximation within the uniform norm by linear combinations of translated functions $f(x-t_i)$, where the shifts $t_i$ are fixed. We demonstrate that for specific functions $f$ exhibiting even symmetry and complete monotonicity for positive $x$, the error in approximating a target function $g$ using a linear operator $L_n$ can be expressed as the supremum over a particular class of functions $\Phi$ of the evaluation $|\Phi(L_n(g))|$. The analysis further establishes that the linear operator $L_n$ achieves optimality if and only if it is equivalent to a quadrature rule.

The LUX-ZEPLIN (LZ) experiment, a successor to LUX, is a leading international endeavor in the search for dark matter. Situated at the Sanford Underground Research Facility in South Dakota, LZ utilizes a 12.7-tonne detector filled with ultra-pure, neon-free liquid xenon to probe the interactions of Weakly Interacting Massive Particles (WIMPs) with ordinary matter. This paper details the initial results from a 300-day data collection period using xenon samples containing 100 parts per billion of $^6$Li. The study analyzes the energy spectrum of events triggered by ionization and scintillation light, specifically targeting spin-dependent couplings between WIMPs and nucleons. The derived 90% confidence level lower limits on the spin-dependent WIMP-nucleon cross-section are 1.1 $\times$ 10$^{-8}$ cm$^2$ for a 1 GeV/c$^2$ WIMP mass, surpassing the prior record set by the LUX experiment. These findings are consistent with the spin-independent cross-section limits previously established by LUX.

Blind image restoration (BIR) is a critical challenge in digital image processing, yet it remains difficult because the unknown point spread function (PSF) is hard to estimate. This paper introduces a new BIR framework based on kernel mixture modeling. The proposed method decomposes an observed blurred image into two components: a low-rank structure representing the underlying clean image and a sparse matrix modeling the blur kernel. To address the difficulty in directly estimating the rank, we employ a low-rank plus sparse unmasking technique, which separates the low-rank component into a low-rank submatrix and a sparse mask. Consequently, the restoration problem is reformulated as a low-rank submatrix recovery task subject to cardinality constraints. The algorithm utilizes an iterative alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM) approach to solve this problem. Experimental results on blind deblurring and blind denoising tasks demonstrate that the proposed method achieves superior performance compared to existing state-of-the-art techniques.

We demonstrate that every strict functorial associateative dual bimodule over a dual algebra naturally generates an associated nonuniform associateative dual bimodule structure on a bialgebra. We propose a framework for translating natural language specifications into formal Hoare triples that accurately capture program semantics. Our method leverages an existing semantic parser to convert natural language specifications into Logic Forms (LoF), a structured interlingua representing meaning. We then introduce a set of Natural rules designed to transform LoFs into corresponding pre- and postconditions as well as assertions, which are integrated into a reasoning engine capable of automatically verifying program correctness based on these translations.

This paper introduces RCanopus, an extension of the Canopus consensus protocol designed to ensure robustness against node crashes and Byzantine faults. While Canopus offers strong consistency and high availability in crash-failure environments, RCanopus expands its capabilities to handle malicious behavior. The protocol maintains the simplicity of Canopus, requiring no new cryptographic assumptions and incurring only a modest increase in communication overhead. RCanopus ensures safety by ensuring all non-faulty nodes eventually agree on a value, provided the number of Byzantine faults does not exceed one-third of the total participants. For liveness, agreement proceeds as long as at least two-thirds of the nodes are non-faulty and at least one node is not experiencing repeated failures. The authors have implemented RCanopus and evaluated it using both simulated and physical testbeds. The results indicate that RCanopus successfully withstands the fault scenarios it was designed for, outperforming existing consensus protocols in these specific conditions.

This study examines how cholesterol influences the bending modulus of a POPC membrane, analyzing both theoretical predictions and experimental findings. We employed the fluctuation method to determine bending modulus via molecular dynamics simulations, utilizing the POPC model validated against experimental data. Our findings reveal that bending rigidity increases with rising cholesterol concentrations, peaking at approximately 50% saturation. This peak aligns with the coexistence of liquid-ordered and liquid-disordered phases, whereas rigidity diminishes in a pure POPC membrane at higher cholesterol levels. These results are corroborated by experimental data from a supported POPC bilayer, which recorded a bending modulus of roughly 14 kBT at 50% cholesterol saturation compared to approximately 20 kBT at saturation.

We present a quantum astrophysical framework for compact objects, extending prior work on the black hole case to general compact structures. This model relies on the canonical ADM Hamiltonian, which is modified through the imposition of an integrability constraint that introduces specific holonomies. Consequently, the resulting dynamics exhibit a discrete temporal evolution characterized by a characteristic scale of approximately the Planck length. We apply this quantum model to the case of compact stars, deriving a corresponding radius-radius relationship. This relationship mirrors the radius-horizon radius relation previously established for black holes, thereby offering a testable prediction for black hole shadows that can be verified via gravitational lensing observations.

This study introduces a catalog detailing the highest-energy cosmic rays recorded during the initial operational phase of the Pierre Auger Observatory. The compilation includes 100 events with energies exceeding 10^17.5 eV, 1,000 events surpassing 10^18 eV, and the 100 most energetic events above the 10^19 eV threshold. For each event, the document provides the date and time of occurrence, the reconstructed energy, the primary interaction's longitudinal depth, and the reconstructed arrival direction. Additionally, the catalog lists the reconstructed energies and longitudinal depths for the 100 most energetic events above 10^18 eV. This dataset offers a comprehensive overview of the highest-energy cosmic rays observed by the largest ground-based detector array globally.

Recent advancements in deep uncertainty assessment for computer vision tasks have primarily focused on pixel-level semantic tasks, such as classification and regression. However, object detection remains largely untouched, with existing uncertainty techniques yielding suboptimal results. This paper introduces a new approach to uncertainty estimation for deep object detectors, grounded in the Monte Carlo Bayesian framework. By addressing the limitations of previous Bayesian detection methods, our method significantly enhances both prediction accuracy and uncertainty assessment reliability. Furthermore, we introduce a novel metric to evaluate uncertainty assessment quality, which surpasses the conventional use of object detection metrics. Experimental results across three benchmarks demonstrate that our method outperforms current state-of-the-art techniques by a wide margin.

Accurately forecasting future traffic states is essential for real-time applications like navigation and traffic control. While most current methods rely on predicting entire road networks, this approach often fails to capture the localized nature of traffic fluctuations. This study introduces a novel strategy that predicts future traffic states specifically on dynamic moving segments, which are extracted by tracking traffic jams. The proposed method employs a deep learning framework that utilizes both historical and current state data to forecast traffic conditions ahead. The effectiveness of this prediction system was validated using the PeMS4 dataset, demonstrating its superior performance.

We introduce a rewriting system designed to operate within Gray classes—structures defined as the union of a set of graphs sharing a fixed vertex set, where each individual graph belongs to a specified class. This system employs a specific type of rule known as an edge configuration rule. These rules consist of a left-hand side and a right-hand side, both being edge configurations over a common vertex set; an application of such a rule replaces the subset of edges in a given graph that matches its left-hand side with the subset defined by its right-hand side. A single such rule can generate multiple distinct rewriting steps. We establish that determining whether a given graph appears in the rewrite closure of a given graph is an NP-complete problem. We also examine the applicability of our framework to the field of consistency management. Our findings indicate that our approach offers a generalized method for addressing consistency management that extends beyond previous techniques.

Accurately segmenting the hippocampus is crucial for diagnosing and treating various disorders, particularly epilepsy. This study introduces a deep learning framework designed to analyze the relationship between hippocampal volume and seizure frequency in patients. The framework partitions the hippocampus into three distinct anatomical regions—head, body, and tail—utilizing multiple Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs). The segmentation model employs two fully convolutional networks (FCNs) enhanced with ResNet-101 and DenseNet-121 backbones, respectively. The partitioning component consists of three fully convolutional networks (FCNs) with DenseNet-121 backbones. The model's efficacy was validated using data from 100 patients with temporal lobe epilepsy (TLE) and 100 healthy controls. The experimental results indicate that the proposed method achieves a Dice coefficient of 0.885 for overall hippocampal segmentation and a Dice coefficient of 0.852 for region-specific partitioning.

We introduce a novel quantum algorithm designed to address the classic Pigeonhole Problem, achieving a speedup of $O(N^{1/3})$ over classical methods. This approach represents an improvement upon the previous best quantum result of $O(N^{1/2})$ while also surpassing the classical limit. Central to this algorithm is the use of transverse modes to encode the problem's inputs. This encoding strategy not only facilitates the implementation of the algorithm but also offers a fresh perspective on the phenomenon of diffraction within the quantum realm.

This paper introduces a Monte Carlo code designed to simulate the trajectories of cosmic ray particles (protons and alpha particles) within the magnetosphere, specifically focusing on their interaction with Earth's magnetic field and the generation of secondary radiation. The study analyzes the flux of these cosmic rays at altitudes of 400 km and 1,600 km, comparing the results for different particle species and energies. The calculated flux values are then contrasted with existing experimental data from the ALTEA and PAMELA satellites to evaluate the model's accuracy.

Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have become a vital tool for analyzing graph-structured data, yet existing models often rely on aggregating information from immediate neighbors, which restricts their capacity to capture global graph patterns. To address this limitation, we introduce a new global learning framework that extends feature aggregation to a pyramid-like structure, progressively linking nodes across varying distances. This approach enhances the representation of both local and global topologies. Furthermore, we propose a dedicated framework for topology link reconfiguration, which optimizes connection weights within the global pyramid to maximize information flow. Experimental evaluations on multiple real-world datasets confirm that our method outperforms current state-of-the-art techniques in graph learning tasks.

We introduce a novel algorithm designed to manage matrix completion tasks with differentially private constraints, drawing inspiration from the Huber method used in private statistical estimation. This approach offers computational efficiency, operating within a time complexity of $O(m \log(1/\epsilon))$, and ensures robust performance across a wide range of input parameters. Furthermore, we establish Huber-type bounds for various scenarios, achieving privacy mechanisms that are stable, precise, and resistant to outliers. We also present Huber variants specifically for tasks like private low-rank matrix fulfillment and rank-one maximum a posteriori estimation, demonstrating that these methods achieve constant additive error.

This study introduces the Astrodust+PAH model, a unified framework designed to characterize the extinction, emission, and polarization caused by sparse interstellar dust. The model relies on a size distribution of silicate and carbonaceous grains, governed by the MRN distribution, which are subjected to the sintering process to ensure size-dependent cohesion. The physical and optical characteristics of these grains are calculated using the T-matrix method, while polarized emission spectra are derived via the dyadic Green's function technique. The results demonstrate that the predicted total extinctions, including those from small polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs), align with observational data from the diffuse interstellar medium. Furthermore, the model successfully reproduces the size distribution of large silicate grains and accurately predicts the size distribution of large PAHs, which are constrained by emission spectra. Additionally, the predicted polarized light in the diffuse interstellar environment matches observations from the Polarization and Emission in the Galaxy Experiment (PoEE). The study also reveals that grain sintering is a critical factor in explaining the extinction and polarization features of the diffuse interstellar medium.

This study presents the discovery of a massive planet, CIDA 1 b, orbiting the extremely low-mass star CIDA 1. The system was identified through a survey of 1,000 brown dwarfs and young stellar objects using the VLT/SPHERE instrument, which revealed a companion with a mass of 11.4 ± 1.1 M_Jup at a projected separation of 1.1 ± 0.2 AU. The system's age is estimated to be 10 ± 2 Myr. Dynamical analysis indicates that CIDA 1 b is gravitationally bound to CIDA 1, with a 99.9% confidence level. The companion exhibits a high projected rotation velocity of 1.1 km s^-1 and a projected equatorial oblateness of 0.11 ± 0.03. These observed properties are consistent with predictions from hydrodynamical models for a young, massive object. The companion's mass is notably higher than the typical mass of hot Jupiters, and its orbit is significantly closer than that of most directly imaged exoplanets. The system's estimated mass ratio is 10^-4.5 ± 10^-6.5. The combination of the host star's low mass and the planet's high mass suggests that CIDA 1 b likely formed via core accretion rather than disk instability.

We investigate a two-player game played on a finite graph $G$ where players alternate pressing vertices, with the objective of toggling unlit vertices to a lit state. A vertex remains lit only if it was initially lit or pressed an even number of times. The game concludes when a player cannot light any new vertex, forcing the subsequent player to move next. We define the "dilemma" as a graph state where the current player can either light a new vertex or deliberately avoid doing so, ceding the move to the opponent. Our primary contribution is a linear algebraic framework that characterizes these dilemmatic configurations. Leveraging this characterization, we derive the maximum number of vertex presses achievable in the dilemma scenario for specific graph families, including trees, cycles, grids, and graphs with diameter three.

This paper introduces a novel image segmentation framework that integrates total variation (TV) regularization with anisotropic diffusion (AD). The model is designed to simultaneously generate a piecewise-smooth segmentation and a denoised, deblurred restored image. By applying the augmented Lagrangian method, we derive an iterative algorithm for solving the resulting system of nonlinear partial differential equations. Theoretically, this paper establishes the convergence of the proposed solution to the global optimum of the model. Furthermore, theoretical analysis demonstrates the convergence of the auxiliary variables to the respective solutions of the TV regularized image reconstruction and the anisotropically diffused image. Experimental results confirm that the proposed method effectively segments and restores images corrupted by noise and blur.

Abstract Interpretation is a technique used to automatically approximate program semantics. While the method's theoretical foundation is well-established, its practical application has historically been hindered by a lack of efficient, scalable tools. This paper introduces a new strategy to accelerate the standard algorithmic framework of Abstract Interpretation. The approach relies on a "decoupling" mechanism that separates the ascending and descending phases of computation. By leveraging the observation that data flow analysis typically advances through a program in lexicographical order, the study demonstrates that the analysis can be executed in two distinct steps: first, the ascending phase is computed using a pre-sorted traversal of the control flow graph to ensure efficiency, and second, the descending phase is derived by applying a specific transformation to the results of the initial stage. The paper further proves that this two-phase division yields outcomes mathematically identical to the traditional single-phase analysis. Finally, the proposed decoupling technique is implemented and evaluated on a leading-scale C/C++ analysis engine, with results confirming a substantial improvement in performance.

Phonons serve as vital mediators of structural and electronic phenomena in condensed matter, yet their manipulation remains difficult. This study demonstrates that topological phononic states can be generated and controlled in the perovskite oxide SrTiO$_3$ through photoexcitation. Utilizing time-resolved inelastic x-ray scattering, researchers observed the emergence of a phonon mode at 4.5 THz within the topological Weyl nodal line of SrTi$_3$'s dispersion relation. This observation coincides with the material's photoinduced transition from a centrosymmetric to a non-centrosymmetric crystal structure. Furthermore, the velocity of this 4.5 THz Weyl node is experimentally tuned by varying the excitation light fluence. These findings establish a pathway for generating and manipulating topological phonons in solids, offering potential applications in phononics and photoacoustics.

Outlier detection is a fundamental task in data mining and pattern recognition, yet it remains difficult in general metric spaces because traditional methods relying on density struggle there due to the absence of a defined density function. This study introduces a novel outlier detection approach for metric spaces that leverages the geometric structure of data points. The method constructs a specific graph based on distances to identify outliers, achieving a balance of speed and accuracy. Theoretical analysis demonstrates that the algorithm is independent of specific metric properties, relying solely on geometric relationships. Empirical evaluations across various datasets confirm that the proposed technique is both efficient and effective.

The interaction between an atom and a metallic surface is examined using an analytical model that accounts for the finite conductivity of the surface material. Analysis reveals that as the atom approaches the surface, it experiences an attractive force; however, if the surface is sufficiently narrow, a local minimum in the atom-surface separation can become stable due to the presence of a minimum. Additionally, the presence of the metallic surface alters the spontaneous emission rate of the atom. It is demonstrated that a slender surface can cause atomic emission to be either suppressed or enhanced, depending on the system's geometry and material properties.

This paper addresses the challenge of bias within graph learning by introducing a new framework for achieving fairness. Our method focuses on ensuring equitable treatment of local communities rather than just individual groups. We introduce a graph learning algorithm that simultaneously optimizes prediction accuracy and this proposed fairness metric. The core of our approach involves formulating the graph into localized communities using a new optimization framework. We then define a graph-based distance metric to measure fairness between these communities and integrate this metric as a regularization term within the learning algorithm. The resulting algorithm is designed to be efficient and scalable, capable of handling large-scale data. We validate our method through experiments on both synthetic datasets and real-world data from a major social media platform. The results demonstrate that our method significantly improves upon existing techniques, achieving a notable balance between fairness and accuracy.

This study introduces a novel iterative algorithm for determining enzyme kinetics, which leverages the iterative approximation of answers to kinetic equations for reversible processes. The method's efficacy is demonstrated through its application to the Michaelis-Menten mechanism, specifically analyzing how the reaction rate varies with substrate concentration and the influence of distinct kinetic parameters. Furthermore, the analysis extends to a two-substrate enzyme reaction, deriving the corresponding kinetic equation and calculating both the reaction rate and its substrate concentration dependencies.

This study presents the measurement of inclusive jet production using jet transverse energy ($E_{\rm T}^{\rm jet}$) and multiplicity at the CMS experiment in proton-proton collisions at 13 TeV. The analysis covers the full 2016 dataset, corresponding to an integrated luminosity of 35.9 fb$^{-1}$. Jet spectra are determined in the forward region, defined by pseudorapidity $|\eta| > 2.4$, across the range $E_{\rm T}^{\rm jet} > 20$ GeV. Results are provided as both absolute cross sections and normalized differential distributions, with the latter compared against predictions from the standard model. Additionally, the study examines the production of jet pairs in the very forward region, $|\eta| > 4.2$, with $E_{\{\text{T}\}}^{\rm jet} > 100$ GeV, to investigate potential deviations from standard model expectations that could indicate the presence of natural or split supersymmetry.

We introduce a new class of mean-reverting, random-time-stopped geometric Brownian motion models designed to capture financial bubbles, where both the start and end points are unknown. These models are estimated using the full dataset of observed bubble trajectories, and the estimation procedure is validated through simulations. We demonstrate that our proposed method outperforms established approaches in accurately estimating both the burst probability and the average burst duration. Additionally, the paper offers a comparative analysis of our results against other existing methods.

This study investigates the ground state and thermal density matrix of a quantum harmonic oscillator subject to a time-dependent driving force. We employ the Euclidean path integral framework in conjunction with Metropolis and Heat-bath Markov Chain Monte Carlo algorithms. To validate these methods, we apply them to a system with an inverse temperature of $\beta=1$ and a driving force defined as $f(t)=\sqrt{2}\cos(t)$. Our results demonstrate that the heat-bath algorithm offers superior performance over the Metropolis approach.

Product reviews serve as a primary source of information for buyers seeking details about a product. While many existing methods suggest products based on review similarity, they often overlook the nuanced sentiment expressed within those reviews. To address this, we introduce a Sentiment-sensitive Interactive Fusion Network (SIFN) designed to perform effective product recommendations by analyzing Review Texts. Our approach extracts semantic features from the reviews and incorporates a Sentiment-Aware Attention (SAA) mechanism to integrate sentiment-specific features into the fusion process. This SAA mechanism not only weights semantic features according to sentiment relevance but also dynamically adjusts sentiment features based on the current semantic context. Furthermore, we employ a multi-task learning strategy to jointly optimize the prediction of product recommendations and review sentiment analysis. Experimental results on two real-world datasets demonstrate that SIFN significantly outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods in terms of both recommendation accuracy and the quality of sentiment analysis.

Code-switching (CS) is a prevalent linguistic trait in many low-resource settings, yet it remains under-researched in the field of natural language processing. This study investigates the utility of lexical substitutions for augmenting Arabic-English (Ar-EN) code-switched text data. We introduce a novel, rule-based approach that leverages lexical and semantic relationships within monolingual Arabic and English corpora to generate Ar-EN code-switched sentences. Evaluating this augmentation strategy on a newly created Ar-EN mixed-language dataset using a BERT-based model demonstrates that our method outperforms existing techniques, including those utilizing transformer-based approaches and existing lexical substitution rules.

The authors demonstrate that any subgroup within the group of diffeomorphisms of a closed surface of genus at least 2 that contains an expansive homeomorphism is not Roelcke precompact. This finding serves as a generalized version of a previous result specifically regarding subgroups containing Thompson's sporadic group, T(49).
