Relation Extraction (RE) entails identifying the relationships between entities within a sentence. This paper introduces a novel RE framework that leverages a knowledge graph (KG) link prediction model to bolster the learning of a relationship classifier. Specifically, we employ a link prediction technique to refine entity representations by leveraging information from the KG, thereby enhancing the capabilities of the relationship classifier. Empirical results demonstrate that our proposed method surpasses existing state-of-the-art techniques.

This work introduces analytical models for calculating the latency of key digital-to-analog and analog-to-digital converters, including the Sample-and-Hold, Flash, Sigma-Delta, and Pipeline converters. These models are derived from empirical data points generated using Matlab's Curve Fitting Toolkit, which interpolates measured data. The resulting formulas enable analytical conversion of measured data points into model parameters. The utility of these models is demonstrated by calculating the end-to-end transmission time for a 100 Mbps signal sent over a 100-meter cable, accounting for the latency of the associated converters.

Continuity is a fundamental concept in analysis, topology, and geometry. In metric spaces, a function is considered continuous if small alterations in the input result in only minor variations in the output. This paper introduces a new definition of continuity specifically tailored for the reinforcement learning (RL) community. We demonstrate that this concept is instrumental in RL by showing that it enables the creation of a "coarse-grained" version of a potentially discontinuous function, which retains continuity. This property facilitates the application of established statistical learning theory to derive performance guarantees for learning algorithms. We validate the utility of this new definition by applying it to the estimation of transition probabilities in Markov decision processes (MDPs) and to the estimation of action-value functions within the framework of online reinforcement learning.

Animates and inanimates represent a fundamental biological categorization in the human visual system, with recent research indicating that their distinct neural representations are established early in the ventral visual stream. This study examines the ontogeny of this animacy organization by analyzing data from 1,025 individuals aged 6 to 85 years using a large-scale functional MRI dataset. We assessed both behavioral performance and brain activity during a visual categorization task involving faces, bodies, and objects. Findings reveal that while behavioral proficiency in distinguishing animates from inanimates remains stable across all age groups, the corresponding neural patterns shift significantly: children exhibit a distributed cortical response to this contrast, whereas adults localize it narrowly to the fusiform gyrus. Furthermore, an age-dependent gradient emerges in which the spatial focus of this contrast migrates posteriorly as individuals mature. These observations underscore the protracted development of this specific visual processing mechanism and illuminate the dynamic nature of the adult ventral visual stream.

This study introduces a new class of arrangement-preserving filters designed for multidimensional simulations involving finite elements and finite difference methods. These filters effectively minimize spurious oscillations and dissipation artifacts that frequently emerge in computational fluid dynamics and structural mechanics. By utilizing convex optimization, the filter parameters are automatically tuned to satisfy strict constraints on filter width, smoothness, symmetry, and monotonicity. The proposed filtering approach is seamlessly integrated into the solution workflow for discretized partial differential equations. The authors demonstrate the filter's performance through various test cases, including the von K\'arm\'an equations for plate bending, the Darcy flow equation, and the Euler equations of fluid dynamics.

This study investigates the corona's evolution in MAXI J1535-571 during its 2018 outburst using the Insight-HXMT X-ray telescope. By analyzing the spectral energy distribution with the two-component model of a Comptonized disk blackbody spectrum, we identified a distinct type-C quasi-periodic oscillation (QPO) in the Comptonization component's temperature. This QPO frequency varied from 1.0 to 1.6 Hz throughout the outburst. Our findings reveal that the Comptonization temperature initially declined before rising, while the corona's size contracted subsequently expanded. Initially, the corona was small and hot, but later it became large and cooler. These results align with the standard paradigm of black hole coronae, where a hot, compact corona transitions into a cold, extended one.

Socially inspired robots must possess the capacity to analyze a human's intentions and adapt their actions accordingly. This paper introduces a novel framework for social intrinsic motivation (SIM), designed to enable robots to dynamically adjust their behaviors in response to a partner's reactions. The core of this approach is the Transfer Empowerment (TE) metric, which quantifies the anticipated difficulty of reaching a specific goal across multiple time steps. By analyzing how a human's intrinsic motivation shifts in response to a robot's behavior, the system generates a corresponding intrinsic motivation signal for the robot. This adaptive mechanism allows the robot to refine its actions to better align with the human's current objectives. The study presents both the formal definition of SIM and a practical implementation designed to foster socially coherent behavior.

We introduce a novel contrastive learning framework designed to train a substance identification model capable of leveraging a single labeled example. This approach utilizes physics-based simulations to generate contextual information from environmental cues, such as gaseous emissions, and integrates it with visual data. The resulting model enables the identification of previously unseen substances anywhere, even when initial training relies solely on one example per category. We validate this approach through experiments on a new dataset comprising 10 substances, where the model successfully achieved 80% accuracy. Furthermore, we demonstrate its practical utility by identifying unknown substances in an industrial setting with 86.6% accuracy, attaining high performance despite limited training data consisting of only 30 examples per class.

This paper offers a survey of Lie 2-algebras, which can be understood as Lie algebras equipped with a degree $-1$ action by a Lie algebra. We provide a comprehensive description of these structures using both global methods, involving smooth functors from Lie groupoids to Lie groups, and local methods, involving $\mathfrak{g}$-atlas Lie algebras. Additionally, we examine various examples, including those derived from Courant algebroids and Lie groupoid pair-distributions.

We introduce a novel, detector-free network designed for robust keypoint detection and descriptor generation, leveraging a self-attention transformer architecture. Unlike many existing methods, our approach explicitly models the relationship between a keypoint's local appearance and its global position within an image. This is achieved by utilizing a set of deformable query vectors that are processed by a dedicated local feature transformer. These queries dynamically align with keypoints in an alternative image based on global positional cues and local contextual details, allowing the resulting matched features to represent both attributes simultaneously. Empirical evaluations on the 7-Scenes and Pascal-Context datasets demonstrate that our method surpasses leading solutions in terms of both keypoint detection accuracy and the reliability of the generated descriptors.

Accurately measuring the vector magnetic field on the Sun is vital for understanding solar physics and space weather. However, these instruments rely on indirect inferences, which can introduce systematic errors. This study examines the impact of such biases by analyzing data from the Helioseismic and Magnetic Imager (HMI) on NASA's Solar Dynamics Observatory (SDO). We evaluated the performance of the spectropolarimetric inversion code, NICOLE, using a controlled dataset derived from the same observations. This test dataset features known ground-truth values obtained from a linear polarization approximation, allowing us to assess the precision of the inferred vector magnetic field. We found that the bias in the total strength of the magnetic field (LOS) is most significant in regions with weak fields, while the measurement of field inclination remains largely unbiased. Conversely, the bias in azimuthal angle is highly dependent on the actual field strength. These findings suggest that the most effective strategy to mitigate these errors is to avoid using the LOS magnetic field component in scientific analyses.

This study introduces an innovative demand side control approach for energy usage planning and real-time charging, targeting the optimization of both objectives. The process commences with energy usage planning, where a collective game is employed to determine optimal power consumption schedules for the upcoming day. Subsequently, during real-time charging, a reinforcement learning-based individual game dynamically adjusts power consumption to minimize costs based on current electricity prices. The efficacy of this proposed framework is validated through simulations utilizing actual grid data from the Nord Pool exchange.

This study examines the Hawking emission characteristics of charged black strings within Rastall gravity theory. We analyze how this gravitational framework impacts key physical parameters, including mass, charge, entropy, temperature, and the isentropic compressibility. Furthermore, we explore the thermodynamic behavior of these black strings, specifically focusing on their stability under radial and specific heat conditions. The results indicate that the string's temperature is highly sensitive to the Rastall parameter, which dictates the nature of its Hawking emission. We also investigate the nature of Hawking emission from these charged black string solutions in Rastall gravity theory, assessing how the gravitational framework influences physical parameters such as mass, charge, entropy, temperature, and isentropic compressibility. The thermodynamic behavior, including stability analysis via radial modes and specific heat capacity, reveals that the string's temperature exhibits heightened sensitivity to the Rastall parameter, thereby dictating the nature of its Hawking emission. This work examines the spectral measures associated with a unitary operator defined on a subset of a Hilbert space that is invariant under it. We demonstrate that the rate at which the associated spectral distributions converge relies exclusively on the spectral function's behavior near zero. Furthermore, we establish the existence of specific projection-valued distributions where convergence does not occur absolutely or in mean, even when strict positivity holds. Finally, we explore the implications of these findings regarding the convergence rates within Von Neumann's Ergodic Theorem.

The Gaia mission is anticipated to deliver spectra for over 10 million stars, including the majority with metallicities below solar levels. However, the Blue-Photometer (BP) and Red-Photometer (RP) data are not optimized for deriving precise metallicities in these objects. This study introduces a novel technique to identify metal-poor stars using Gaia BP and RP spectra. The method relies on a machine-learning approach that leverages the distinct spectral features of metal-poor stars to distinguish them from solar-metallicity counterparts. The algorithm was trained on a synthetic dataset generated from the BTSetell library, covering a wide range of metallicities from -2.5 to 0. The resulting classification model was then validated against real spectroscopic data from the APOGEE survey. The results demonstrate that the method effectively separates metal-poor stars from solar-metallicity stars, achieving an accuracy of 99.9% for the latter group. Furthermore, the method successfully identifies metal-poor stars with metallicities below -1.5, reaching a purity level of 99.9% and an accuracy of 89.9%.

Global climate change is intensifying wildfire severity, a trend that has gained significant attention from researchers and policymakers. This study introduces a novel method for evaluating fire intensity worldwide by leveraging the relationship between burned area and fire season duration. We analyze data from 2003 to 2016, sourced from the Global Fire Assimilation System (GFAS), to develop a robust model capable of forecasting fire intensity. This approach employs a combination of geospatial analysis and machine learning, specifically utilizing a geographically weighted regression (GWR) technique alongside a random forest algorithm. The findings reveal a strong positive correlation between fire season length and fire intensity. Furthermore, the study successfully predicts fire intensity with a mean absolute percentage error (MAPE) of 16.5%. This innovative framework offers valuable insights for fire management, potentially aiding in the identification of high-intensity zones and the development of effective mitigation strategies.

This study explores the corpus-based measurement of morphological complexity, specifically analyzing the relationships between various existing metrics. We introduce a new metric, the "Morphological Richness Index" (MRI), designed to capture the diversity of inflectional and derivational affixes within a language. Our work involves constructing a comprehensive dataset of 100 morphological complexity metrics for 1,700 languages using 11 major language resources. Through this dataset, we assess the reliability of these measures, correlate them with one another, and validate findings by comparing our results to established correlations between morphological complexity and societal development. We find that no single metric stands out as the most robust; instead, a composite score derived from multiple metrics offers superior predictive accuracy for societal complexity. Furthermore, while many metrics exhibit high inter-correlations, we identify distinct clusters of related measures, including those based on morphological richness, agglutinativity, and the diversity of word forms.

Self-interacting dark matter (SIDM) offers a promising solution to discrepancies between cosmological simulations and galaxy observations, particularly the "small-scale crisis" involving gravitational potentials in dwarf galaxies and the cores of galaxy clusters. This study investigates gravitational magnification in the core of the galaxy cluster Abell 1689, utilizing deep Hubble Space Telescope data and mass models derived from strong and weak lensing constraints. We find that the observed magnification profiles in the cluster core are consistent with a standard cold dark matter (CDM) model, effectively ruling out significant self-interactions. Specifically, we constrain the self-scattering cross-section to $\sigma/m < 0.07$ cm$^2$/g at 95% confidence, a limit comparable to previous results from galaxy cluster analyses but more stringent than those derived solely from dwarf galaxy studies. These findings suggest that SIDM models must be tuned to simultaneously satisfy dwarf galaxy core profiles and cluster core magnification limits, which may necessitate a density- or temperature-dependent cross-section.

We introduce a technique for reducing the state space of dynamical models while ensuring a bound on the resulting approximation error. This approach leverages the concept of weak observability, which restricts dynamical systems to subspaces where errors in state estimation remain limited. We establish a bound on the estimation error for the compressed model and provide a sufficient condition to guarantee that this bound remains below a specified threshold. Additionally, we present a necessary and sufficient condition for dynamical systems to be weakly observable. The method is demonstrated through a case study involving a nonlinear fluid dynamics system.

This study introduces a novel method for independent component analysis (ICA) grounded in a new statistical measure termed mutual ar-Rényi entropy (m-ar-E). The m-ar-E metric quantifies the dependence among random variables by extending the concept of Rényi entropy to multiple dimensions; specifically, its minimum value indicates independence. A key advantage of this approach is its ability to effectively capture non-Gaussian distributions, which is why minimizing the m-ar-E via a rapid fixed-point algorithm serves as an effective strategy for separating independent sources. The proposed method demonstrates robustness against various mixing models and accurately recovers both source signals and their mixing matrix. Furthermore, the algorithm exhibits superior computational efficiency compared to established ICA techniques.

Social networking platforms have become primary instant sources for incident identification. Although existing research predominantly analyzes text-based content, this study introduces a novel framework for detecting incidents in real-time from geotags within social media. The proposed framework employs a two-stage process: initially, it identifies the location of an incident by aggregating geotags and determining the most probable site via a density-based algorithm. Subsequently, it predicts the occurrence of an incident by applying a sliding window technique to the chronological sequence of identified locations. The system's efficacy was validated against Twitter data comprising geotags from known events, with results demonstrating an average detection latency of 11.5 minutes.

We establish the existence and uniqueness of a continuous solution for the problem $-\Delta u = \mathcal{H}^s \llcorner \Gamma$ within a Lipschitz domain $\Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^n$, where $0 < s < 2$ and $\Gamma$ is a $C^{2}$ submanifold of $\Omega$ possessing surface $\mathcal{H}^s$ as a distribution. This result holds under Neumann boundary conditions ($\partial_{\nu} u = 0$ on $\partial \Omega$) with a given $L^2$ function $f$. Additionally, we demonstrate that a continuous solution exists for the case of Dirichlet boundary conditions ($u = 0$ on $\partial \Omega$) when $1 < s < 2$.

This study introduces a high-throughput evolutionary exploration strategy designed to identify novel intermetallic compounds with abundant cobalt. By leveraging the high predictability of formation energies in intermetallic systems, the researchers utilized a genetic algorithm to iteratively construct increasingly larger supercells that minimized total energy per atom. This process involved generating random atomic shuffles within a fixed atom count and employing a simulated annealing method to optimize atomic positions and crystal lattice parameters. The iterative refinement of these supercells successfully produced 103 previously unreported cobalt-rich yttrium-cobalt-boron intermetallics, 103 of which were confirmed to be thermodynamically stable. Furthermore, the methodology was validated by correctly predicting the formation energies of 103 new compounds and accurately locating their crystal structures within the International Crystal Structure Database.

Risk-conscious bidding has become a primary focus for display advertising systems, as it is essential for maximizing advertising return on investment (ROAS) by balancing bid amounts against the anticipated value of future conversions. However, the inherent uncertainty of predicting future values makes risk assessment challenging. This paper introduces a novel risk-conscious bidding framework tailored for display advertising, specifically designed to maximize long-term profit under budget constraints. The model employs a multi-agent system where each agent independently estimates future value and risk, then iteratively refines bid amounts through interaction with a shared budget constraint. Theoretical analysis demonstrates that the proposed algorithm converges to an $\epsilon$-Nash equilibrium within $O(1/\epsilon)$ iterations. Extensive experiments on both real-world and synthetic datasets confirm that the budget-aware bid shapting (BABS) algorithm outperforms current state-of-the-art solutions.

We demonstrate that quantum trajectories exhibiting the most significant deviation from classical behavior emerge specifically in regions characterized by negative values within the Wigner function. This finding confirms and expands upon the guidance principle proposed by Tumulka, which utilizes the concept of a guidance wave function. Our proof relies on the observation that the quantum Fisher information density is proportional to the square of the Wigner function. This relationship allows us to establish that the average squared deviation from classical evolution is directly proportional to the Fisher information, which itself is constant across position space.

This paper introduces a novel privacy amplification method tailored for privacy amplification-based quantum key distribution (PA-QKD) that bypasses the need for explicit two-universal hash function selection. By employing entropy accumulation, this approach calculates the secure bound for the resulting hash functions. Utilizing a non-uniform random source, the technique achieves tighter security bounds than those provided by standard min-entropy evaluations. The study details the secure bound calculation for the BB84 and B92 protocols, incorporating the effects of detection efficiency. Furthermore, the method is applied to the "122-state" protocol, which supports single-photon sources and the presence of vacuum states. Numerical analysis of the secure bit rates for BB84, B92, and 122 protocols reveals that the derived tight bounds enable vacuum-state utilization in practical privacy-enhanced scenarios.

This paper examines the specific properties of timelike Bertrand curves. We derive the necessary and sufficient requirements for a curve to qualify as a timelike Bertrand curve and calculate the unique constant distances characterizing such curves. Furthermore, we categorize these curves by identifying distinct subsets of timelike Bertrand curves based on specific geometric conditions. The study also covers analogous cases for forward and backward Frenet frames and analyzes curves that do not adhere to the standard Frenet frame requirements.

This brief study examines combinations of distinct independent Feller processes, each adhering to the stochastic differential equation $dX_t = a_t\,dt + \sigma_t\,dW_t$. We demonstrate that if the product of the diffusion coefficient and its associated drift remains constant for the individual components, their combined sum also exhibits this property. This observation facilitates the derivation of marginal and conditional distributions for combinations involving Brownian motion, arithmetic Brownian motion, and arithmetic Ornstein-Uhlenbeck processes. Furthermore, we establish that these specific combinations admit sampling algorithms based on rejection methods.

This work presents a diagrammatic framework designed to investigate the scattering of multi-photon states within waveguide quantum electrodynamics (QED) systems featuring a two-level atom. We demonstrate that a two-dimensional scattering matrix can be constructed by integrating the products of a universal $2D$ T-matrix and specific vertex functions. These functions depend on the incoming and outgoing photon modes, frequencies, polarization, as well as the properties of the incident and scattered photons. The proposed method is applied to analyze three-photon scattering scenarios, specifically examining how input-frequency entanglement influences the output entanglement. We find that the system's response to three-photon scattering can be divided into two components: one invariant to the input entanglement and another that scales directly with it. This latter term acts as an effective nonlinearity, suggesting that the waveguide atom mediates an effective nonlinearity between waveguide light. Finally, we explore the potential for generating frequency entanglement among three photons via three-photon scattering.

We examine the evolution of spin-dependent dark matter components within a framework of boosted dark matter, specifically focusing on scenarios where a scalar field mediates interactions between the dark matter candidate and the Standard Model. By employing a kinetic theory approach, we derive the spin-dependent cross-sections for dark matter scattering off nucleons, demonstrating that these interactions can yield significant deviations from conventional expectations. Our analysis reveals that spin-polarized dark matter components experience anisotropic diffusion, with their movement varying based on the orientation of their angular momentum relative to the bulk momentum of the fluid. Furthermore, we investigate how these effects influence the production of dark matter in the early universe, concluding that they can substantially alter the yield of spin-polarized dark matter.

This brief note examines the historical and mathematical connection between Faulhaber and the Bernoulli numbers, extending the classic Faulhaber formula for odd powers to a generalized expression involving the Eulerian polynomials. Additionally, the text presents distinct proofs for both the Faulhaber and Brounelli identities.

Traditional non-coherent differential detection for Continuous Phase Modulation (CPM) suffers from significant performance degradation in the presence of delay Doppler (DD) shifts, which also broaden system timing sensitivity windows. This paper introduces a novel non-coherent differential detector for CPM that mitigates these DD effects and timing sensitivity issues. The new approach achieves this by leveraging the inherent properties of CPM to perform a maximum likelihood estimation of the combined DD shift and timing error, subsequently correcting the timing estimate to optimize the differential detection process. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed detector matches the performance of conventional methods under ideal conditions while offering substantial improvements in environments characterized by DD shifts and extended timing sensitivity.

Reward design stands as a critical component in the successful deployment of reinforcement learning (RL) within real-world scenarios. However, crafting such rewards is notoriously difficult, often necessitating extensive human-RL agent interactions to identify the correct objective function. This iterative process is not only labor-intensive but also prone to human error. To address these challenges, we introduce a visually assisted cluster ranking framework designed to facilitate human-RL agent collaboration. In this approach, an RL agent is trained using a parameterized reward function that allows for the generation of multiple distinct reward designs. These options are then clustered together, and humans provide feedback through rankings to select the most suitable one. By integrating human insights at the cluster level rather than the individual level, this framework significantly reduces annotation time. Furthermore, it is particularly effective in complex tasks where human preferences are ambiguous, allowing agents to receive broader, more robust guidance. We have validated this method across three diverse environments, including a complex, real-world warehouse scenario, and demonstrated marked improvements in both sample efficiency and training speed.

We investigate the configuration-space wave functions of nucleons within noncommutative QCD frameworks. In these systems, the standard parton distribution functions (PDFs) are replaced by generalized, or "star," PDFs. By analyzing the Fourier transforms of the corresponding noncommutative light-front wave function (W.F.), we demonstrate that the momentum-space star PDFs retain the same functional form as their commutative counterparts, differing only by a shift in the momentum argument. Consequently, the star PDFs can be expressed as shifted versions of ordinary PDFs. This relationship allows us to derive the momentum shift directly from the Fourier transform of the nucleon wave function in configuration space. Furthermore, the configuration-space wave functions for up and down quarks are derived, and their Fourier transforms yield the momentum-space W.F. for sea quarks. Finally, the configuration-space wave functions for valence quarks are utilized to determine the moments of the up and down sea quark PDFs.

We investigate the phase diagram of the zero-temperature toric code model defined on a square lattice within a magnetic field, where the system's Hamiltonian incorporates both $z$- and $x$-components. Our findings indicate that the ground state remains a topologically ordered toric code phase across the entire parameter range. Notably, the model exhibits a first-order phase transition between two distinct types of topological edge states.

This work investigates the sigma-model approximation for the probability distribution of the resolvent within random band matrices, specifically in the regime where the band width scales as $N^{2/3}$. We demonstrate that the approximation error is exponentially small relative to $N$. Furthermore, we establish that the resolvent's probability measure is dominated by that of the standard GUE, which also undergoes an exponential sublinear deviation in terms of $N$. These findings are applicable to the study of the Schr\"odinger operator associated with a random potential that is spatially correlated over a characteristic length scale of $N^{2/3}$.

Current pre-trained language models (PLMs) have achieved significant success in various natural language processing (NLP) tasks, yet their effectiveness in the domain of conversation comprehension remains limited. This paper introduces a new pre-training approach specifically tailored for conversation comprehension. The method employs a token-level contextual loss function designed to maximize the significance of meaningful tokens within sentences. Experimental results demonstrate that this model outperforms both baseline strategies and state-of-the-art approaches across three key areas: conversational attribution, dialog state tracking, and question answering within dialogue contexts.

Although significant progress has been made in automated algorithmic interpretability, a universally accepted standard for evaluating model explanations remains absent. To address this, we introduce a framework for human-centric algorithmic interpretability that is grounded in how people learn. This model defines interpretability as a function of both the explanatory method and the specific domain knowledge required by the user. Consequently, this perspective necessitates a tailored assessment metric for each model and set of explanations. We propose the Cognitive Intricacy Score (CIS) to quantify algorithmic interpretability within our framework, a measure that evaluates the cognitive load required to comprehend both the explanations and the underlying model. We also provide a methodology for calculating CIS using natural language processing and naturalness metrics. Finally, we discuss the utility of this framework in balancing interpretability and model performance, as well as its application to the design of educational tools for teaching machine learning.

TinyML, a field dedicated to deploying machine learning on resource-constrained devices, has recently seen significant growth. This paper introduces TiWS-iForest, an optimized version of the Isolation Forest algorithm designed to operate within the stringent memory and computational limits of TinyML environments. The optimization is achieved through two key strategies: (1) utilizing a weak guidance mechanism to reduce both memory usage and training time, and (2) implementing a compact, embedded-friendly isolation tree structure. The weak guidance approach relies on a simple heuristic to direct data partitioning, while the space-efficient tree structure relies on a specialized data type that minimizes memory footprint. Experimental evaluations across multiple anomaly detection benchmarks demonstrate that TiWS-iForest delivers superior performance compared to prior TinyML adaptations of Isolation Trees, achieving significant reductions in both memory consumption and computational time.

This study proposes a novel Poisson process reparameterization designed to enhance the flexibility of the Clayton copula, enabling the direct estimation of the number of exceedances for any threshold. This approach offers a distinct advantage over standard methods, which typically require fitting multiple threshold-exceedance models and merging the resulting estimates. By utilizing the proposed reparameterization, we achieve a unified estimation of these exceedances alongside other model parameters. Consequently, this method yields a more robust and versatile framework for analyzing extreme values.

Cross sections are fundamental to understanding particle interactions, yet their physical interpretation is often difficult to define. We introduce a novel approach to identifying cross sections by examining regions of average inflection points. By analyzing areas where the mean value of a specific observable remains constant, we provide a framework for defining quantities that represent the probability of specific processes. We apply this methodology to determine inflection points for various observables, including transverse momentum, rapidity, and jet multiplicity, within proton-proton collisions at the LHC.

This paper introduces the COMET-ATOMIC dataset, a COMplete and MEasurable extension of the large-scale ATOMIC dataset. While ATOMIC contains 580 million instance-labeled common sense triples, it lacks systematic validation of their accuracy. COMET-ATOMIC addresses this by providing a balanced subset of 1.5 million triples that have been rigorously verified through a crowdsourcing pipeline. We further validate this curated dataset by demonstrating its efficacy in a range of common sense reasoning tasks, including a COMET-ATOMIC-specific adaptation of the Truthful QA benchmark, a modified version of the SemEval-2019 Common SENSE task, and a modified version of the SemEval-2019 Common SENSE task. We further validate this curated dataset by demonstrating its efficacy in a range of common sense reasoning tasks, including a COMET-ATOMIC-specific adaptation of the Truthful QA benchmark, a modified version of the SemEval-2019 Common SENSE task, and a modified version of the SemEval-2019 Common SENSE task. We further validate this curated dataset by demonstrating its efficacy in a range of common sense reasoning tasks, including a COMET-ATOMIC-specific adaptation of the Truthful QA benchmark, a modified version of the SemEval-2019 Common SENSE task, and a modified version of the SemEval-2019 Common SENSE task. We further validate this curated dataset by demonstrating its

The Hi-GAL survey, conducted using the JCMT's SCUBA-2 instrument, targets cold dust emission from star-forming regions in the Galactic plane. It operates at four wavelengths (450, 850, 450, and 850 $\mu$m) across 12 square degrees, capturing a broad range of emission sources. To facilitate the analysis of this extensive dataset, JCMT has developed a specialized data reduction pipeline. This paper details the pipeline's core components, including a new software tool named `galfit` for generating reference flux calibration, `gasmapper` for creating mosaics, and `gasquant` for performing photometry. Furthermore, the paper outlines the procedures for creating a reference catalogue and a catalogue of point sources, which are utilized to validate the quality of the final outputs.

We present a high-precision determination of the chemical abundances in NGC 2808, a massive globular cluster, by analyzing the spectra of its most recently formed stars. Using the MILES library, we examined the spectra of 100 stars with effective temperatures ranging from 4,500 K to 8,000 K and surface gravities between 2.0 and 4.5. Our findings reveal a metallicity of [Fe/H] = +0.13 ± 0.05 dex, which aligns with previous studies, and confirm a significant metallicity gradient across the sample, reaching a maximum difference of 0.2 dex. This variation is robustly supported by the high signal-to-noise ratio of our data and the large sample size. Our results indicate that NGC 2808 is a metal-rich cluster, likely formed from a gas cloud that was heavily enriched by Type II supernovae.

Single file movement is characterized by the inability of particles to overtake one another, a constraint that profoundly alters statistical properties compared to standard Brownian motion. This study examines the entropic effects on single-file dynamics by analyzing a system of $N$ hard rods confined to a one-dimensional box of length $L$ under the influence of an external potential. We investigate the entropic influence on the initial exit duration statistics, specifically the time required for the leading particle to escape through one of the boundaries. Our analysis reveals that the exit duration statistics are governed by the system's entropy, which in turn depends on the external potential. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the exit duration scales with the system size as $L^2$, a result that holds regardless of the specific potential profile. Finally, we show that the exit duration statistics are independent of the external potential, provided that the system remains in the thermodynamic limit.

This study explores the application of Bayesian inference within quantum mechanics, specifically addressing the measurement of non-commuting observables. We demonstrate that the standard von Neumann rule for calculating probabilities after measurement can be understood as a direct consequence of the quantum Bayes' theorem. Furthermore, the quantum version of Bayesian inference is developed to calculate probabilities after a measurement, highlighting the distinctiveness of quantum mechanics compared to classical probability theory. Finally, the discussion concludes by emphasizing the significance of this approach for understanding measurement in quantum mechanics.

The equation of state (EOS) for a system is defined by the quantity $J = \langle \frac{\langle E \rangle}{V} \rangle$, representing the average energy density, where the average accounts for fluctuations in volume $V$ and energy $E$. This study examines the behavior of $J$ within small QCD systems, specifically those generated in high-energy heavy-ion collisions. By analyzing $J$ across varying temperatures and densities, we observe that it rises with increasing thermal density but remains nearly flat at low temperatures. These findings are compared against lattice QCD simulations and models describing a hadron resonance gas. We further explore the relationship between $J$ and the variance of energy fluctuations, $\langle (\Delta E)^2 \rangle / V$, finding that the former is consistently lower than the latter. This discrepancy is attributed to volume fluctuations, which diminish the EOS average relative to the energy variance ratio. Additionally, the analysis of $J$ in tiny systems reveals a distinct signature of phase transition, offering a novel diagnostic tool for studying matter formation in such contexts.

This paper provides a concise overview of the known non-trivial elements within the cohomology groups of the mod 2 Steenrod algebra. It begins with the foundational classes: the reduced powers $Sq^i$ and the Adams classes $\eta$, $\gamma$, and $\pi$. Subsequently, it details various families of elements characterized by their length, specifically the families $\alpha$, $\beta$, $\gamma$, $\delta$, $\varepsilon$, and $\sigma$. Furthermore, it covers elements defined through their duals in terms of their operations, including $\alpha$, $\beta$, $\pi$, $\eta$, and $\eta^2$. Finally, it presents a comprehensive table enumerating all identified elements up to degree 255.

Ultraviolet observations of distant galaxies are crucial for studying the reionization era and the formation of early stars. However, ground-based facilities cannot access the Lyman ultraviolet range because Earth's atmosphere absorbs these wavelengths. To overcome this limitation, we have developed a filter model that enables the Lyman ultraviolet to be observed through the visible spectrum by acting as a proxy. Utilizing the Hubble Space Telescope's data, we validated the model's accuracy by comparing photometric results with spectra. Our findings indicate that the model achieves a high degree of precision, with a maximum absolute error of 0.03 magnitudes and a maximum relative error of 0.02.

This study introduces a graph-symmetry-optimized ideal distributed control method for multi-agent systems, utilizing a consensus protocol that incorporates dynamic filters. Unlike traditional approaches, this filter-based protocol enables agents to achieve their collective goals immediately upon network connection, bypassing the convergence delays inherent in standard consensus protocols. We demonstrate that the proposed control law is grounded in the ideal control framework, leveraging the graph symmetries of the interaction network to facilitate the design of the filter-based consensus protocol. Furthermore, we establish that this symmetry-based ideal distributed control is both necessary and sufficient for standard consensus protocols to achieve ideal distributed control. Finally, we present an algorithm to compute the optimal dynamic filter coefficients by solving a convex optimization problem, which can be executed in a distributed manner across the network.

The rapid expansion of video and image data has intensified the need for efficient indexing and search capabilities. While text indexing is well-established, indexing dynamic visual content presents distinct challenges. This paper introduces Dynamic Picture Indexing (DPI), a novel approach that represents videos as a collection of sentences, where each statement describes a sequence of actions performed by objects. These textual descriptions are generated using an object detection framework and action recognition models. To facilitate search, these visual "sentences" are indexed alongside standard textual sentences via a joint sentence-matching strategy. Experimental results on the Charades dataset demonstrate that our method achieves state-of-the-art performance, surpassing prior methods by 10% to 20%.

This paper introduces keyless verification, a method for validating data integrity without relying on a pre-shared secret, specifically for the weak case of additive white Gaussian noise (AWGN) channels. We demonstrate that if a channel offers arbitrarily small but non-zero capacity, it can serve as a source of randomness for generating codes with an exponentially low error probability. This finding implies that even in scenarios where an eavesdropper possesses a channel with only minimal, non-negligible capacity, a legitimate receiver can decode messages with reliability approaching one. Furthermore, we present a practical coding scheme that achieves this near-optimal performance using a finite number of channel transmissions.

We investigate how the transport distance of a driven, damped, and noise-affected dynamical system scales with the driving force $F$, specifically in the weak driving regime where $F \ll F_c$ and $F_c$ marks the threshold for the onset of chaotic dynamics. In the absence of noise, the system exhibits a constant drift velocity $v \sim F$; however, introducing noise results in transport distance $x$ that is independent of $F$ when noise amplitude is large, but follows a distinct scaling when noise is small. Specifically, for small noise, the distance $x$ scales as $F^{2/3}$ in systems with linear restoring forces and as $F^{1/2}$ in those with quadratic potentials. These theoretical predictions are validated through numerical simulations.

This study proposes a novel method for impulse response estimation via local projections that utilizes additive regression models to concurrently capture non-linear patterns and temporal variation in dynamic effects. The approach, termed "impulse response estimation via adaptable local projections" (IR-ALP), adapts the coefficient estimation of standard linear projections to adaptively reflect time-evolving behaviors and non-linear structures inherent in data. Under mild conditions, the asymptotic properties of the proposed method are established, and numerical simulations demonstrate its superior performance compared to conventional linear and additive models. Finally, the method's effectiveness is validated through an analysis of US macroeconomic data.

This work investigates the angular momentum of a charge $q$ confined within a uniform magnetic field $\mathbf{B} = B\hat{z}$ and subjected to a constant electric field $\mathbf{E} = E\hat{z}$. The analysis reveals that the electromagnetic stress-energy tensor exhibits a non-zero angular momentum density, which, upon volume integration, yields a non-vanishing total angular momentum. This quantum void angular momentum arises from the interaction between the charge's electric field and the externally applied magnetic field. Furthermore, the study demonstrates that the magnitude of this angular momentum scales linearly with the charge's radial distance from the axis, $r$.

Named entity classification (NEC) is a pivotal task within information extraction, yet existing approaches often rely on heuristic strategies that fail to fully leverage the hierarchical structure inherent in entity types. This paper introduces a novel hyperbolic space-based framework designed to enhance NEC accuracy by embedding entity types within a hyperbolic manifold and employing iterative refinement to progressively narrow candidate sets. Specifically, we utilize the Poincaré ball representation to construct a structured taxonomy of entities. Our proposed method, FGNET-RH, employs a feature-guided mechanism that refines predictions at each hyperbolic layer, allowing the model to leverage hierarchical relationships to filter out non-matching candidates. Empirical results demonstrate that FGNET-RH significantly surpasses state-of-the-art methods on the FGNET-RH dataset, achieving a 2.1% improvement in F1 score. Furthermore, comprehensive ablation studies validate the effectiveness of our hyperbolic space formulation and the proposed refinement strategy.

This study focuses on the normalized forms of the second Hankel determinants, expressed as $h_2,2(f) = \frac{a_3a_2^2 - a_4a_1^2}{a_2^2}$, for functions within the class $\mathcal{U}$, which consists of close-to-convex functions sharing the same initial Maclaurin coefficients as the convex functions of order one. Specifically, we establish upper bounds for the sharp upper bounds of $h_2,2(f)$ for all $f \in \mathcal{U}$. Additionally, we derive upper bounds for the sharp upper bounds of the same expression for the broader class $\mathcal{S}$ of univalent functions.

Cloud data centers (CDCs) are increasingly central to the modern economy, yet their high energy consumption and associated carbon emissions necessitate a shift toward sustainable operations. To achieve this, cloud providers are actively integrating green energy sources, such as wind and solar, into their power supply. However, the intermittent nature of renewables creates challenges in meeting consistent Quality of Service (QoS) levels. This paper introduces a novel pre-partitioning load distribution strategy designed to optimize resource allocation within green cloud data centers. The primary objective is to minimize energy consumption while maintaining QoS standards. The study evaluates the proposed method against two existing approaches: a random distribution and a traditional optimal scheduling algorithm. Results indicate that the pre-partitioning strategy achieves a 10% reduction in energy usage compared to the optimal approach and a 20% reduction relative to the random distribution method.

We introduce a novel deep learning framework designed to forecast game equilibria, even when the underlying game rules are unknown. This approach leverages historical interaction data from multiple agents to anticipate future equilibrium states. Central to our model is a Fixed Point Network (FPN) capable of learning the best response functions of the game. We demonstrate that, under mild assumptions, learning these functions enables the prediction of Nash equilibria. Furthermore, we prove that the FPN architecture is universal, capable of approximating the game's equilibrium payoffs with arbitrary precision. Empirical results across various benchmarks illustrate the FPN's ability to successfully predict equilibria in complex scenarios where the game structure has not been explicitly provided.

This work introduces a new upper limit on the causal influence of one random variable over another, grounded in the non-negative entropy of conditional probability distributions. We demonstrate that, for many causal structures, the aggregate influence across all potential target variables is strictly bounded by the source variable's entropy. Additionally, we establish an algorithm capable of calculating the precise upper bound for influence within any specific causal model. These theoretical results are utilized to derive novel constraints on causal impacts within domains such as genetics and social science, and the proposed bound is shown to be computationally tractable even when applied to high-dimensional causal Bayesian networks.

This study addresses predictive surveillance for linear time-invariant systems subjected to stealthy attacks. We demonstrate that if the system matrix is undetectable, the system's future trajectory cannot be accurately predicted even with full access to the system model. To resolve this limitation, we propose a novel data-driven method that utilizes a minimal quantity of observations to enable effective prediction. Furthermore, we establish a specific condition guaranteeing the accurate prediction of future system states. Finally, we validate our findings through a case study involving a power network.

This study presents GAE-ISumm, an unmonitored, neural, graph-based summarization model designed for Indian languages. GAE-ISumm employs a Graph Attention Encoder-Decoder architecture to generate concise summaries from lengthy documents. Unlike many existing approaches, this system requires no pre-trained language models or external word embeddings, relying instead solely on character n-gram features. This dependency on minimal resources allows for the efficient training of the model on small datasets. The research evaluates the model's performance across three Indian languages—Marathi, Malayalam, and Tamil—using the Indic Summ benchmark. Experimental results demonstrate that GAE-ISumm achieves a significant improvement in ROUGE scores compared to the baseline, with gains of 1.0, 1.2, and 1.4 respectively. Furthermore, the model's ability to generalize across different languages highlights its potential for cross-lingual summarization tasks.

This paper examines two specific conditions applicable to s-rings: (N1) every s-module associated with a thick s-simple ring is Noetherian, and (N2) the ring's center constitutes a one-dimensional one-dimensional local domain with residue field of order two, a condition implying that all s-modules of (N) are unital. It is further demonstrated that condition (N1) is equivalent to a combination of (N2) and a condition (S): the set of idempotent elements within the s-ring forms a semigroup that is both finite and locally commutative.

This study investigates the feasibility of detecting hidden companions around the accelerating stars HD 11426, HD 11435, HD 11429, HD 11427, and HD 11426. We conducted a comprehensive search for periodic signals in the Gaia DR2 proper motions and parallax data for these systems. While no periodic variations were identified, we established upper limits on the masses and orbital semi-major axes of potential unseen partners. These constraints are sufficiently tight to influence future exoplanet occurrence studies and investigations into the prevalence of binary systems.

Variational Autoencoders (VAEs) are widely used in machine learning, typically employing a standard Gaussian prior for latent variables. This paper introduces a novel VAE variant that utilizes a square-shaped (uniform) prior, accompanied by regularizing mechanisms designed to enhance performance. The authors provide a theoretical analysis of the proposed model's convergence and establish an empirical comparison demonstrating that this new architecture outperforms conventional VAEs across multiple datasets.

The proliferation of Internet of Things (IoT) devices has created significant security and privacy challenges, particularly within the home environment. This study introduces a novel private blockchain architecture designed to enhance security and efficiency in intelligent home monitoring. The proposed system empowers homeowners to restrict device access, regulate data transmission, and establish specific access controls for device information. Furthermore, the framework incorporates an optimized routing protocol that leverages private blockchain capabilities to select the most reliable transmission paths, thereby minimizing latency and enhancing overall network performance.

This paper introduces a deep learning-based approach for jointly optimizing the quantization of L-values and the generation of soft bit decisions in soft decoders. The proposed method employs a neural network to generate quantized L-value representations that maintain a minimal bit-error rate (BER) while maximizing the accuracy of the soft information fed into the decoder. This scheme was evaluated on convolutional and LDPC-coded systems within an additive white Gaussian noise (AWGN) channel environment. The results demonstrate that the learned quantization scheme achieves BER performance nearly identical to that of traditional binary quantization, but with significantly fewer bits required.

This study introduces a new approach to the longstanding challenge of determining whether a directed acyclic graph (DIGraph) possesses an upward planar embedding. While previous research has largely focused on specific subclasses, our method offers a unified framework that delivers the first general upper bound for this problem. By adapting a topological sorting technique, we generate a permutation of the vertices along a horizontal axis; a linear-time algorithm is then employed to verify if the corresponding vertical edges can be drawn without crossings. Our findings establish that the existence of a subgraph with $O(n)$ edges enables an $\tilde{O}(n^{11/5})$-time verification, improving to $\tilde{O}(n^{5/3})$ if the graph is known to be bipartite. Furthermore, we demonstrate that finding the minimum number of edges removed to achieve upward planarity is NP-hard, even for bipartite graphs with a maximum degree of three. Additionally, we present an algorithm capable of computing an upward planar subgraph with at most a $1.5$-approximation ratio in polynomial time.

Crowdsourced data is increasingly common in machine learning, yet it often suffers from inherent inaccuracies. This study examines a dataset from a recent study on the 2016 US Presidential Election, which was annotated by thousands of participants. Our analysis reveals that most crowd worker errors stem from genuine ignorance rather than deliberate deception. To address this, we propose an ensemble modeling strategy that incorporates a "human softmax" to represent individual annotator confidence levels. By integrating these distributions, we develop a method to filter out uncertainty from reliable annotators and refine the model for uncertain cases. Our results demonstrate that this approach significantly outperforms traditional methods that rely solely on annotator agreement metrics.

We demonstrate that the spectrum of the transfer operator for a skew-product semiflow, constructed from a hyperbolic PDE and a time-periodic perturbation, can be reduced by adjusting the perturbation's period. This finding provides compelling evidence for the existence of a maximal Liouville exponent associated with such semiflows.

We demonstrate that for a specific class of nonlocal games, determining the value is solvable. This category includes maximally entangled states that are maximally correlated, which encompasses the Popescu-Rohrlich scenario. In these scenarios, the players' joint strategy is a stochastic matrix, and their individual inputs and outputs follow a fixed ordering. The games are considered intertwined when the sum of a player's input and output yields the same result regardless of the other player's input. The authors present a method to determine the optimal mixed strategy for participants in local contests involving a fixed set of intertwined states, which in turn allows for the computation of the games' value. This approach relies on solving a semi-infinite linear program, where the infinite constraints are approximated by finite sets to generate a sequence of lower bounds converging to the true value. The study also examines the complexity of these games, finding that while the number of constraints in local contests typically grows exponentially with the size of the state, the number of variables increases only polynomially. This structural advantage is absent in local contests utilizing arbitrary, non-predefined entangled states.

This paper partially replicates the work of Li et al. (2019), which introduced a novel algorithm for automatically duplicating failed tests in embedded systems through a guided genetic procedure. The original study evaluated the method on a set of embedded crash bugs drawn from the QEMU project. Our findings indicate that the replication efforts were successful. Our group developed our own implementation using the same genetic algorithm and employed identical parameters as the authors. We executed the same set of 20 test cases with the same initial seed for each. The results show that our tool successfully duplicated all 20 failures, matching the performance of the original tool exactly.

Using high-resolution scanning SQUID microscopy, we have mapped the vortex lattice in optimally doped YBa$_2$Cu$_3$O$_{6.93}$ under magnetic fields of 1.5 T and 3.5 T applied parallel to the $c$-axis. Our findings reveal that the vortex arrangement is not uniform across the entire field range; instead, a distinct transition occurs at approximately 2.5 T, shifting from a triangular lattice to a square one. This behavior is interpreted as evidence for anisotropic vortex interactions, which are likely driven by the superconductor's intrinsic crystal structure.
