We introduce a versatile framework for zero-, few-, and no-shot analysis tasks that leverages the contextualized representations of a pretrained language model. By utilizing a cluster-based scoring mechanism, our approach generates class scores for input instances. We validate this method across multiple domains, including text classification, clustering, and a new task we term "cluster-based scoring." Specifically, in cluster-based scoring, the objective is to assign each item to an appropriate category by identifying the most similar cluster without relying on labeled examples. Our results demonstrate that the method performs competitively in both text classification and standard clustering scenarios. Furthermore, it achieves state-of-the-art performance on the cluster-based scoring task, particularly when utilizing zero-shot strategies.

This paper introduces a paper on the development of an open-source Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) system for the German language. It details the methodology for developing this system, covering the construction of a speech corpus, the training of a neural network, and the implementation of a decoder. Furthermore, the study evaluates the system's performance using the Common German Speech Benchmark (GEB) and compares these findings with results from the German Speech Challenge (GSC).

This study presents a comprehensive investigation of 30 candidate Be stars within the 30 Doradus (N36) nebula, utilizing multi-epoch optical spectra and photometric data. The analysis reveals that 26 of these objects exhibit Be star characteristics, with the remaining four classified as non-Be stars. The 26 Be stars are categorized into two distinct groups: 14 in the "Be high" (BeH) category and 12 in the "Be low" (BeL) category. The distinction between these groups lies in their emission line profiles; BeH stars display single-lined profiles, whereas BeL stars show double-lined profiles. Notably, the majority of double-lined profiles are associated with emission lines in the H$\alpha$ region. Furthermore, the study examines the correlation between emission line strength and stellar rotation velocity, noting that the relationship is not uniform across all stars. Instead, a correlation emerges only when restricting the sample to stars rotating below 200 km s$^{-1}$.

In recent years, the proliferation of internet-connected devices has led to a significant rise in the online dissemination of non-standardized text. To counter this, inverse text standardization (ITS)—a process that converts such non-standardized text back into properly formatted standard text—has become a crucial area of study. While current ITS research predominantly relies on data-driven approaches, there is a notable scarcity of publicly available datasets. This paper introduces a novel data augmentation strategy designed to generate synthetic training data for ITS tasks. Experimental results demonstrate that incorporating this augmented data yields marked improvements in model performance. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that the proposed method is versatile, successfully extending to related text processing domains beyond ITS.

This paper establishes the Faber-Krahn inequality concerning the Hermitian operator subject to Robin boundary conditions defined on the sphere. Additionally, we derive optimal constants for domains involving spherical sectors under the same operator and boundary conditions. As extensions, the Hermite operator's Robin eigenvalues are analyzed within these geometries.

Non-exchangeable processes, which lack stationarity and isotropy, are frequently employed to model intricate natural phenomena. This work introduces a new class of kernels designed for such processes: the non-exchangeable tangent kernel (NFT-K). This framework extends the well-established family of tangent kernels used for exchangeable processes, specifically those based on Laplace-type functions. We demonstrate that the resulting NFT-K can be interpreted as a neural network kernel and proven to be positive semidefinite. Furthermore, we examine the characteristics of these kernels and outline a methodology for their empirical estimation. Finally, we validate the approach through experiments on synthetic data and within the context of spatio-temporal forecasting.

We investigate how non-equilibrium one-dimensional point-gap topological systems are affected by correlated disorder. Our findings indicate that, in contrast to the depolarizing channel, correlated noise can dismantle the point-gap topology. We demonstrate that, unlike the depolarizing case where the bulk point gaps remain robust against disorder, this protection is fragile and can be stripped away by the introduction of correlated noise.

This study examines the incorporation of social speaker traits into synthetic speech. We introduce a novel methodology for embedding these traits by leveraging a pre-trained speech synthesis model capable of generating speech from text-to-speech prompts. Our approach involves creating an encoder-driven architecture that maps trait values to a latent space, effectively conditioning speech generation. Experimental results demonstrate that the system successfully synthesizes speech reflecting specified social traits. Furthermore, analyses reveal that the latent representations encode these social attributes in a continuous and interpretable manner.

We introduce a dark matter (DM) framework grounded in modular $\Delta$ symmetry, featuring a single DM candidate that forms part of a complex scalar doublet alongside a fermion. This model is extended by incorporating a $U(1)_{B-L}$ gauge symmetry, which spontaneously breaks to yield the observed dark matter relic abundance and generate neutrino masses. The framework naturally accounts for the large $\bar{\theta}_{13}$ angle and the observed non-zero neutrino mass spectrum. The model's parameter space is constrained by current experimental data, including dark matter relic density measurements, perturbativity bounds, electroweak precision tests, Higgs boson observables, and neutrino oscillation data. The resulting predictions for the effective neutrino mass ($m_{\beta\beta}$) and the effective $\bar{\theta}_{ee}$ fall within the reach of upcoming experiments such as KATRIN and the neutrinoless double-beta decay searches.

This study investigates the collective dynamics of triaxial nuclei within the framework of the modified Schrödinger equation derived from Heisenberg's uncertainty principle, which includes a minimum length. We employ a potential energy surface based on the Nilsson model to determine the corresponding potential fields. Solving the associated differential equation yields the differential equation for radial motion. To address this, we apply the Laplace transform method, obtaining explicit analytical expressions for both radial and angular components. Subsequently, we calculate the energy eigenvalues and corresponding wave functions for triaxial nuclei. Finally, we analyze how the minimum length parameter influences collective nuclear motion and discuss the implications of these findings.

This paper introduces multiple new methods for constructing and creating polyphase complementary sets (PCSs), specifically utilizing symmetries, complex conjugates, and the Hadamard product. A novel generalization of the Hadamard product is defined to define new families of complementary sets, leading to a new class known as $H_{poly}$. Furthermore, several new creation techniques for $H_{poly}$-sets are developed, and a method for generating additional $H_{real}$-sets is provided. Finally, a new family of complementary sets is defined based on the Hadamard product of real Golay complementary sequences.

Detecting local modifications in a scene is a fundamental challenge across various computer vision tasks, including image forensics, security, and surveillance. While current methods have largely focused on natural images, hyperspectral imagery (HSI) offers significantly higher dimensionality and detail, making it a more difficult yet critical area for detection. This paper introduces an unsupervised deep learning framework capable of detecting local changes in hyperspectral images. The approach utilizes a convolutional autoencoder to extract latent features, which are subsequently aggregated through a feature combination strategy. The entire model is trained in an unsupervised manner, eliminating the need for extensive labeled datasets. The method's efficacy is validated using an unsupervised classification technique to identify local alterations in hyperspectral images of both synthetic and real-world scenarios.

This study investigates molecular fluids to determine the relationship between residual entropy and viscosity, utilizing a statistical mechanics framework to calculate reduced entropy and a molecular dynamics simulation to determine reduced viscosity. The analysis reveals a robust, nearly universal logarithmic relationship between these two properties, which holds across diverse fluid models and temperature-density conditions. Notably, this relationship persists even when molecular fluids possess residual entropy close to that of simple hard spheres, provided they maintain significant orientational ordering. The findings further indicate that fluid viscosity correlates with residual entropy through the same logarithmic function observed in self-diffusion coefficients. Consequently, this suggests that the logarithmic link between viscosity and self-diffusion is not merely coincidental but stems from the shared dependence of both transport properties on residual entropy.

We explore a cyclic cosmological framework where the universe undergoes repeated phases of expansion and contraction. In this model, the universe alternates between a classical regime and a quantum one, with phase transitions occurring at the boundary between these states. While classical phases resemble the standard $\Lambda$CDM cosmology, quantum phases are characterized by a specific effective Lagrangian. We demonstrate that within a single cycle, the universe naturally transitions between these two Lagrangians. Furthermore, the model offers a theoretical explanation for the cosmological constant problem and the nature of dark matter.

The Invariant-set hypothesis offers a superdeterministic, non-local explanation for quantum phenomena, positing that specific dynamical systems evolve deterministically within phase space, where only trajectories confined to geometrically invariant sets yield observable reality. This article introduces a hidden-variable model designed to test the hypothesis by analyzing photon polarization correlations in a Bell scenario. By employing this model, we can replicate quantum mechanical predictions for entanglement experiments without relying on standard assumptions such as parameter independence, parameter determinism, or realism.

Keyphrase detection, a well-established Natural Language Processing (NLP) task, involves locating key short phrases within a document. Although it has broad applications, current research predominantly relies on large-scale neural architectures that are computationally expensive and unsuitable for environments with limited resources, such as those found in the Internet of Things (IoT). This study investigates the viability of deploying neural networks for keyphrase detection on highly constrained IoT hardware. We evaluate several models, including BERT, Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), and Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs), across three specific devices: a Raspberry Pi Zero W, a BeagleBone Black, and a Google Coral. Our findings indicate that BERT and RNNs are not only infeasible for these devices but also fail to meet real-time processing requirements. In contrast, we demonstrate that a lightweight CNN can successfully execute the task on the Google Coral, delivering both high accuracy and efficient performance.

The paper examines the critical dimer model on a two-dimensional square lattice in the presence of a background gauge field, a setup that mirrors the lattice regularization of a massless Dirac fermion theory. We analyze the relationship between the fermionic and dimer descriptions, demonstrating that the latter captures the fundamental physics of the former. Specifically, we demonstrate that the chiral anomaly emerges from the non-invariance of the dimer partition function's normalization factor under local gauge transformations. Additionally, we show that the expectation values of the fermion current and the chiral density in the Dirac framework correspond exactly to those of the dimer variables.

Group Lasso serves as a popular high-dimensional variable selection technique by leveraging prior knowledge of group structures to perform selection within those structures rather than at the individual level. Although effective when structures are defined by continuous features, it struggles with nominal variables because traditional distance metrics, such as Euclidean distance, are ill-suited for handling discrete categories. This study introduces a novel approach to constructing distance metrics specifically for group nominal variables, which forms the basis of a new variable selection method. We demonstrate through simulations that our technique outperforms existing methods in high-dimensional settings involving nominal data.

The hypervisor is a crucial component in modern virtualization architectures, yet its ability to guarantee real-time performance in mixed-criticality embedded environments remains a significant challenge. To address this, we introduce a new hypervisor named T-Visor, designed specifically to ensure hard real-time execution by leveraging hardware virtualization support. T-Visor utilizes the Intel VT-x framework to create a streamlined architecture that minimizes overhead and guarantees precise timer access for both guest operating systems and bare-metal tasks. Furthermore, the system employs a paravirtualization technique to reduce context-switching delays. Experimental results from an actual embedded board demonstrate that T-Visor achieves superior performance compared to existing hypervisors, delivering less than 100 nanoseconds of context switching while maintaining strict real-time capabilities.

We introduce a novel minimal answer strategy for stitching 360-degree panoramas, designed to eliminate the need for external sensors by relying on gravity. Our system captures images using a single camera and a two-axis gimbal; by recording the gimbal's orientation during each shot, we can align images based on these directional priors. This approach bypasses the computationally heavy feature matching and bundle adjustment processes typically required. Instead, we employ a neural network to generate a compact set of control points for each panorama, which a subsequent network refines into an image warp. Experimental results demonstrate that this framework achieves high-quality stitching with only two input images and minimal human intervention.

Chimera states are characterized by the coexistence of coherent and incoherent dynamics among identical nonlocally-coupled oscillators. This study investigates chimeras arising from a system comprising two large, equally sized, and homogeneously coupled oscillators, where each oscillator possesses a uniform random coupling offset. The heterogeneity in offsets is constrained to a narrow range, ensuring that the coherent cluster maintains zero internal phase variance. The analysis reveals that the degree of offset variation significantly influences the Chimera regime, potentially yielding two distinct states: a chimera featuring two spatially uniform groups or one with an additional phase gradient within the synchronized cluster. The findings are substantiated through both numerical simulations and analytical derivations.

Resilience in cyber-physical systems (CPS) refers to the capability to maintain essential functions despite attacks or failures. While resilient control strategies are typically developed through offline analysis, this paper introduces a data-driven reinforcement learning (RL) method for generating resilient policies. The proposed approach integrates a probabilistic, data-driven model of the environment, which is trained concurrently with the agent's policy. To assess resilience, the method employs a probabilistic attack model to simulate potential adversarial actions. The objective is to learn a policy that minimizes attack-induced damage while simultaneously learning a model capable of predicting attack outcomes. The underlying algorithm combines policy gradient techniques with sequential Monte Carlo methods, such as Sequential Monte Carlo Heuristic (PMC), to enable joint optimization of both the policy and the environmental model. The effectiveness of this framework is validated on two case studies: a nonlinear vehicle dynamics system and a water treatment facility.

We establish Milnor-style higher slice algebras as the homotopy groups of the higher slice spectra developed by Hill-Hopkins Ravenel. Subsequently, we apply a Bousfield localization technique to present multilayer diagrams as an alternative computational method for determining these higher slice rings.

In chaotic quantum systems, the von Neumann entropy of a subsystem within a canonical ensemble surpasses the thermodynamic average by an extent proportional to the subsystem's area. This phenomenon, known as area-law violation, mirrors the behavior of entanglement entropy in pure states, which is governed by the Page curve. We demonstrate that this violation persists in the von Neumann entanglement entropy of subsystems within random tensor networks, even when the subsystem size is significantly smaller than half the total system size. Specifically, the entropy exceeds the trivial thermal expectation by a quantity scaling with the smaller dimension of the area. We attribute this effect to the refraction of entanglement lines at the system's boundaries. Furthermore, we show that this mechanism explains the emergence of the area-law violation in the thermal state of a quantum black hole.

In the realm of complex systems, the capacity to gather and process data is essential for survival. While physical or chemical entities can endure brief data exchanges through delicate, short-lived states, the ability to persist significantly longer necessitates a mechanism to safeguard this data against inherent noise. This study demonstrates that systems exhibiting stochastic dynamics can support such robust information storage through a far more efficient approach: by leveraging heritable traits in their own dynamic evolution to maintain a persistent signal indefinitely. This phenomenon, illustrated using a minimal model of a traveling agent, reveals that even a solitary individual can transmit substantial knowledge across multiple generations without relying on specialized hardware or the high fidelity of reproduction. This finding expands the theoretical framework of information storage, suggesting a more accessible pathway for persistent memory within the vast and varied landscape of natural systems.

This paper investigates the three-dimensional generalized H\'{e}non map, a mathematical model capable of producing chaotic behavior across a broad range of parameters. We introduce a computational approach to calculate the map's three-dimensional inverse function and demonstrate its application in generating the three-dimensional Julia set. Additionally, we describe a method for constructing three-dimensional surfaces representing the map's three-dimensional surfaces of attraction. We further illustrate how these surfaces of attraction can be utilized to create three-dimensional surfaces depicting the map's three-dimensional surfaces of repulsion. Finally, we present a technique for generating the three-dimensional surface of the map's three-dimensional surface of recurrence.

This article examines the spread of hook lengths in partitions where these values can be expressed as the product of two or three integers. For partition sizes up to $10^6$, we calculate the relative frequencies of these distributions and offer conjectures regarding their asymptotic behaviors. Additionally, we identify specific patterns in the cases of $n=3$ and demonstrate how our findings for this scenario can be utilized to derive an asymptotic expansion for the count of such partitions.

We investigate a two-component Bose-Einstein condensate described by the Gross-Pitaevskii equations, analyzing both the full model and a simplified approximation. We demonstrate that when intercomponent interactions are sufficiently strong, the system exhibits a nonlinear quantum switch. This phenomenon is characterized by the emergence of two stable quantum ground states, where the quantum realm of one field transitions into that of the other based on the initial amplitude of the second field. Furthermore, our analysis reveals the presence of traveling waves that facilitate this switching process.

We examine the connection between asymptotic symmetries at null infinity and the S-matrix, focusing on two-dimensional soft graviton theories. We demonstrate that the BMS algebra, when augmented with a central extension, emerges as the zero-mode sector of the Dirac-quantized Hamiltonian governing soft graviton dynamics. Furthermore, the zero-mode sector of the S-matrix, derived from a specific class of two-dimensional soft graviton actions, is shown to correspond to the exponential generator of this same BMS algebra plus its core representation. In three dimensions, the analysis extends to the soft graviton sector of the Einstein-Hilbert action, revealing a similar underlying structure.

This study introduces an innovative neural ensemble architecture designed to process online streams of tasks indefinitely. By leveraging task-specific gating mechanisms, the model dynamically regulates the activation of a fixed set of shared weights, enabling continuous adaptation to new challenges without forgetting previous ones. Empirical evaluations on both synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate that this approach achieves superior performance compared to current state-of-the-art methods. Furthermore, the research offers a theoretical analysis of the model's behavior, including an examination of how the distribution of these task gates influences learning capabilities.

We introduce a broadened definition of a pair consisting of a closed, connected, oriented surface and its enclosing volume, applicable to any compact set in $\mathbb{R}^4$. This framework allows us to construct a canonical family of smooth, conformally equivalent metrics on the region bounded by such sets. Specifically, we demonstrate the existence of a unique metric within this family that is flat when equipped with the induced measure derived from the surface's geometry. This canonical flat metric serves as a powerful tool for defining measures on compact sets within $\mathbb{R}^4$. We illustrate the utility of this approach by recovering existing results concerning the isoperimetric inequality and Shapo's conjecture in $\mathbb{R}^4$.

This paper constructs several families of complete permutation functions of degree $q^2+q+1$ and $q^2+2q+1$ defined over the finite field extension $\mathbb{F}_{q^3}$. Additionally, we present new examples of complete permutation functions of degree $q^2+q+1$ over $\mathbb{F}_{q^3}$ and provide novel examples of complete permutation functions of degree $q^2+2q+1$ over the same field.

This study introduces a new approach to classifying adult intestinal worms into three species—*Ascaris lumbricoides*, *Hookworm*, and *Trichuris trichiura*—utilizing a Deep Belief Network (DBN). The proposed method involves extracting image features through the GoogleNet convolutional neural network (CNN) and training a DBN with these representations. The dataset comprises 1,000 images for each species, sourced from the ISIC 2017 Grand Challenge Intestinal Worm Categorization track. The results indicate that the hybrid CNN-DBN architecture outperforms other established methods, achieving an accuracy of 99.99% and an F1-score of 99.98%.

This study examines the optimal reinsurance and investment strategies for two competing insurers operating within a shared financial market. The insurers, who compete for a fixed market share, employ distinct underwriting and investment approaches. Their collective surplus is modeled using a regime-switching process driven by a Markov chain, where the underlying financial market dynamics and individual risk exposures are influenced by simultaneous jumps and diffusion noise. Specifically, each insurer's surplus incorporates a Poisson process to represent claim arrivals, alongside an investment portfolio allocated between a risk-free asset and a risky asset. The objective is to determine optimal investment and reinsurance policies that maximize the expected utility terminal surplus for both insurers, evaluated under a constant absolute risk aversion (CARA) framework. The analysis employs the stochastic analysis method combined with a verification theorem to establish the existence and uniqueness of the optimal strategies. Furthermore, the study derives closed-form expressions for these optimal strategies and the corresponding maximum expected utility values.

This study introduces a PID controller designed to ensure stable and smooth vertical takeoff and landing (VTOL) drone operations, with a specific focus on maintaining a constant altitude. The primary objective is to regulate the aircraft's vertical speed and acceleration to remain within minimal, steady bounds. To achieve this, the paper presents a novel dual-stage architecture: a primary feedback loop utilizing a Proportional-Integral-Derivative (PID) controller for altitude management, and a secondary feedforward loop engineered to actively suppress vertical speed and acceleration deviations. The derivative component of the feedback mechanism is implemented via a novel acceleration estimator, which leverages the Stochastic Dual Asynchronous Simplex Algorithm (SDA) to solve the vertical position optimization problem inherent in minimum-time control. This approach offers a significant advantage over traditional numerical differentiation methods by eliminating the need for finite difference approximations, thus enhancing estimation accuracy. Furthermore, the feedforward stage employs a Genetic Filter (GF) to predict and counteract anticipated disturbances. The efficacy of this hybrid control framework is validated through experimental results.

This study employs a dispersive analysis of low-energy pion-nucleon scattering to derive a model-independent, analytic representation of the $s$-wave isospin amplitudes. By integrating experimental data with a rigorous mathematical framework, the research establishes the fundamental constraints on these interactions, offering significant implications for chiral perturbation theory and lattice QCD studies.

This paper details the reconstruction of particle tracks within the outermost layer of the CMS Phase-1 pixel detector, which CMS utilized following its upgrade. This layer features a new readout system designed to enhance tracking capabilities and mitigate radiation damage. We present the performance outcomes of the edge track reconstruction within this layer and evaluate various strategies for handling layers with limited coverage. Furthermore, we introduce the edge track reconstruction algorithm and provide a comprehensive examination of its parameters.

We present a study utilizing the Hyper Suprime-Cam Wide Survey (HSC-SSP) to classify the morphologies of active galactic nucleus (AGN) host galaxies with redshifts $z<1$. Our dataset comprises 1,000 AGN host candidates identified through X-ray observations from the XMM-Newton satellite, which were matched to HSC imaging data. We employed the SExtractor tool to derive galaxy structural parameters and utilized the Galaxy Zoo-Machine Learning (GZML) model to assign morphological types. Our analysis reveals that the majority of these AGN hosts are disk galaxies, with only a minority classified as ellipticals. Furthermore, we examined the relationship between the morphological type and the X-ray luminosity of the central AGN. We observed that elliptical galaxies tend to harbor more luminous AGNs compared to disk galaxies, a relationship that strengthens at higher luminosities. This trend is likely driven by the fact that massive elliptical galaxies are more prone to hosting high-luminosity AGNs, a selection effect rather than a direct physical correlation.

We investigate the phase-space profile of short-range correlations (SRCs) within atomic nuclei by analyzing two-body momentum distributions alongside Wigner functions. Our findings reveal that while the radial structure of these SRCs remains consistent regardless of the nuclear environment, their characteristic angular profile is highly sensitive to it. Specifically, the anisotropy observed in the derived Wigner functions is driven by nuclear deformation, whereas the overall phase-space profile is governed primarily by the total nuclear mass. These results offer a robust framework for interpreting recent experimental data on sub-saturation momentum two-body correlations in deformed nuclei.

This study introduces a method for generating complex-valued representations of images and graph data, utilizing complex-valued neural networks to classify these multi-modal datasets. The primary motivation stems from the observation that complex numbers naturally encode both magnitude and phase, offering richer information capacity than their binary or real-number counterparts. The core contribution is a novel architecture that extends complex-valued deep learning techniques to handle images and graphs simultaneously. The model's performance is evaluated against established baselines, demonstrating competitive results across multiple tasks. The codebase is publicly available at https://github.com/robin-lee/cde.

The saturation of parton densities in small-x regimes is a fundamental aspect of QCD, with its significance extending from the interpretation of deep inelastic ep scattering to the dynamics of heavy nucleus collisions. This overview outlines the historical context of this phenomenon and its theoretical foundations, specifically focusing on the nonlinear evolution of parton densities at small-x and the concept of geometric scaling. The discussion concludes by examining experimental signatures of saturation and geometric scaling within both ep scattering and heavy nucleus collisions.

We investigate the abundance spread observed in low-metallicity stars by examining the chemical abundances of 1,100 stars with metallicities ranging from -1.5 to -0.5 dex, utilizing spectroscopic data from the APOGEE survey. Our analysis reveals that this spread is most pronounced in elements produced by massive stars (e.g., Mg, Si, Ca) and least significant in those synthesized by intermediate-mass stars (e.g., Na, Al). Furthermore, we find that the spread in these intermediate-mass products is more prominent in stars with lower metallicities and higher surface gravities. These findings indicate that the observed abundance variations in low-metallicity stars primarily reflect differences in the chemical yields of massive stars, while also implying that the observed spread in intermediate-mass products is largely driven by measurement uncertainties.

This study introduces a novel toolkit designed to assess the sensitivity of machine learning models, offering a means to gauge the stability of variable importance estimates derived from these algorithms. Stability serves as a critical metric for evaluating the dependability of a variable's established significance. We demonstrate this toolkit through an application to financial literacy forecasting, utilizing data from the National Financial Education Coalition. Our findings reveal that while machine learning models can effectively predict financial literacy, their reliance on financial knowledge is surprisingly low in stability. This suggests that financial knowledge should not be considered a robust predictor, even if it appears significant in initial analyses.

This paper introduces a novel method for quantum machine learning that leverages the quantum state of a Superconducting QUantum Interference Device (SQUID). The proposed algorithm utilizes the SQUID's physical parameters as a quantum memory to store classical data labels and data values. Consequently, this approach allows for the execution of multiple matrix operations within a single two-level SQUID system. The efficacy of this learning algorithm is demonstrated through its application to the MNIST dataset.

This paper introduces and examines the novel concepts of pointwise semi-slant and distorted product submanifolds within the framework of nearly contact metric structures. We establish the necessary and sufficient conditions required for a nearly contact metric submanifolds to be classified as both a distorted product and a pointwise semi-slnd submanifolds. Furthermore, the study explores the relationships among various classes of pointwise semi-slnd submaniflds, specifically focusing on the distortions inherent in the structure.

The PALEOCCENE project aims to create a novel neutrino detection technique utilizing a 100-liter crystal enriched with germanium, leveraging the impact of nuclear recoils on the crystal's color centers. This study presents a thorough analysis of the primary background sources anticipated in PALEOCCENE, employing state-of-the-art Monte Carlo simulations to forecast recoil examination outcomes. We evaluate the sensitivity of this neutrino detection approach to various parameters, including the neutrino cross-section, recoil energy thresholds, and germanium enrichment levels. Furthermore, this work offers a comprehensive analysis of the neutrino recoil spectrum, providing a valuable resource for future neutrino detection initiatives.

This study investigates the dynamics of active colloidal particles within a stationary background fluid subjected to a spatially non-uniform activity field. We demonstrate that the resulting effective force acting on the moving particle is proportional to the first-order gradient of this activity field, with its magnitude and direction depending on the specific swim pressure profile of the particle. Furthermore, we examine the modifications to the effective diffusion coefficient and the associated noise structure. These findings are validated through numerical simulations, which also assess the influence of the swim pressure profile on the particle's mobility and its capacity to generate a directed drift in response to an activity gradient.

u=e^2/\hbar$ regime. Notably, it uncovers a new property of fractional quantum Hall systems: the existence of multiple magnetorotron branches. This mechanism accounts for the experimentally observed linear temperature dependence of longitudinal resistance in the $
u=5/2$ state and aligns with the theoretically predicted linear behavior associated with the $
u=1/3$ state under high magnetic fields.

Clustering constitutes a fundamental challenge in analyzing the spread of epidemics on contact networks, where the disease transmits from infected individuals to susceptible ones. This work introduces a geometric approach to modeling outbreak evolution, utilizing the concept of a "contagion radius" to define the set of susceptible nodes that could become infected given a specific initial set of cases. We demonstrate that this set expands continuously and exhibits a quasi-convex behavior within the configuration space of the network. Leveraging these properties, we develop a clustering algorithm that effectively identifies the most likely source of the outbreak. We validate this method's performance through simulations involving both synthetic networks and real-world data.

The processing of CMB temperature data from satellite missions like Planck involves smoothing the sky with Gaussian kernels to generate a maximum likelihood map. This procedure can inadvertently create artificial artifacts known as "X artifacts" near map origin points, which stem from the data processing sequence. This study examines the mechanisms behind these artifacts and demonstrates that they can be circumvented by adjusting the order of operations, specifically by applying pixelization before deconvolution rather than afterward. Furthermore, these artifacts are expected to be eliminated in the upcoming SMICA 2018 data release from Planck, as this upcoming processing pipeline is anticipated to utilize a revised approach.

Communication is a fundamental human ability, yet animals and individuals lacking speech often struggle to acquire complex, multi-step tasks. This research investigates how introducing language as a medium for social interaction can facilitate goal-directed learning in artificial agents. We specifically examine the challenge of language referential ambiguity, which arises when multiple objects in an environment match a given description. We propose that agents overcome this obstacle by utilizing shared knowledge of object referents as a regularizer during joint learning of both communication and behavior. Our findings demonstrate that this social pressure to maintain consistent references within groups leads agents to develop more sophisticated linguistic capabilities, enabling them to learn and execute multi-step tasks more effectively.

Quantum channel tomography is essential for characterizing how quantum states evolve, a process that can be computationally demanding for channels with large Hilbert spaces. This paper introduces a new tomographic approach termed shadow procedure tomography, which leverages classical data from specific measurements to reconstruct a channel's complete description through a procedure analogous to machine learning. The study outlines a tomographic protocol capable of estimating a chosen parameter of a channel using a number of measurements that is polynomial relative to the channel's Hilbert space dimension. The paper further explores the capabilities and constraints of this tomographic framework.

This paper introduces a new class of inequalities that bound the Cheeger constant in terms of planar convex shapes' isoperimetric ratio, with a focus on convex domains in $\mathbb{R}^n$. We establish a novel inequality applicable to all such shapes, with special emphasis on those possessing reflectional symmetry. Additionally, we outline a method for estimating the Cheeger constant of shapes with multiple local minima by utilizing inequalities derived from their individually separated minimal components.

This study addresses the challenge of optimizing flight paths for Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) to minimize energy usage while maintaining a specified endurance. To model this, we introduced a new framework that accounts for wind effects, atmospheric drag, UAV weight, and battery capacity. Utilizing the Oberett-Bliss equation, the framework enables the calculation of optimal velocity and corresponding altitude for any given flight path segment. Additionally, we developed a dynamic wind forecasting model capable of predicting wind patterns at various altitudes and locations. This model was validated using actual measurements from the NOAA buoy situated in the North Sea. Finally, we developed a dynamic programming algorithm designed to determine the most energy-efficient trajectory for a UAV operating within a defined 2D area.

We employ the renormalization group method to investigate the instability of bilayer graphene with Coulomb interactions, demonstrating that the system decomposes into three-body and four-body bound states. This breakdown occurs at the energy scale of the BCS gap, which is determined by the system's coupling constant. Our analysis reveals that the three-body bound state possesses a negative total energy, whereas the four-body state exists in resonance. Furthermore, the energy of the bound state correlates with the interaction strength; as the coupling constant increases, this energy rises.

We utilized scanning tunneling microscopy and angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy to examine the conformational states and electronic properties of Sc2TbN@C80 fullerene on an h-BN/Ni(111) substrate. The study reveals that the molecules initially adopt a single dominant conformer, which transforms into a mixture of multiple conformers as the temperature rises. This transition is attributed to the thermal excitation of the molecules from their ground conformational state to higher-energy excited conformer states. Furthermore, the analysis of spin- and angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy data indicates that the hybridization between the molecular orbitals of Sc2TbN@C80 and the nickel substrate remains consistent across varying temperatures.

The Internet of Things (IoT) is rapidly expanding, connecting billions of devices to the internet. These devices are characterized by their low cost, limited computational power, and minimal memory capacity. The primary objective for IoT is to transmit data to a central server for analysis, yet a significant hurdle remains: securing the communication channel between the device and the server. This paper introduces a novel lightweight encryption algorithm designed specifically for IoT applications. The proposed method leverages a novel approach to bitwise operations to achieve a superior balance of security and efficiency. Experimental results indicate that the algorithm offers enhanced security while maintaining high efficiency, surpassing existing methods.

This study introduces a sequential Bayesian trial formulation designed to optimize the parameters for an adaptive Ramsey sequence in trapped ions. Specifically, the optimization targets the estimation of the b-field's magnitude, which causes the qubit energy splitting. The proposed framework employs a likelihood function to evaluate parameter sets, which can be assessed via Bayesian methods to determine subsequent steps in the measurement process. The trial formulation is executed using both quantum and classical resources in an alternating cycle. The adaptive Ramsey sequence, realized through digital quantum simulation, leverages mid-circuit measurement and feed-forward capabilities of the IonQ system. The experimental results demonstrate that this adaptive approach significantly enhances estimation precision by a factor of 3.3 compared to a non-adaptive method using an equivalent number of resources. The study concludes that the proposed trial formulation offers a viable methodology for optimizing future adaptive protocols.

This study introduces Gromov Centrality (GCS), a novel approach to quantifying node importance in complex networks. Grounded in metric geometry, GCS leverages the triangle inequality surplus to assess centrality. The GCS metric is computationally efficient, requiring only the calculation of shortest paths, and offers a multi-scale perspective that captures both immediate local influence and broader global significance. By utilizing a continuous centrality spectrum, GCS can be fine-tuned to prioritize either local or global network dynamics. Furthermore, GCS demonstrates high versatility by adapting to diverse network structures, including directed and weighted connections. Empirical evaluations across various synthetic models and real-world datasets confirm that GCS exhibits strong predictive power for multiple node-specific attributes.

This work introduces a new theory of gravity built on the concept of azimuthal symmetry. We begin by examining the properties of null cones and their relation to light speed, followed by a discussion of spherical and cylindrical coordinate systems. We also explore the connection between space, time, and mass, alongside the principles of relativity and the equivalence principle. Furthermore, we analyze how mass and energy relate and introduce the fundamental postulates of our new gravitational framework.

We define the rigorous equivalence of collections of matrix pencils, a relationship that subsumes rigorous right and rigorous left equivalence individually. Our work centers on characterizing this relationship via the rigorous right invariant factor matrix, a structure we also utilize to establish both necessary and sufficient conditions for right invariant subspace majorization in the context of collections of matrix pencils.

We present a geometric formulation of T-duality for twisted tori, extending the framework established by Halmagyi, Hull, and Tolda within the context of string theory. This approach relies on the application of Courant algebroids, specifically those constructed as semi-direct products of the tangent bundle and exterior forms, which are then twisted by a 3-form and vector distribution characteristic of the twisted torus. Our derivation demonstrates the emergence of a dual twisted torus structure, achieved by inverting specific structural constants. Furthermore, we establish that the entire dualization process corresponds to a sequence of operations utilizing Lagrangian subbundles defined within a semi-direct product framework that incorporates both the exterior forms and the dualized tangent bundle.

This paper presents a quasi-polynomial time algorithm capable of embedding any $g$-gonal metric space into a tree structure of size bounded by $O(g^{O(1)} \log^{O(1)} n)$. This result improves upon the quasi-polynomial time, quasi-linear embedding of subgraph-free hyperbolic metric spaces previously established by Chepoi and V\'{a}rady [1]. Furthermore, we demonstrate that for any fixed genus $g$, such a subgraph-free hyperbolic metric space can be embedded into a planar graph with $O(n)$ vertices and treewidth $O(g^{O(1)} \log^{O(1)} n)$. These findings are applicable to the analysis of metric spaces derived from data sets, including those generated by neural networks and Euclidean distance graphs.

This paper investigates the long-term dynamics of strongly monotone discrete-time dynamical systems with smooth maps. We establish that the $\omega$-limit sets for generic initial conditions exhibit a consistent structure: they consist of a finite collection of periodic orbits interspersed with a continuum of invariant sets forming a measure-zero set. This finding extends the seminal work of de Vries (2009) on weakly contractive systems to the broader category of strongly monotone systems. Our proof relies on demonstrating that a specific generic property holds: every trajectory either converges to a periodic orbit or becomes trapped within an invariant set defined by a complex graph structure.

The variational quantum eigensolver (VQE) is a hybrid quantum-classical algorithm designed to determine the ground state energy of quantum systems. In this study, we introduce a modified VQE approach that leverages a single excitation to drive the adiabatic evolution of the quantum state. We demonstrate that this excitation-assisted variant achieves convergence to the ground state using fewer circuit gates than the standard algorithm. Our results indicate that the gate reduction is proportional to the energy gap between the ground state and the nearest excited state. We validate these findings through numerical simulations applied to hydrogen molecules and various lattice Hubbard models.

Addressing the challenge of generating high-quality outputs is a fundamental issue in deep learning. While deep generative models have achieved remarkable success in producing realistic data, they typically rely on optimizing parameters to maximize the likelihood of observed samples. This conventional approach often results in overly smooth outputs and a failure to capture the full data distribution. In this work, we introduce a novel strategy that leverages attention mechanisms within the encoder to extract meaningful information from unobserved samples. By employing this enhanced encoder, we can create more accurate generative models that better reflect the true distribution of data. Furthermore, we integrate a sophisticated decoding stage that utilizes attention mechanisms to synthesize high-quality outputs. This proposed framework has been validated on two prominent benchmarks—the CelebA dataset and the CIFAR-10 dataset—demonstrating superior performance compared to existing state-of-the-art methods.

The recent findings from the Hubble Space Telescope (H0SH0) regarding the Hubble constant ($H_0$) have created significant tension with Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB) predictions derived from the standard $\Lambda$CDM model. This "Hubble tension" might be resolved if a gravitational-wave background (GWB) from primordial inflation were detected, as such a GWB would increase the sound horizon at recombination ($r$), thereby lowering the inferred value of $H_0$ from CMB data. This study investigates the feasibility of detecting the inflationary GWB using the NANOGrav 12-yr data set, the H0SH0, and the Advanced LIGO-Virgo observatory. We demonstrate that NANOGrav's sensitivity to the inflationary GWB is comparable to that of the Laser Interferometer Space Antenna (LISA), which will operate in the future. If confirmed, the inflationary GWB would yield a predicted H0SH0 value of $H_0 = 67.6 \pm 1.4$ km s$^{-1}$ Mpc$^{-1}$, consistent with the CMB prediction. Furthermore, the Advanced LIGO-Virgo network could detect the inflationary GWB at a significance level of $5\sigma$ within the next decade.

This study reports the first observations of comet C/2015 ER61 (PanSTARRS) using the Atacama Compact Array (ACA) of the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA). Data were gathered on 12 April 2015 at a heliocentric distance of 2.8 AU, utilizing the 7 mm band to detect carbon monosulfide (CS) emissions. The analysis of these observations indicates that the coma of comet PanSTARRS is not uniform; rather, it is structured into two distinct source regions. The first region is located approximately 10 arcseconds from the nucleus, while the second extends to about 20 arcseconds. The spatial distribution of the CS gas suggests a distributed source mechanism, likely driven by the sublimation of a refractory CS ice mixed with dust. This finding challenges previous models of cometary activity, which typically assumed a point-source origin for outgassing. Furthermore, the study measured the expansion velocity of the coma at roughly 0.5 km/s.

This paper presents a straightforward and potent framework for the unsupervised speech modeling task. We utilize a sequence-to-sequence architecture incorporating attention, trained exclusively on an unsupervised corpus of speech. To differentiate between generated and actual audio samples, we introduce a discriminator that operates on both the time-domain waveform and the frequency-domain spectrogram. Experiments conducted on the TTS challenge benchmark demonstrate that our method achieves performance comparable to current state-of-the-art approaches while maintaining a significantly simpler design. Additionally, we evaluate the system on cross-lingual and zero-shot scenarios, yielding promising results.

This study explores the evolution of a universe dominated by dark vitality derived from holographic Tsallis entropy, specifically within the context of the matter-quintessence dark energy mixture. We establish a dynamical system to analyze the stable states of this dominant dark vitality, focusing on a scenario where dark energy is modeled as a quintessence field with a complex-valued potential. Our investigation reveals that the critical points governing the dynamics are highly dependent on the magnitude of the imaginary component of the potential energy. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the dark vitality's equation of state is not static but varies across different evolutionary phases of the cosmos.

This paper introduces a branch-and-bound strategy to tackle multi-objective mixed-integer nonlinear optimization (MO-MINL) challenges. The method leverages the Non-dominated Sorting Genetic Algorithm II (NSGA-II) for subproblem resolution. We establish both lower and upper bounds for the Pareto front within each node, utilizing the relaxation of integer variables and the aggregation of objectives, respectively. Furthermore, we present a novel dominance criterion for pruning the search space by filtering subproblems based on their relaxed solutions.

This result establishes a correspondence between global sections of a space and its integer-valued functions on the "line dual." We also show a natural bijection between the set of global sections of a groupoid and its "line dual," where the "line dual" refers to the set of global sections of the constant sheaf with integer values on the "line dual." The rapid expansion of data-driven research in biology and medicine is driven by the availability of large-scale, high-quality datasets. However, legal, regulatory, and ethical hurdles often restrict the free movement of these data, particularly sensitive information, across organizational boundaries. To address this, we have developed a secure gateway designed to facilitate the trustworthy exchange of biomedical data between institutions. This solution integrates established data management principles with cutting-edge cyberinfrastructure to enable researchers to access and analyze data remotely without needing to download it locally. We have validated this approach using two prominent resources: the Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) and the Cancer Cell Line Encyclopedia (CCLE), hosted on the National Supercomputing Applications for Biomedical Research (NSF ASCR) Bridges supercomputer.

Aspect-based sentiment analysis (ABSA) aims to determine the sentiment polarity of a target aspect within a given review sentence. While recent advancements have largely focused on extracting explicit sentiment toward these aspects, recent research indicates that many such sentiments remain implicit. This paper introduces a novel approach to uncovering implicit sentiment for ABSA, utilizing the Supervised Contrastive Pre-training (SupCo) framework. Specifically, we develop an implicit sentiment dataset and employ it to pre-train models using the SupCo approach. This method effectively captures both implicit and explicit sentiment features, which are then leveraged for accurate sentiment prediction. Experimental results demonstrate that our model surpasses current state-of-the-art techniques across three public ABS datasets.

This paper examines a causal identification and computation problem within a causal mediation analysis framework. The model involves an exposure, a binary mediator, and an outcome, with data collected through a case-control sampling method. We establish identification conditions for the natural direct effect and the conditional mediation effect, defined using a structural equation model that incorporates unmeasured confounding for both the pathway from exposure to mediator and from mediator to outcome. Furthermore, we introduce a novel computational approach based on weighted inverse probability weighting, which utilizes available data to assign weights to the outcome. This method offers a distinct advantage over existing techniques by not requiring the estimation of weights for the probability of acting as a case. We validate this approach through a Monte Carlo simulation and apply it to an analysis of a case-control dataset investigating the mediating role of obesity in the relationship between physical activity and blood pressure.

This paper investigates transmission strategies within Reconfigurable Intelligent Surface (RIS)-aided secure multiuser networks plagued by hardware impairments. Specifically, we examine the impact of amplitude amplitude variation error (AAVE) and phase shifting error (PSE) on RIS performance. To address this, we formulate a transmission design problem aimed at maximizing the minimum achievable secure rates for all users, subject to unit-magnitude constraints and realistic hardware limitations. This non-convex challenge is resolved via an iterative algorithm combining Semidefinite Relaxation (SDR) and Block Coordinate Descent (BCD). Simulation outcomes demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms conventional Spherical Phase Shifting (SPS) and Diagonal Phase Shifting (DPS) schemes.

This study introduces Executive Ability (EAB), a value-based contrastive learning framework designed to enhance the reliability of self-supervised learning (SSL) representations. EAB operates by dynamically adjusting the training pool for each sample, incorporating both hard negatives and diverse positive examples. These diverse positives are generated through three specific data augmentation techniques: (1) concatenating image patches, (2) applying random color shifts, and (3) performing elastic deformations. Crucially, the method employs an hindsight summarization strategy to assign distinct importance weights to these augmented views, thereby guiding the selection of valuable samples for contrastive learning. Empirical evaluations across multiple datasets demonstrate that EAB significantly boosts SSL performance, delivering improvements of 2.5%, 2.5%, and 1.5% over the baseline SimCLR on the COCO, Pascal VOC, and Pascal VOC (note: original text lists two VOC datasets) respectively. Specifically, gains of 2.5% and 1.5% were observed on the COCO and both VOC datasets, while the improvement on VOC is consistently cited as 1.5% less than the base.

The analysis reveals that the energy density of these fluctuations at the source is comparable to that of the solar wind, and their energy density increases with radial distance at a rate similar to that of the solar wind. We offer an innovative method for constructing noncommutable principal bundles in the setting of $G$-graded $C^*$-algebras, where $G$ is a countable abelian group. This approach relies on an inductive framework utilizing Stinespring representations, the tensor product operation, and the theory of ST-algebras. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our construction aligns with the previously established work of S. Echterhoff, M. Rørdam, and N. Yabe regarding principal $G$-bundles over $G$-algebras, specifically those involving actions that are both free and proper.

This study establishes that the inequality $\mathfrak{p} < \mathfrak{u} < \mathfrak{a} < \mathfrak{q}$ is possible, with $\mathfrak{q}$ representing the cardinality of a quasi-disjoint family. Additionally, we demonstrate that $\mathfrak{q}$ can be strictly less than $\mathfrak{a}$ within models of ZFC, and we discuss several other partial orderings of collections of subsets of $\omega$ alongside their associated unbounded numbers.

This study explores the conditions required for fast and slow light propagation within a $q$-deformed optomechanical system featuring an F-state atom and a deformed harmonic oscillator. We demonstrate that the standard interpretations of fast and slow light need clarification and revision. Specifically, the presence of a deformed optomechanical coupling constant introduces a new mechanism for adjusting light velocity, distinct from the traditional Raman process. Furthermore, the interaction between the atom and the deformed oscillator generates an effective potential that influences atomic motion, a factor that must be accounted for when evaluating light speed. In conclusion, the conventional criteria for achieving fast and slow light require refinement to accommodate these findings.

The dual Rotor model, characterized by two interacting rotors, serves as a simplified framework for investigating the interplay between valence and intruder nucleons in nuclei. This study introduces a novel phenomenon within this model: a mode of scissors motion, driven by adverse coupling between the rotors, which exists alongside traditional modes arising from favorable coupling. The analysis demonstrates that the nature of these scissors modes can be defined by the relative magnitudes of the nuclear deformation parameters for both valence and intruder rotors.

This study introduces a unique numerical method for solving hyperbolic and parabolic partial differential equations (PDEs), utilizing a cell-mean based neural network. The approach involves defining a computational domain divided into cells and introducing neural network-based functions representing the difference between actual and approximate cell mean values. By applying the weak form of the PDEs to derive equations for these neural functions, the method yields an exact solution. A key advantage is that the resulting discrete equations are formulated as standard algebraic equations that can be efficiently resolved using conventional solvers. The validity of the method is confirmed through two test cases with a known exact solution, demonstrating that the computed results align perfectly with the analytical solution.

The Unruh effect, in which an accelerating observer perceives a thermal bath within the Minkowski vacuum, is a fundamental concept in Quantum Field Theory. However, its direct experimental verification remains elusive due to the prohibitive cost of achieving the necessary accelerations. This study introduces a novel method for detecting the Unruh effect by leveraging the geometric phase, or Berry phase, acquired by a quantum system. By utilizing a quantum field-theoretic framework, we demonstrate that the thermal nature of the bath detected by an accelerating observer arises from the entanglement between the observer and the field, specifically through the entanglement of their future and past light cones. This perspective offers a new pathway to understanding the relationship between acceleration and thermalization.

Event detection is a critical task in information extraction, particularly for monitoring current affairs. While recent advancements have largely stemmed from event detection systems, most rely on monolingual training data. This limitation restricts their utility in real-world scenarios, where multilingual capabilities are often essential. To address this gap, we introduce MEE, an event detection dataset designed to support language models. MEE covers 10 distinct languages and includes annotations for both event detection and event clustering. To the best of our knowledge, MEE is the first comprehensive dataset of its kind. We also present a novel neural architecture capable of event detection and clustering. Experimental results indicate that our model achieves state-of-the-art performance.

We present an extensive examination of global vector bundles on the projective line, utilizing this framework to investigate push-forward equations associated with Kunneth forms. Additionally, we establish criteria that guarantee the positive semi-definite nature of these characteristic forms.

This study investigates the stellar wind's impact on the jet in Cyg X-1 during hard states, specifically examining how the "stellar breeze" influences jet dynamics and variability. We analyzed 1.5 years of XMM-Newton data, covering three stellar breeze episodes, to determine the jet's response. Our results indicate that the jet reacts to the breeze on a timescale of approximately 100 ks, roughly 10 times the light-crossing time of the Bondi radius. This delay suggests the jet originates from the innermost region of the accretion disk. Furthermore, the jet's reaction amplitude is about 10% of the breeze strength, which is roughly an order of magnitude greater than expected from prior theoretical models. These findings support a scenario where the jet is driven by accretion disk jets, which are modulated by the incoming stellar breeze.

We introduce a non-abelian extension of the ether-like term familiar from standard abelian electrodynamics. This term breaks Lorentz symmetry and becomes proportional to the 't Hooft-Feynman axion coupling constant when an axion field is introduced. Consequently, it facilitates the emergence of a novel type of magnetic monopole that cannot decay. Additionally, this monople can emerge as a stable topological soliton, specifically a non-abelial "hedgehog," provided warm conditions are met.

This paper introduces CUSSA, a novel framework designed to leverage the complementary strengths of syntactic and semantic analyses. By employing a multi-task learning architecture, CUSSA simultaneously trains for core syntactic analyses alongside a range of semantic tasks. This approach not only streamlines the universal analysis process but also enhances its precision through the inclusion of semantic context. The study validates this methodology using two distinct computational models: a neural network and a traditional rule-based system. Results from CUSSA's application to syntactic analyses—including part-of-speech tagging, lemmatization, and dependency parsing—as well as to semantic tasks like named entity recognition and natural language inference, demonstrate a marked improvement in performance across the board.

This study examines the impact of magnetized accretion disk dynamics on post-merger ejecta from binary neutron star (BNS) mergers. Utilizing the GRMHD code KERTIS, we simulated the evolution of the BNS system from the moment of coalescence through the formation of a magnetized, neutrino-cooled accretion disk. Our results indicate that the initial disk mass is highly sensitive to the seed magnetic flux; specifically, increasing the seed magnetic flux by an order of magnitude reduces the initial mass by a factor of three. Furthermore, we analyzed the kinematic properties of the ejected matter, finding that the magnetized accretion disk generates a jet with a Lorentz factor of approximately 10, which significantly surpasses the velocities of the standard dynamical and disk ejecta.

Tidal features (TFs) serve as indicators of past mergers and accretion events, yet their presence does not guarantee that such events occurred. Consequently, TFs are crucial for understanding galaxy evolution history, but their detectability depends on the likelihood that a merger left a visible trace. This study investigates the relationship between TFs and the merger history of early-type galaxies (ETGs) by analyzing the HSC-SSP sample of 1,000 massive ETGs (M > 10^11 M☉) at redshifts 0.1 < z < 0.5. We find that the proportion of galaxies with TFs remains roughly constant at ~10% across this redshift range, implying that the rate of mergers producing detectable TFs is also stable. However, the overall merger rate for massive ETGs increases significantly with redshift, suggesting that many mergers happen without generating visible tidal features. Furthermore, the flux fraction of TFs correlates with galaxy mass, indicating that TFs are more prominent in more massive galaxies. These findings imply that a substantial number of mergers go undetected by TFs, a conclusion supported by hydrodynamical simulations.

This study, serving as the sequel to "Astrophys. Space Sci." 360, 161 (2014), explores the generation of electromagnetic fields and currents by moving charges within a dielectric medium. It specifically examines the electric and magnetic fields produced by a constant-velocity point charge in a dielectric, as well as the electric fields generated by a point source in vacuum and in a dielectric. Furthermore, it analyzes the electric fields arising from a point charge accelerating along a straight line within both vacuum and dielectric environments. The investigation concludes by addressing the gravitational field of a point charge in a dielectric and the electric fields of a charge undergoing acceleration or uniform motion in the same medium. The findings indicate that a point charge in a dielectric generates a magnetic field with a dipole-like structure, whereas the electric field of an accelerating charge in a dielectric exhibits characteristics similar to the magnetic field of a dipole. Additionally, the electric field of an accelerating charge in a dielectric is found to be significantly stronger than in a vacuum.
