We introduce a homology theory for Steadfast $\alpha$-structures, which serves as a chromatic refinement of the homology theory developed by Dwyer and Weyer for $\mathbb{T}$-structures. Additionally, we demonstrate that this refinement yields a map from chromatically twisted Steadfast $\mathbb{T}$-homology to the standard Steadfast $\mathbb{T}$-homology.

This paper investigates the performance gap between binary power control and the optimal strategy in terms of sum symmetric degrees of freedom (GDoF) for $K$-user interference channels (ICs). We demonstrate that, under optimal power allocation, the Extremal GDoF gain of binary power control scales as $\Theta(K^{2/3})$. Conversely, when compared against the optimal sum GDoF, the corresponding gain for binary power control is bounded by $\Theta(\sqrt{K})$.

The escalating volume of business data has intensified the need for auditing, a process that necessitates the classification of individual data items into predefined categories. This study introduces a classification framework that leverages the attributes of these items to determine their respective classes. We utilize a dynamic knowledge structure to identify the optimal classification for each item. Furthermore, we apply the evidence theory framework to quantify the degree of certainty associated with each classification decision. The proposed methodology is validated through an auditing auditing case study, with results demonstrating that the approach is both effective and applicable.

This work presents a novel, exact, parallel Markov chain that generates realizations from the Strauss model, an interaction point process widely utilized in spatial statistics. The proposed method, which is exact and capable of leveraging spatial parallelism, is rigorously evaluated against two existing Monte Carlo algorithms through simulations involving the hard-core and Strauss point processes. The results demonstrate that the new approach achieves superior performance, particularly when dealing with large datasets.

We investigate the influence of the generalized uncertainty principle (GUP) on Lorentz transformations, utilizing the canonical formalism alongside a momentum-space deformation that maintains the Lie algebra structure of the Poincaré group. Our analysis demonstrates that the Poincaré algebra remains closed only when the deformation parameter is set to zero, indicating a conflict between the GUP and Lorentz symmetry. We further examine the Galilean limit of this framework, observing that a closed algebra emerges exclusively under two specific conditions: either the deformation parameter is zero, or the product of the GUP parameter and Planck's constant vanishes, effectively nullifying the commutator between space and momentum. Consequently, the Galilei algebra closes without the GUP, or if the deformation parameter is zero, the first modification of Lorentz transformations becomes independent of Planck's constant.

This study addresses the challenge of scheduling courses and classes, a problem categorized as NP-hard. We introduce a novel algorithm that prioritizes student preferences by allowing multiple courses to be scheduled simultaneously within overlapping time slots. This multitasking capability is made possible by the shared use of facilities, such as lecture halls and laboratories, during these concurrent sessions. To solve this, we developed a Mixed-Integer Programming (MIP) model and conducted computational experiments on both small and large datasets. Our results demonstrate that the algorithm effectively manages large-scale scheduling tasks, delivering high-quality solutions that align well with student desires.

This research investigates the performance of a monopod hopping robot operating on soft ground. The investigation involves creating a mathematical model to simulate the robot's reaction on yielding surfaces, which are defined by their ability to deform. The results indicate that the rate of soil deformation is directly proportional to the magnitude of the normal force exerted by the robot's foot. The study also analyzes how the robot's center of mass (CoM) vertical acceleration correlates with the forces acting upon it. Theoretical predictions were validated through physical experiments. The report concludes with a discussion on the theoretical findings and experimental data, followed by a proposal for improving the robot's stability.

The Internet of Things (IoT) is rapidly expanding, with a significant portion of devices relying on wireless mesh networks (WMNs) for communication. In this architecture, nodes autonomously route data to the network, enabling seamless coverage even in areas lacking traditional infrastructure. However, the constrained processing power and memory of these nodes often result in outdated firmware, which can cause security vulnerabilities and operational inefficiencies. This study evaluates a dependable WMN firmware distribution strategy that leverages a specialized upgrade path. The proposed method ensures that nodes successfully update without disrupting network operations, regardless of their current software version. The authors conducted a large-scale field experiment on a 100-node WMN to assess the effectiveness of this approach. The results demonstrate that the system achieves a 99.9% success rate in upgrading nodes while maintaining uninterrupted data transmission throughout the network.

Multifractal properties characterize the eigenstates of many-body localized (MBL) systems, which are distinct from single-particle fractal states found in Anderson insulators. In contrast, ergodic states are defined by extended eigenstates. This study examines the Fock-space propagator $P(r,t)$, where $r$ represents the distance between sites and $t$ is time, to explore many-body systems. We demonstrate that the eigenstate participation ratio (EP R) scales with a single exponent, $\gamma$, as a function of distance, and that the eigenstate Fock-space velocity (EF S) scales with a single exponent, $\delta$, as a function of time. These findings confirm that the eigenstate F S propagator $P(r,t)$ can be described by a scaling function dependent on the ratio $t^{1/\delta}r$. We observe that the eigenstate F S velocity exponent, $\delta$, remains constant across both single-particle fractal and Anderson insulator regimes but changes in the ergodic phase. We also note that the eigenstate F S velocity exponent, $\delta$, is related to the eigenstate participation ratio exponent, $\gamma$, by a simple relationship. We further find that the eigenstate F S velocity exponent, $\delta$, is related to the eigenstate participation ratio exponent, $\gamma$, by a simple relationship. We also note that the eigenstate F S velocity exponent, $\delta$, is related to the eigenstate participation ratio

We examine the online knapsack problem, a framework where a user seeks to identify $k$ items of unknown quality within a budget of $b$ interactions, each costing one query. The user can only assess an item's value through interactive search, which involves querying an oracle for a specific question; the oracle's response guides the next query. While prior research primarily addressed scenarios with a single target, we investigate the multi-target case. We demonstrate that for specific query models, the problem remains NP-hard even with a single item, yet for others, we establish polynomial-time solvability. In these interactive contexts, we analyze two primary query types: binary search, where the oracle answers if an item's value exceeds a threshold, and numerical search, where the oracle provides the exact value. We further examine the impact of noisy oracle responses, which may deviate from the true value. Finally, we present a novel query model that accommodates both noise and arbitrary response distributions, proving it is solvable in polynomial time for the multi-target scenario but remains NP-hard for the single-target scenario.

To assess the robustness of quantum neural networks (QNNs), this paper introduces a novel framework for generating global adversarial instances and disturbances. The proposed method employs a gradient-based algorithm that optimizes an objective function to maximize the discrepancy between QNN outputs on original and adversariously manipulated inputs, effectively ensuring resilience across the entire input feature space. Additionally, the study presents a specific technique for generating adversarial disturbances within the quantum input qubits' state space. Experimental results demonstrate that these generated threats successfully compromise the integrity of the tested quantum classifiers.

This paper investigates the Steklov eigenvalues of specific simply connected planar domains, which are described as "almost spherical" because they result from the union of a closed disk and a finite collection of disjoint closed disks situated outside it. We demonstrate that, for regions created by adding $n$ such disks to a primary disk, the first $n+1$ eigenvalues correspond precisely to those of the original large disk alone. This finding extends the earlier result by Brock and Wehrheim (2011), who examined only the case of adding two disks. Our approach relies on the method of unfolding, combined with techniques from spectral graph theory and the analysis of singular integral operators.

Compliance constitutes a fundamental aspect of contemporary business processes, where it is defined as the requirement that process executions must strictly follow specific rules. While existing compliance checking approaches typically evaluate entire execution traces against process models, these methods often overlook the necessity of verifying specific trace segments for partial compliance. This paper introduces a novel compliance verification method that utilizes segment traces and a designated compliance constraint to determine whether a specific trace segment adheres to its requirements. The proposed method is built upon infix and postfix alignments, offering a computationally efficient approach that avoids the performance bottlenecks of traditional techniques. The authors also present a formal definition of compliance verification and provide a theoretical analysis of its computational complexity.

Accurate signal propagation modeling is essential for the planning, optimization, and deployment of cellular networks. While traditional models rely on empirical measurements and often lack the flexibility to account for diverse environmental variables, data-driven deep learning approaches have emerged as a promising alternative. This study introduces a deep convolutional neural network (CNN) designed to predict pathloss using high-resolution satellite imagery. Leveraging the image-based architecture of the model, we demonstrate that it can effectively capture the impact of various terrains and structures on signal attenuation. Evaluated against extensive real-world drive-test datasets, the proposed method achieves significantly lower root mean square error (RMSE) compared to conventional models. Furthermore, the research highlights the model's adaptability to different environments and its scalability for use in large-scale networks.

This work introduces a standardized set of semantics for temporal planning, formally defining key concepts such as plan validity, deadlock, and deadlock. Furthermore, we establish a semantics-independent framework for formally confirming plan validation, which serves as a universal reference for temporal planners and validates the correctness of various temporal planners and validation algorithms. We also provide formally confirmed validation algorithms and implementers in Python, which can be used to verify the correctness of other temporal planners and validation algorithms. Finally, we discuss the implications of these results for future research and development in temporal planning.

Power system expansion planning (ESP) models are essential for determining the most cost-effective infrastructure investments to meet future demand. These models typically rely on a demand forecast, which is constructed using demand response (DR) strategies that lower electricity consumption through incentives. This study introduces a mathematical framework to quantify the sensitivity of ESP outcomes to variations in DR levels. The analysis utilizes a mixed-integer linear programming (MIP) model based on a simplified network and a simplified, piecewise linear cost function for generation and investment. The authors derive both necessary and sufficient conditions for plan sensitivity and demonstrate that these sensitivities are constant within specific intervals of a plan's MIP objective function value. The research further proves that the sensitivity regarding DR levels is non-negative and that the sensitivity concerning generation and investment levels is monotonically increasing. The study also establishes a connection between the proposed model and a variant of the subgradient method for MIP optimization. Finally, numerical experiments conducted on a simple three-bus network illustrate the model's application and validate the theoretical findings.

This paper examines a Vlasov–Maxwell system defined on a bounded domain, featuring a Neumann boundary condition that ensures the preservation of particle count. We establish the existence of global-in-time weak solutions and demonstrate their uniqueness. The core of this investigation relies on a novel application of the push-forward technique, which enables the transformation of the kinetic equation into an equivalent characteristic (Lagrange) formulation. This transformed representation is crucial for deriving the necessary a priori estimates. The primary innovation of this work is the extension of the push-forward method to Vlasov–Poisson-like models within bounded regions, thereby generalizing the approach previously validated for the Vlasov–Poisson equation in all three spatial dimensions by Pfaffelmoser and others.

This paper introduces a novel approach to identify search queries that retrieve relevant data from knowledge repositories for specific concepts. While prior work has primarily focused on crafting queries for entire concepts, our method targets the identification of queries for individual subconcepts. We name this approach STRICT (Subconcept Retrieval-based Term Identification for Concept Positioning). The proposed method employs a subconector extraction technique and a query suggestion strategy grounded in data retrieval. Extensive experiments on the DBpedia dataset demonstrate that our method surpasses existing approaches, achieving an F1 score of 0.515.

Colloidal gels are highly attractive for numerous applications, yet their inherent structural complexity and sensitivity to external factors often make it difficult to tailor their mechanical and flow behaviors for specific uses. This study demonstrates that applying ultrasonic vibrations can effectively modify the viscoelastic properties of colloidal gels, enabling the creation of materials with customized mechanical and flow characteristics. This approach offers a highly efficient method for designing and fabricating tailored materials.
This paper examines the well-known, yet unresolved, Collatz Conjecture.

Automatically categorizing STEM documents is essential for supporting STEM education and research. While current methods typically rely on isolated features like mathematical entities, physical concepts, or STEM tags, they often fail to capture the nuanced relationships between these elements. To address this, we introduce a new framework for categorizing STEM documents through the analysis of how these entities are associated. Our approach involves two key steps: first, automatically generating category-specific entity associations by analyzing co-occurrence patterns within the text; second, leveraging these associations to enhance categorization accuracy. Experimental results across three distinct datasets—covering calculus, physics, and general STEM content—demonstrate that our method improves performance by 1.5% to 10.5% compared to existing baselines. Additionally, we conducted a qualitative analysis of our computed entity associations to reveal insights into how these entities coexist within different academic categories.

The primary objective of stable matching is to pair individuals into mutually satisfactory relationships. In the context of stable *pairing*, prospective participants may propose additional options beyond those automatically accepted, with the goal of the system to select a subset of these proposals to create a more efficient and productive pairing. This research proposes a new framework for stable pairing that operates on proposals submitted by all agents, offering a flexible environment for expressing preferences. We establish the existence of a valid pairing within this model and demonstrate that it can be computed in polynomial time. Furthermore, we analyze the sensitivity of this pairing to changes in submissions and prove that it exhibits robust stability properties. Finally, we validate the practicality of our approach through experiments on real-world data, showing that incorporating these pairings significantly enhances user satisfaction.

Generating high-quality summaries is a critical natural language processing task. Although numerous models have been developed to address this, the current evaluation metrics used to measure summary quality are often inadequate. These existing metrics rely on comparing a generated summary against one or more reference summaries via external resources, such as WER, BLEU, and ROUGE. However, they fail to capture the nuanced aspects of summary quality that human evaluators consider, including relevance, coherence, and informativeness. To bridge this gap, we introduce SummScore, a metric that leverages a cross-encoder pre-trained on summary pairs. SumScore functions as a regressor that outputs a single score reflecting summary quality. We trained this model using a dataset of 1.2 million summary pairs annotated with human scores from the Summary Creation Shared Task of WMT 2018. Our model achieves a Pearson correlation coefficient of 0.688 with human judgments, surpassing all currently available metrics. Furthermore, we demonstrate that SumScore can effectively identify superior models and highlight specific areas for improvement in generated outputs.

We introduce a rapid algorithm for recovering a signal from noisy quadratic observations. This method leverages the fact that, given a fixed, sparse support, the associated maximum likelihood estimator can be expressed as the unique fixed point of a contraction mapping. We establish that this algorithm converges to the exact solution, which is known to exist, provided the contractiveness constant is sufficiently small. Furthermore, we demonstrate that under specific conditions, the number of iterations required for convergence is significantly lower than the total degrees of freedom. Numerical experiments indicate that this approach is highly effective for sparse support recovery and achieves convergence in very few steps.

This study presents a straightforward yet potent framework for multi-modal fusion, designed to enhance the efficiency of LiDAR-camera integration. While current research predominantly focuses on complex architectures with extensive modularity to address specific issues, our approach emphasizes a unified, cohesive design. We introduce BEVFusion, a LiDAR-camera fusion model that performs early fusion by aligning features from both sensors within a unified bird's-eye view (BEV) space. This method avoids the need for intricate multi-stage processing or feature concatenation, streamlining the workflow. By utilizing a shared BEV representation, BEVFusion not only accelerates inference but also enhances feature compatibility. Experimental results on the KITTI benchmark demonstrate that BEVFusion surpasses existing state-of-the-art fusion techniques, achieving a 2.0% improvement in Object Detection (OJ) and a 0.2% improvement in Object Interaction (OIO) metrics. Furthermore, the model exhibits robustness across diverse scenarios, including adverse weather conditions.

This study examines the impact of temperature fluctuations on liquid turbulence across the inertial and dissipative regimes. The research focuses on three-dimensional turbulence subjected to uniform mean heating, where heat is transferred from a heated lower wall to an upper, cooler ceiling. The primary objective is to determine how this heat transfer alters the turbulent kinetic energy (TKE) spectrum at the drain range. The simulations employ the direct numerical simulation (DNS) method, modeling a channel with dimensions of 1024 x 128 x 128 and a Reynolds number of 10,000. The results indicate that the TKE spectrum in the drain range is significantly lower than that of isothermal turbulence. This reduction is primarily caused by the cooling effect at the upper wall, which suppresses the energy dissipation in that region. The findings suggest that the presence of the cooled ceiling substantially diminishes the overall TKE spectrum at the drain range.

This study presents a numerical model to explain the complex diffraction patterns generated when a laser scans a liquid surface, driven by thermally induced variations in the refractive index. The research focuses on analyzing the relationship between laser parameters and the resulting diffraction features. The investigation reveals that the laser beam's travel time significantly influences the spatial distribution of the laser-induced temperature within the liquid. Furthermore, the study demonstrates that the evolution of diffraction patterns over time is governed by the interplay between laser parameters and liquid properties. The findings offer a quantitative framework for understanding the formation of these diffraction patterns, serving as a reference for future investigations into this phenomenon.

This study investigates the effectiveness of using natural language techniques to extract information from design dialogues. We evaluated the approach on a dataset of 1,000 sessions, achieving 80% accuracy in identifying software features and 70% in determining code ownership. To ensure reliable results, we employed a conclusion robustness methodology that involved repeatedly executing the extraction process on a smaller subset of data and validating the outcomes against a complete analysis of the entire dataset. We also assessed the stability of the extracted conclusions by comparing them with those generated by alternative algorithms.

H-STREAM is a novel data streaming framework designed to facilitate the development of analytics pipelines for big data streams. It features a streamlined programming model that enables developers to build pipelines using a straightforward pipeline abstraction, where each step applies a function to the incoming stream. While this model offers simplicity, it often sacrifices the performance required for processing large-scale streaming data. To address this, H-STREAM provides a comprehensive library of operators that support parallelization, data filtering, and aggregation. Additionally, the framework offers mechanisms for state management, allowing operators to retain intermediate results for subsequent processing. H-STREAM also provides tools for data transformation, which convert stream operators into batch processing tasks. This paper outlines the core principles of the H-STREAM framework, presents specific design choices, and includes experimental results that validate the system's performance.

This work examines non-resonant graphs for the single-production of a top-antibottom pair, specifically within the $t\bar{b} + X$ framework where $X$ represents additional particles. We analyze the graph set for the process $q\bar{q}' \to t\bar{b} + X$ in the $N$-body final state, incorporating contributions from $X = \emptyset, \gamma, Z, H, W^{\pm}, \text{and } t\bar{t}$. For the $t\bar{b} + W^{\pm}$ channel, we further include $t_R = t_R$ contributions. We demonstrate that the standard non-resonant graphs for $t\bar{b} + X$ (where $X = \emptyset, \gamma, Z, H$) are insufficient to accurately model the $t\bar{b} + X$ cross section. To address this, we propose an extended non-resonant graph set that accounts for the top and bottom quark masses. We find that this expanded set yields results in excellent agreement with the exact cross section. Additionally, we explore the impact of the top and bottom masses on the angular distribution of the $t\bar{b} + X$ process.

Knowledge-based neural machine translation (KB-NMT) leverages a knowledge base (KB) to generate translations for queries lacking sufficient context in data-driven approaches. While recent methods have achieved notable success, they often suffer from incomplete translations or excessive repetition of base elements. This study introduces a novel duplicate mechanism designed to regulate these base components within the SPARQL-NMT framework. By leveraging the predictive power of a dedicated duplicate predictor, the system effectively suppresses unnecessary duplications while preserving those essential for maintaining semantic accuracy. Evaluated on the FB15K-2376 dataset, this method demonstrates an improved F1 score of 1.8 over the current state-of-the-art, alongside a 23.6% reduction in base duplicate errors.

Scholarly citations are fundamental to the academic community, serving as the primary mechanism for disseminating knowledge and enabling research. However, the current citation-based metrics are often insufficient for evaluating venue quality, particularly for newer or smaller conferences. In this paper, we introduce Venue Insights, a lightweight, venue-based alternative to venue-based evaluation metrics. Our approach involves a two-step process: first, we cluster papers by similarity, and second, we calculate a venue's quality score by determining the proportion of similar papers it hosts relative to the broader community. Our findings indicate that Venue Insights can effectively identify high-quality venues, including emerging and smaller conferences, while remaining computationally efficient.

This paper presents a validation approach for neural network control systems, which are often opaque and difficult to analyze using traditional methods. We focus on a specific class of feedforward neural networks featuring ReLU activation, finite weights, and finite biases. By partitioning the state space into regions where the network output remains constant, we transform the resulting control task into a finite collection of problems with linear control constraints and linear dynamics. We then apply randomized Kriging-based approximate dynamic programming to address these sub-problems. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this proposed framework through a controlled example.

This paper introduces a functorial approach to grouping elements within a collection into nested clusters of varying sizes, where each cluster is allowed to overlap with others. Our method employs a weighted cluster tree to represent the entire hierarchy of groupings. We define a grouping functor that constructs this tree from an element set and a similarity matrix, utilizing an optimization algorithm to determine the tree's structure. We also present a method for computing groupings through iterative application of the grouping functor. We demonstrate the utility of our functorial grouping framework by applying it to a set of human faces.

Restoring visual data from streaming tensor inputs is vital for numerous real-world applications, including medical imaging, satellite photography, and remote sensing. However, conventional tensor recovery methods are often unsuitable for this streaming context because they demand storing the entire data stream in memory, which is impractical for massive streams with limited memory capacity. To address this challenge, we introduce a monitoring framework that leverages the local patch structures of streaming tensors to enable efficient restoration. This approach employs a new iterative algorithm to track patch recovery status, allowing the system to adaptively select key patches for memory retention while discarding less critical ones. This selective strategy significantly reduces memory usage while maintaining, or even enhancing, restoration quality. The proposed method is built on the Tensor Ring (TR) framework, a recent advancement over traditional low-rank tensor completion models that offers superior flexibility and efficiency. We further develop a specialized TR-based patch monitoring algorithm that surpasses existing state-of-the-art techniques in both performance and speed. Extensive experiments on various real-world datasets confirm the method's effectiveness, demonstrating substantial memory savings alongside high-quality, competitive restoration outcomes.

This study investigates the fundamental properties of certain finite-dimensional Nichols algebras over Weyl groups, specifically focusing on types $D_4$, $E_6$, $E_7$, and $E_8$. For each case, we establish the dimension, degree, and Poincaré polynomial. Additionally, we determine the structure of the coradical and the associated graded algebra for these examples.

This study provides the first direct numerical demonstration of Zakharov-Kolmogorov (ZK) spectral laws governing inertial wave turbulence (IWT) in three-dimensional fluids. The study focuses on periodic cubic domains with periodic boundary conditions, where a magnetic field is imposed along the z-axis. We analyze a system of 1024 massless particles interacting via a Yukawa-like potential, which supports weakly dispersive inertial waves. Our results reveal that, under specific driving conditions, the system develops a Kolmogorov-Zakharov stationary cascade. This cascade is defined by a constant flux of energy and angular momentum across inertial wave modes, which are characterized by a fixed frequency. The observed spectral exponent for the ZK cascade aligns with the theoretically predicted value.

This paper establishes a novel proof of the submodularity of the weight function associated with graph autonomous sets, utilizing the iterative graph standardization technique developed by Benczúr and Kővári. Furthermore, we present an algorithm capable of computing the Benczúr-Kővári autonomous set for graphs with $n$ vertices and $m$ edges in $O(mn^2/m^{2/3})$ time complexity.

Monolayer graphene, a single-atom-thick form of carbon, has garnered significant attention for its remarkable electronic and mechanical properties. This study investigates the thermodynamic behavior of electrically controlled graphene within a canonical ensemble, deriving its partition function and key thermodynamic quantities. We demonstrate that the graphene layer's temperature rises with an increasing electric field; however, this heating effect is contingent upon the sign of the charge carriers. Furthermore, we show that the system's entropy and heat capacity are non-zero exclusively at finite temperatures, while the internal energy and entropy vanish at absolute zero.

This study presents the detection of low-frequency radio emissions from the binary system CR Draconis, a binary composed of flare stars. The observations, conducted using the UTR-2 radio telescope, spanned a 10-year period from 2010 to 2019. The recorded radio bursts were analyzed to determine their spectral characteristics, temporal profiles, and polarization. The spectral range of the detected emissions spanned from 10.5 MHz to 15.5 MHz, with peak fluxes reaching up to 100 Jy. The majority of bursts were detected in right-hand circular polarization, with polarization degrees ranging from 10% to 80%. The duration of the bursts varied between 10 seconds and 10 minutes. The study also identified a correlation between the star's optical flares and the radio bursts, noting that the majority of the radio events were associated with optical flares. The analysis of the radio bursts' polarization and duration provided insights into the physical parameters of the emitting plasma. The study concludes that the radio emissions from CR Draconis are likely generated by the electron-cyclotron maser mechanism, which is consistent with the observed low frequencies and polarization characteristics. The study also notes that the radio emissions from CR Draconis are likely generated by the electron-cyclotron maser mechanism, which is consistent with the observed low frequencies and polarization characteristics. Articulated Neural Rendering (ANR) is a novel system designed to synthesize realistic images of a human-like virtual character from arbitrary camera angles, utilizing a single real photograph and one or more motion capture sequences. Unlike traditional methods, ANR employs a differentiable, hierarchical skeletal model that represents an amorphous, continuous volume. This approach enables the generation of novel views from unseen angles and creates images corresponding to specific frames from the input motion capture data. The system's key advantage lies in its ability to capture fine-grained, high-frequency surface details—such as hair strands and fabric folds—while maintaining the capacity to model large-scale body deformations. Experimental results indicate that ANR surpasses existing state-of-the-art techniques in both visual fidelity and rendering efficiency.

The widespread adoption of computer vision has led to a surge in image manipulation techniques, many of which alter visual intensity. Although humans are often drawn to vivid imagery, it remains unclear whether these alterations positively influence machine performance. This study investigates how varying levels of intensity impact both human and machine accuracy across three specific tasks: image retrieval, visual question answering, and object detection. We conducted experiments using both human participants and state-of-the-art machine learning models across varying intensities. Our findings indicate that while humans consistently perform better under higher intensity conditions, machines achieve peak results with lower intensity. These observations suggest that future research should explore how altering intensity can simultaneously benefit human and machine performance.

We investigate the connection between the $SU(2)$ Chern-Simons path integral and the action of the Askey-Wilson algebra on the space of link symbols. Specifically, we demonstrate that the Reshetikhin-Turam-based link symbols serve as the eigenstates of the algebra's generators, with the eigenvalues for the Casimir operator for the spin-$j$ representation calculated explicitly. Additionally, we show that the link symbols correspond to the matrix elements of the algebra's vector representation. Finally, we establish that the Casson invariant emerges as the intersection pairing defined among these link symbols.

This study explores how to enhance large language models (LLMs) for zero-shot classification by fine-tuning on diverse datasets and classification cues. Drawing inspiration from meta-learning, we introduce a framework that dynamically selects appropriate data based on specific task requirements. The approach is designed to be flexible, accommodating various data formats such as individual examples, entire datasets, or aggregated collections. The method is demonstrated through experiments on 102 zero-shot tasks derived from 18 different datasets, with results showing significant improvements over both standard zero-shot baselines and few-shot learning methods.

We examine the impact of electroweak phase shift (EWPS) on the $Z_3$-invariant Next-to-Minimal Supersymmetric Standard Model (NMSSM), specifically regarding LHC phenomenology and the implications for gravitational wave detection. In this framework, the Higgs sector comprises five complex scalar fields, and the lightest CP-odd scalar, $a_1$, acquires a non-zero vacuum expectation value (VEV) that spontaneously breaks the $Z_2$ symmetry while preserving the $Z_3$ symmetry. This mechanism generates a distinct electroweak phase shift alongside the standard Higgs phase. Our analysis indicates that the LHC's High-Luminosity phase could detect the $Z_3$-invariant Higgs doublet and the complex singlet, provided their masses fall within the accessible range. Furthermore, the phase shift influences the relic density of dark matter candidates, particularly neutralinos and singlino-like states, which are crucial for understanding dark matter stability. Finally, the transition associated with the $Z_3$-invariant sector may produce stochastic gravitational waves, offering a complementary probe to direct particle searches at the LHC.

The next generation of (sub)millimeter-wave interferometers promises to transform our understanding of the early universe, yet this potential relies on the ability to precisely detect and correct for telescope position errors. We introduce "High-z Sudoku," a diagnostic tool designed to evaluate an instrument's capability to identify and correct these submillimeter-level shifts. The method involves observing a cluster of sources within a compact field of view; by analyzing the resulting image, one can determine the magnitude and direction of any positional deviation. We demonstrate the utility of High-z Sudoku by applying it to a simulated observation of a high-redshift field with the ALMA array. We have conducted comprehensive quantum Monte Carlo simulations of the spin-1/2 Heisenberg antiferromagnet on a triangular lattice, utilizing the sign-free stochastic series expansion method. By examining the temperature-dependent dynamical spin structure factor, $S(\mathbf{q},\omega)$, we identify two distinct phases: a conventional antiferromagnetic state and a novel phase characterized by symmetry disruption. This nonmagnetic phase exhibits a six-fold symmetric spin excitation spectrum, which we attribute to a "liquid" state. Our findings align with recent theoretical predictions regarding the existence of a symmetry-broken liquid phase in this system.

We demonstrate that the $SU(3)-$Higgs theory, defined by an $SU(3)$ gauge coupling and an adjoint Higgs field, undergoes a transition between restricted and derestriction phases as the Higgs mass parameter increases. This conclusion is supported by an analytical derivation of the effective potential and numerical evidence from measurements of the Polyakov loop susceptibility. Furthermore, this study elucidates the connection between the $SU(3)-$Higgs mechanism and the standard Standard Model sector, specifically the $Z$ boson mass and the confinement-deconfinement transition within Quantum Chromodynamics (QCD).

The study of the hexagonal intermetallic compound Cr$_2$Al, which exhibits a layered structure, reveals a complex magnetic order characterized by in-plane antiferromagnetic (AFM) and ferromagnetic (FM) interactions. While the AFM coupling between neighboring Cr atoms is significantly stronger, the FM interaction between next-nearest-neighbor Cr atoms is sufficiently robust to generate a spiral antiferromagnetic state at low temperatures. This behavior is confirmed through a combination of magnetization, specific heat, and neutron scattering analyses.

This study evaluates a kinetic model featuring a velocity-dependent collision frequency to simulate rarefied gas flows characterized by weak intermolecular forces. The model's performance is benchmarked against the Bird model and the Boltzmann equation across a range of Knudsen numbers and intermolecular potential parameters. Results indicate that the proposed model matches the Bird model in terms of accuracy, computational efficiency, and simplicity, yet it is more precise than the Bird model when interaction potentials are weak.

We introduce a new approach to training semantic analyzers, which are neural networks designed to determine if a given sentence matches the meaning of a query. Our method centers on the concept of "familiarization," where the model is exposed to examples containing variations of a sentence that still retain its original meaning. By incorporating these augmented samples into our training regimen, we achieve significant improvements in performance, particularly when working with extremely limited datasets. Our experiments demonstrate that this technique yields a 10% boost in performance for datasets with fewer than 1,000 examples per category and a 4% boost for those with 1,000 to 5,000 examples.

The future Electron-Ion Collider (EIC) is planned to explore the internal structure of protons and nuclei by colliding them with high-energy electron beams. To achieve this, the EIC will utilize advanced silicon pixel and strip tracking sensors that provide precise three-dimensional position measurements. These measurements are essential for determining the scattered leptons' momentum transfer and ensuring the accuracy of the scattered electron's longitudinal momentum. To meet these requirements, the tracking system must deliver high spatial resolution, low material density, and high radiation hardness. This paper reviews the current status of silicon sensor fabrication and testing at the National Research Centre for Laser Radiation (NRCLR) in Russia, an institution that is a key partner in the EIC project.

This study examines the variability of the low-mass active galactic nucleus (AGN) 2M1229+1755, which has a mass of approximately 1.5 solar masses. The object was monitored using the 1.2-meter telescope at the OHP observatory, recording its optical (V-band) and near-infrared (I-band) fluxes over a 12-hour span. The resulting light curves reveal a significant fluctuation of roughly 10% in both bands, with the variations appearing nearly synchronous. The observed behavior is consistent with an oscillation mode, specifically the fundamental radial pulsation of the accretion disc. The analysis of the amplitude of these fluctuations indicates that the accretion disc is the primary source of the emission. Furthermore, the fluctuations are interpreted as a response to the thermal instability of the disc, a phenomenon previously identified in the context of dwarf novae.

This study presents a novel method for measuring the radial component of the magnetic field in stars by analyzing the polarization of spectral lines during a discharge event. The technique relies on the distinct sensitivity of line polarization to the radial magnetic field at line cores versus the influence of the equatorial field at line wings. The method was validated using a laboratory discharge of iron, and the resulting data were applied to observations of HD58260, a rapidly rotating A-type star. The findings indicate that the star's magnetic field strength decreases by a factor of 2.5 from the surface to a depth of 0.5R*. This observed gradient aligns with predictions from magnetohydrodynamic simulations of rotating stars. Additionally, the study confirms that the magnetic field in HD58260 is organized in a toroidal configuration.

We present a representation of the one-dimensional bosonic system introduced by Roger Coquereaux and Paul L. Dunkl (Phys. Rev. D 42, 3127 (1990)) utilizing unitsary irreducible representations of the one-dimensional Euclidean group, $E(1)$. This approach extends the well-established connection between the two-dimensional isotropic harmonic oscillator and $E(2)$, as described by Perelomov (Phys. Rep. 22, 42 (1974)). Notably, the Coquereaux-Dunkl system features bosonic variables that fail to commute with the Hamiltonian, a behavior analogous to position and momentum operators in standard quantum mechanics.

We present ALMA observations of the H30$\alpha$ line emission within the starburst galaxy NGC 5253, a region known for its low metallicity. This study aims to evaluate the H30$\alpha$ emission as a potential tracer for star formation in galaxies with low metal content. Our data reveal a compact source measuring 1.6" x 0.8" (FWHM) with a flux of 0.042 mJy, located in NGC 5253's central starburst region. This discrepancy suggests the presence of a high-velocity outflow driven by massive star formation. This paper establishes a new concept known as continuous orbital similarity rigidity for topologically axiom systems. We demonstrate that minimal free continuous actions of non-solvable groups, as well as certain minimal free actions of the homeomorphism groups of the line and the circle, exhibit this property.

This work examines the asymptotic properties of the Nadaraya-Watson estimator for conditional mean functions. The analysis covers the rate of convergence and bias behavior under minimal assumptions, specifically within the framework of functions exhibiting local smoothness characterized by a given order of derivatives. Additionally, we establish conditions ensuring that the estimator remains bounded in probability, provided the underlying conditional mean functions are continuous.

This study introduces a novel framework designed to estimate the current state of an epidemic. It posits that the core challenge of monitoring an epidemic process can be effectively addressed using observer theory. This approach relies on a rigorous, rigorous mathematical model of the epidemic dynamics, a set of observation equations, and specific assumptions regarding the error dynamics. By integrating these components, a unique observer architecture is constructed. This structure enables the estimation of unobservable variables based on available data. Furthermore, the framework establishes sufficient conditions necessary to ensure that estimation errors converge asymptotically. Finally, a set of illustrative examples is provided to demonstrate the practical application of this proposed framework.

Knowledge graphs (KGs) serve as valuable resources for representing real-world entities and their interrelations. While most KG completion techniques concentrate on predicting missing existing relationships, this study introduces a novel framework designed to forecast future relationships within a temporal KG context. The work begins by outlining the challenges of this task, which involves balancing the need for high precision with the requirement to identify a sufficient number of valid future links. It then proposes a new method that leverages a static graph representation to effectively integrate temporal information. The approach is evaluated on three benchmark datasets, demonstrating that it outperforms current state-of-the-art methods. Furthermore, the results of an in-depth analysis highlight the importance of temporal information and provide insights into the distinct characteristics of the datasets employed.

Ultrashort pulse lasers operating in the mid-infrared spectrum are essential for advancing fields such as spectroscopy, medicine, and fundamental physics. To achieve higher peak power, there is a critical need to develop oscillators capable of supporting shorter pulses and larger apertures. This study presents a geometric analysis of the Kerr-lens mode-locking stability for oscillators utilizing large apertures and high peak power. The investigation reveals that the conventional approach of optimizing pulse duration by adjusting the cavity dispersion is insufficient, as it neglects the impact of Kerr-lens stability. The authors introduce a straightforward method to assess stability by calculating the cavity's effective lensing power. The stability criterion is defined by the intersection of this effective power with the cavity's stable lensing region. The analysis further demonstrates that the cavity's effective lensing power is highly sensitive to the location of the laser crystals. Consequently, the placement of these gain or nonlinear crystals must be carefully considered to ensure stable operation of Kerr-lens mode-locked oscillators.

This paper introduces an asynchronous online federated learning framework specifically for nonlinear regression tasks. In this setup, the learner accesses data streams from multiple sources, each managed by an independent agent. A key challenge addressed is the varying computational and communication capabilities among these agents, which can lead to significant delays in asynchronous learning. To resolve this, the study proposes a novel Nonlinear Regression Asynchronous Federated Averaging (NRAFA) algorithm. The convergence of NRAFA is rigorously analyzed, and simulation experiments confirm that the method offers superior performance compared to existing asynchronous federated online learning algorithms.

This paper explores the asymptotic behavior of a function defined by $a^{x \log^{\infty} a} = \text{tet}_a(x)$, where $a > e^{e^{-1}}$. We establish that $\text{tet}_a(x)$ admits an asymptotic expansion in powers of $e^{-x}$, with each successive term involving higher powers of logarithms of $x$. This expansion is constructed using iterated logarithms of $x$ in the exponents of $e^{-x}$. Our asymptotic series is expressed through coefficients derived from the Riemann zeta function and powers of the inverse of $a$. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the resulting formula can be represented as a Laplace-type integral.

We introduce a novel method for constructing novel high-dimensional expander (HDX) graphs by utilizing group actions on finite groups. This approach relies on the quotient of a finite group $G$ by a subgroup $H$, where the subgroup is the point stabilizer of a transitive group action. We demonstrate that these newly created graphs possess the property of being HDGs. Furthermore, we establish that a broad category of these graphs fits within the established category of canonical HDGs. This class is distinguished by the property that the adjacency matrix commutes with the action of the stabilizer subgroup $H$. We illustrate the utility of our construction by identifying a specific family of HDGs that are not currently recognized as canonical. This family is derived from the action of $PSL(2, p)$ on the projective line over the field with $p$ elements, where $p$ denotes a prime number.

This study examines the magnetic properties of GdInO$_3$ through magnetization and specific heat measurements across a broad temperature range and various magnetic fields. The data indicate a layered, honeycomb-like network of Gd ions, which interact via antiferromagnetic coupling. The material undergoes a phase transition to an antiferromagnetic state at $T_N = 10.5$ K, characterized by a specific heat anomaly. Theoretical analysis of the specific heat, utilizing the spin-1/2 Heisenberg model on a honeycomb lattice, supports the proposed structural arrangement of the Gd ions. Furthermore, the application of a magnetic field induces a transition to a ferromagnetic state at $T_C = 5.5$ K, with the specific heat peak shifting to lower temperatures as the field strength increases. The observed magnetization behavior is consistent with a spin-flop transition.

Link prediction is a critical task in network analysis, with the ability to anticipate future connections being particularly valuable. While embedding methods have become a standard approach for this, they often rely on dense graph representations that can be computationally expensive and fail to capture the inherent sparsity of most real-world networks. To address this, we introduce Sparse Sparse Network Embedding (SSNE), a novel framework designed to predict links in sparse networks. SSNE employs a graph neural network (GNN) that generates node representations by aggregating information solely from a node's immediate neighbors. By utilizing a message-passing mechanism, SSNE effectively captures both local topology and higher-order structural patterns. Furthermore, the method employs an adaptive sampling strategy to select informative neighbors, thereby enhancing both computational efficiency and predictive performance. Experimental results across multiple real-world networks demonstrate that SSNE surpasses existing state-of-the-art techniques in link forecasting accuracy while significantly reducing runtime.

We describe the fabrication and evaluation of two silicon-based atomic vapor chambers utilizing deep silicon micromachining techniques. The first design is a flat chamber with a 10 cm² area and a 2 mm depth, while the second is a serpentine configuration with a 2.5 cm² area and 0.5 mm depth. Following a 2-hour bakeout, the vacuum pressure in the vacuum chamber settled at approximately 10⁻⁸ mbar. After introducing 100 µL of Rb into the chambers, the resulting vapor density was roughly 10¹³ cm⁻³. Pressure measurements taken via a capacitance manometer indicated that the pumping speed for atomic vapor was 0.035 m³/s for the flat chamber and 0.016 m³/s for the serpentine chamber.

This paper introduces a modeling approach for estimating nonlinear disturbance power in dual-polarization 4D transmission formats. Initially, we outline the methodology for creating a linear power model for 4D signals. Subsequently, we develop a nonlinear disturbance power model for dual-polarization 4D modes by leveraging the previously established linear framework. Finally, we validate the accuracy of this model through computer simulations.

This study introduces FIRe-GAN, a novel deep deep learning framework for fusing infrared and visible imagery to produce realistic visible light images. The architecture employs a generator and a discriminator, with the generator's loss function augmented by a novel, groundbreaking metric termed the Gradient Frequency Infrared Enhancement (FIRe-GAN) metric, which evaluates the generator's output against the input infrared image. The FIRe-GAN metric is formulated as a function of the input infrared image and the generated visible image, with the visible image being iteratively refined to minimize this loss function. The proposed framework is evaluated on a publicly available dataset of wildfire imagery, with the results indicating that the generated images exhibit superior realism compared to those produced by other state-of-the-art methods. The source code for the implementation is made available at the following URL: https://github.com/your-repo/firegan.

Depression is a prevalent mental health condition that can be identified through the analysis of social media activity. This study details the collection of a social media dataset designed to identify indicators of depression, specifically focusing on Twitter users who have been diagnosed with the condition. It also presents an empirical study that evaluates the effectiveness of various machine learning algorithms in detecting depressive markers within these social media posts.

Unlike traditional compartmental models that rely on deterministic ordinary differential equations, this approach employs stochastic differential equations to capture the randomness inherent in the outbreak. The model's parameters are calibrated using empirical COVID-19 data from China and Italy. This study investigates the Isoscalar Giant Monopole Resonance (ISGMR) in $^{24}$Mg and $^{28}$Si using a microscopic Random Phase Approximation (RPA) framework. The methodology employs a density-dependent Skyrme force, augmented by a coupling between isoscalar monopole and quadrupole RPA modes. The calculated RPA+ISGMR spectra for these nuclei align well with experimental data, specifically matching the observed centroid energies and full width at half maximum (FWHM). The analysis reveals that the monopole-quadrupole coupling significantly influences the ISGMR centroid energy in $^{24}$Mg, whereas its effect is negligible in $^{28}$Si. Furthermore, the microscopic RPA approach successfully reproduces the experimental isoscalar giant dipole resonance (ISGDR) spectra for both nuclei.

This study examines the long-term behavior of finite-dimensional feedback-regulated systems that are coupled with resistive loads subject to dry friction. We demonstrate that the resulting closed-loop dynamics can exhibit both con vergence and stick-slip oscillations. Specifically, the system is proven to possess a global Lyapunov function, which ensures that all trajectories converge to an attractor with a finite dimension. Furthermore, we establish that these dynamics admit a representation as the solution to a differential inclusion involving set-valued monotone operators. This property enables the derivation of a sufficient criterion guaranteeing global asymptotic con vergence to a unique equilibrium point. Finally, we illustrate the validity of this criterion through a two-degree-of-freedom mechanical example exhibiting stick-slip behavior.

This work addresses the challenge of optimizing long-term utility for an agent within a partially observable Markov decision process (POMDP) subject to a budget constraint. We demonstrate that this problem is mathematically equivalent to finding the optimal solution to Bellman Hedging—a corresponding problem in a fully observable setting that alternates between a risk-neutral MDP and a risk-averse utility maximization. Leveraging this formulation, we introduce a novel deep reinforcement learning framework capable of jointly discovering both the optimal risk-averse dynamic and the corresponding hedging strategy. Empirical evaluations across various control and navigation scenarios confirm that our method surpasses traditional approaches in both sample efficiency and final performance.

Sequential recommenders are increasingly prevalent in online environments, where they infer user preferences by analyzing interaction sequences. However, these models often overlook the underlying motivations driving user behavior. This paper introduces HUM (Hidden User Motivation Modeling), a framework designed to explicitly model sequential interactions by integrating motivation states. By jointly training a HUM system alongside a sequential recommender, it uncovers motivation states that enhance performance. Evaluations across three datasets demonstrate that HUM significantly boosts the accuracy of state-of-the-art systems. Furthermore, it effectively identifies motivation drivers behind specific user interactions, offering valuable insights for both researchers and practitioners.

This paper addresses the challenge of approximating a rank-one matrix from noisy observations, where data is partitioned into $G$ groups, each possessing distinct heterogeneity characteristics. We demonstrate that the minimax optimal error rates for this approximation task are dictated by the count of groups with heterogeneity significantly exceeding the baseline. Specifically, these extreme groups dictate the convergence speed, while those with only moderate variations have negligible impact. Our findings establish both upper and lower bounds for the risk, which match within a constant factor. Additionally, we present a specific estimator designed to efficiently leverage the inherent groupwise heterogeneity.

The topological classification of materials with symmetry breaks is currently an active area of research. This paper introduces a simplified model featuring a topological phase transition driven by the breaking of $U(1)$ gauge symmetry. This framework serves as a fundamental building block for constructing more intricate topological phases that emerge solely from the absence of symmetries. The model is defined by a quadratic Hamiltonian composed of two components: the first term is a standard Bogoliubov-de Gennes Hamiltonian, while the second arises from the coupling of Nambu spinors to the complex order parameter of the broken $U(1)$ symmetry. This interaction creates an effective non-Hermitian term within the Bogoliubov-de Gennes formalism, resulting in the disappearance of the bulk band gap upon reaching a critical threshold of the control parameter. This analytical model is further supported by numerical simulations of the corresponding Hamiltonian mean-field theory. Furthermore, the study examines the topological phase diagram of the system, including the analysis of edge states and the calculation of the non-trivial winding number in the topological phase.

This work presents a distributed control method for linear multi-channel systems that achieves both decentralized stability and adaptability to new components. The proposed design relies on a consensus-based controller utilizing a balanced communication graph, where each node's update rule incorporates a specific gain. This gain is determined by solving a Riccati equation that accounts for the local system dynamics and the count of available inputs. The construction ensures stability without requiring knowledge of the global system model, while the gains for each agent depend only on its local model and communication topology. Furthermore, the approach facilitates plug-and-play operations: when new nodes are added, the existing consensus protocol requires no parameter adjustments, and stability is maintained automatically as long as the gain selection respects an established upper bound.

The ongoing global pandemic has caused widespread devastation, resulting in countless deaths and economic collapse. As the world grapples with the virus's impact, there is an urgent need to develop effective tools for its detection and management. While existing research has created various machine learning models to assist in categorizing COVID-19 cases, these approaches often struggle with the inherent complexity of the disease and its multifaceted effects on the human body. To address these limitations, we propose a new dual-stage categorization framework designed to handle the inherent class imbalance in data. Our method employs a BERT-based classifier for initial detection, followed by a Random Forest model to further categorize the disease. Experimental results demonstrate that this dual-stage strategy significantly outperforms existing single-stage models, achieving an accuracy of 90.1%, a precision of 89.1%, a recall of 89.9%, and an F1-score of 89.5%.

This work serves as a foundational guide for researchers entering the field of network science, covering essential concepts, tools, and resources. It begins by defining core network elements, including nodes, edges, and graphs, before exploring fundamental metrics such as degree, centrality, and clustering. The text then examines key phenomena like small-world properties, scale-free distributions, and network evolution. Furthermore, it outlines major research domains, including social network analysis, epidemiology, and the study of the brain. Complementing this overview is a dedicated section on computational methods, featuring Python code examples that utilize the NetworkX library to demonstrate practical applications. Finally, the authors provide curated lists of textbooks, online courses, and scholarly articles to support continued learning and development.

Time scales are fundamental to the study of eco-evolutionary dynamics, yet the mechanisms governing their variation and impacts on system behavior remain incompletely understood. This study investigates how temporal fluctuations in time scales influence eco-evolutionary processes, with a specific focus on the modern era. We examine the drivers of these time scales, including the pace of environmental change, the speed of phenotypic shifts, and the magnitude of demographic fluctuations. Furthermore, we explore how these factors interact to shape the dynamics of eco-evolutionary systems. We also analyze the roles of time scales in the context of life history traits, phenotypic plasticity, and population dynamics. Finally, we discuss the implications of these findings for understanding how time scales affect the emergence of eco-evolutionary feedback loops and the stability of ecosystems.

This study investigates the susceptibility of speech deep learning models to adversarial attacks, specifically examining how such attacks impact the fundamental premise of self-supervised learning (SML) in speech. By utilizing the SML framework to derive robust speech representations, we explore the effects of applying adversarial noise during both the pre-training and fine-tuning stages of these models. Our findings indicate that while clean data remains essential for the core SML process, generating adversarial examples during these phases can still produce effective speech representations. Furthermore, we assess the impact of training on data contaminated with clean versus corrupted inputs and analyze the role of random initialization. Our results demonstrate that employing random initialization yields significantly superior performance compared to continuing from a pre-trained model trained with corrupted data. Finally, we examine the efficacy of adversarially contaminated data in the context of speaker verification and emotion recognition tasks.

The decentralized nature of blockchain technology has enabled the creation of trustless, decentralized marketplaces that facilitate the exchange of both digital and tangible goods. These platforms are gaining significant traction among users and businesses alike. This article examines the foundational elements of blockchain-enabled decentralized marketplaces, including their operational mechanisms, associated benefits, and remaining hurdles. It further outlines the current state of the field and anticipates future developments within this domain.

This study presents a sensitivity analysis approach for missing data problems, grounded in the concept of the E-value. The E-value functions as a metric for quantifying how robust a research conclusion remains against the potential influence of missing information. We employ E-values within the Bayesian framework to construct a posterior distribution of E-values, thereby enabling the calculation of the proportion of posterior probabilities where E-values exceed a specified threshold. This method offers a means to assess the uncertainty surrounding the magnitude of an E-value. Additionally, we introduce a novel Bayesian sensitivity index designed to facilitate comparison across different E-value distributions. The approach is demonstrated through applications to both simulation studies and actual data analysis.

This paper presents a comprehensive classification of $U_q(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$-symmetries for the quantum plane. We establish that the equation of every invariant subalgebra relative to a homogeneous skew-pairing is equivalent to that generated by any other such subalgebra via an automorphism of the quantum plane itself. Furthermore, we provide a catalog of the corresponding skew-pairings modulo the action of the quantum group's automorphism group.

The rapid proliferation of connected devices and the Internet of Things (IoT) has generated vast amounts of data, enabling more precise and efficient services. However, traditional data-centric models face significant hurdles, primarily concerning data privacy and the high costs associated with data sharing. Consequently, a shift toward model-centric approaches, known as Federated Learning (FL), has emerged as a decentralized alternative. In FL, data remains local to individual devices, with only model parameters shared globally to train a collective model. Despite its benefits, FL still encounters challenges regarding data heterogeneity and the risk of data leakage. To address these issues, this paper examines how blockchain technology can enhance FL. It outlines the core components of both technologies, analyzes their integration potential, and reviews existing frameworks that leverage blockchain to bolster FL. Furthermore, the study highlights current research gaps and proposes future research avenues in this evolving field.

This study presents the measurement of beauty and elegance quark production using non-prompt and prompt D mesons in proton-proton collisions at a center-of-mass energy of $\sqrt{s}=5.02$ TeV. The data were collected by the LHCb experiment with an integrated luminosity of 1 fb$^{-1}$. Beauty and elegance are identified through the decay of B mesons into D mesons accompanied by at least one additional charged hadron. The analysis covers the kinematic region defined by transverse momentum $p_{\rm T} > 0.5$ GeV/$c$ and pseudorapidity $-2.5 < y < -0.5$. The results are expressed as differential cross-sections for the variables $p_{\rm T}$ and $z_{\rm E}$, where $z_{\rm E}$ represents the fraction of the B-hadron's momentum carried by the D meson. These measurements are compared with predictions from the PYTHIA 6.4 and 8.2 Monte Carlo event generators, as well as the CTEQ15 parton distribution function (PDF) set combined with the MRST2004QED1.45 and MRST2004QED1.45 parton splitting functions. The results are also contrasted with LHCb's previous measurements of beauty and elegance at $\sqrt{s}=7$ TeV.

The millikelvin temperature range is essential for the development of quantum computing. Situated within Fermilab's Integrated Quantum Computing System, a dedicated dilution refrigerator provides a temperature platform of 10 mK, featuring 16 low-loss microwave lines and 4 low-loss DC bias lines. This line infrastructure is coupled to a custom control system that allows for the automated calibration of transmission and reflection parameters, as well as the monitoring of DC bias voltages and currents at each line's endpoint.

This paper examines the misuse of cryptographic methods within the Pytho n ecosystem. While Python's standard library offers a limited set of tools, the widely adopted third-party PyCryptodome package expands these capabilities significantly. Despite these options, developers frequently encounter challenges due to a lack of comprehensive documentation and the overwhelming complexity inherent in cryptography. Consequently, errors often arise from improper usage. We present a collection of such cases drawn from public repositories, analyzing the specific issues and proposing corrections for each scenario.

Accurate and efficient data collection is crucial for developing reliable machine learning models. However, gathering large volumes of high-quality labeled data remains a significant challenge, particularly in complex domains like urban planning and autonomous driving. This paper introduces a novel, fully automatic labeling framework designed to generate precise annotations for complex scenarios such as urban planning and autonomous driving. Our method employs a voting mechanism based on scaled values to determine the optimal placement and dimensions of geometric primitives, including lines, polygons, and free-form curves. We evaluated the system on two major datasets: the OpenStreetMap (OSM) and the Waymo Open Dataset (WOD). The results demonstrate that our approach achieves state-of-the-art performance on both datasets, surpassing existing state-of-the-art automatic annotation methods.

Proximal operators are essential tools in optimization, particularly for solving inverse problems. While recent advancements have introduced general operators for diverse regularization functions, they often struggle with seismic reflectivity reconstruction due to excessive computational costs. This paper introduces a new operator tailored for the proximal mean network within a nonuniform sparse framework, designed to address these limitations. The proposed method is evaluated using synthetic and field data for reflectivity reconstruction, demonstrating that it achieves superior image quality compared to existing operators. Additionally, the approach offers significantly faster processing times, making it highly suitable for real-time applications.

This study explores the properties of semigroups of composition operators acting on specific subspaces of the little analytic function space, denoted as Little OA. These operators are defined by holomorphic mapping functions mapping the unit disk into itself. A primary focus is placed on computing the generator of such operator semigroups and characterizing composition semigroups that exhibit growth of order at most linear. Additionally, sufficient criteria are established to determine when a given semigroup is uniformly bounded.

We investigate the conformal field theory governing the critical point of the Haagerup quantum chain, a system notable for its non-lie algebraic symmetry. By performing numerical renormalization group calculations, we identify this governing theory as a new central charge $c=3/2$ model featuring four primary fields. We introduce a method for calculating operator merging rates via wavefunction overlaps, finding it to be significantly more efficient than traditional matrix product state operator basis methods. This approach also allows for the determination of universal finite-size corrections, specifically $k=1/49$ and $k=1/36$, corresponding to the fusion of identity operators with the primary field $\psi$.

Historical texts present unique challenges for part-of-speech (POS) tagging because standard definitions of these categories often fail to apply due to evolving linguistic norms. To address this, we propose a set-valued POS tagging framework that predicts a range of possible categories for each token rather than a single fixed label. This approach is particularly beneficial for ambiguous words and enables the identification of cases where a modern category definition simply does not fit historical usage. Our method utilizes a conditional computational generation model to produce these sets of POS tags, with the output quality assessed using a specialized set-theoretic metric. Experimental results on a 19th-century German corpus demonstrate that the proposed method achieves superior accuracy compared to single-label models. Furthermore, we present a qualitative analysis of instances where the system correctly identifies words that should not be confined to a single category under contemporary rules.

The primary objective of formal methods is to create software that is free of errors. However, the high cost and complexity associated with these methods have restricted their adoption in the software industry. To address this, we have developed an intelligent assistant that converts user requirements into formal specifications. This tool is designed to facilitate the use of formal verification by industry professionals. To achieve this, the system employs a machine learning model capable of automatically generating first-order logic specifications from natural language inputs. To date, the tool has been tested on a dataset of 1,000 manually curated requirements for city services, which were developed by domain experts.

This paper introduces a Concealed Inverses (CI) protocol for Quantum Error Correction (QEC) tailored to the superconducting quantum computing architecture. In this framework, the syndrome is determined by a quantum circuit that integrates both the logical qubit and an auxiliary system, with the latter's final state concealing the error syndrome. We demonstrate that the overall probability of fault errors can be mitigated by reducing the occurrence of circuit faults within the segment dedicated to error concealment. To validate the protocol, we employ a logical qubit subject to bit-flip errors, protected by three logical qubits and two ancilla qubits arranged in a linear configuration. Results indicate that the total error probability under the CI approach is lower than that of the conventional measurement-based method. Furthermore, the study explores the influence of noise on the ancilla qubits and the logical qubit, establishing a quantitative relationship between the circuit error rates in the two segments of the protocol.

We demonstrate that within a regular category, the existence of all cocartesian morphisms for preorders serves as a necessary and sufficient condition for their existence across all small relations. This stands in contrast to the behavior observed in regular (and more broadly, exact) categories concerning functors between equivalence relations. We also establish that in any regular category capable of forming cocartesian morphisms for bi-unique relations, these cocartesian structures automatically extend to cover all small relations.

This study examines the spatial peaks of a bivariate ocean wave model, specifically utilizing a bivariate linear process and a bivariate linear process with a spatially varying coefficient. We establish the asymptotic distribution of the maximum values observed within conditional frameworks, specifically targeting specific realizations of the process's components. These theoretical findings are applied to address the problem of predicting extreme oceanic wave conditions.

Contemporary vision-language models (VLMs) have achieved significant success in zero-shot generalization by aligning textual and visual features. However, these models typically struggle with complex tasks that require deep semantic understanding. To address this limitation, we introduce VT-CLIP, an enhanced VLM architecture that integrates visual-assisted texts to boost performance on intricate reasoning. Our framework introduces two key components: (1) an Image Captioning Module (ICM) that extracts salient objects and details from images to generate descriptive captions, and (2) a Visual-Text Fusion Module (VTFM) that synthesizes image captions with original text prompts to create enriched, semantically complex queries. These visual-enhanced queries are then aligned with image features to generate robust representations. Empirical evaluations on established benchmarks demonstrate that VT-CLIP surpasses existing methods, achieving a +2.0% average gain in performance across multiple challenging reasoning tasks.

This work addresses the fundamental challenge of estimating a low-rank matrix from noisy observations. We present an operator transitioning method that effectively handles various noisy matrix recovery scenarios, including the noisy singular value problem, completion of a low-rank matrix, and the recovery of a rank-one signal within a noisy subspace. Our findings demonstrate that, for a broad range of these problems, the proposed method converges to the optimal recovery rate. Our results further indicate that, in several instances, the method achieves optimal performance even without relying on any specific dimensionality assumptions regarding the underlying matrices.
